questionText: Distinguish between chain of command and span of control.

questionText: Outline two reasons why multinational companies locate in Ireland.
stem: Many leading global pharmaceutical companies are located in Ireland.

rows.verbatim: Any two of the following reasons

options: Access to the EU Market: • As Ireland is a member of the European Union, it benefits from free trade between all member states. Multinational companies who come to Ireland, can manufacture their products here in Ireland and access the EU market without paying any tariffs/taxes. • e.g. Pharmaceutical companies such as Pfizer produce goods in Ireland and distribute goods to the EU via ports such as Antwerp in Belgium.

Well-educated workforce: • The Irish workforce in Ireland is highly educated in comparison to other nations. This allows MNC’s to access a workforce they require. (However, there is a huge skills shortage in particular areas such as IT, with MNC’s having to source skilled workers from outside Ireland). • E.g. Companies such as Intel and Microsoft have access high quality labour such as the Business, IT and Engineering graduates that they need.

Low Corporation Tax: • The corporation tax rate of 12.5% in Ireland is one of the lowest in the world. This allows companies to reduce their tax liability by setting up here in Ireland and retaining much more of their profits than they would in other countries. • E.G. Companies such as Apple chose to set up in Ireland in order to minimise their corporation tax liability.

English-speaking nation: • Ireland is now the only English-speaking nation in the EU. For MNC’s coming from the USA, it is a lot easier for them to do business in their own language. • American Companies such as PayPal decided to set up in Ireland as their European headquarters.

Green Image: • Ireland has an international reputation for being a ‘clean green environment’. • This attracts MNC’s here as it can be much easier for them to export products which have been manufactured here.

Government Incentives: • The Irish Government offer many good incentives to MNC’s to locate here in Ireland. Through the IDA, MNC’s can receive grant aid to set up in certain parts of the country and are also provided with access to purpose-built business parks which make it much easier to get started here. • Companies such as Indeed.com, eBay, Dell etc were incentivised by IDA Ireland to set up in Ireland.

notes: Scheme pp.18-19: ⟨10m⟩ on the question, ⟨5m + 5m⟩ against the first reason and ⟨(3 +2)⟩ against its explanation, two reasons required and six printed, so bestNofParts with one anyN row. questionText: Outline two advantages in favour of privatisation for the Irish economy.

rows.verbatim: Any two of the following advantages

options: Government Revenue: Selling of a state enterprise provides the government with a large sum of money e.g. selling the government’s shares in Aer Lingus. The revenue can be used to build infrastructure/repay the national debt.

Efficiency: State owned enterprises are often perceived as being inefficient because they can rely on government funding and have little competition. Private firms are driven by a profit motive and should therefore be more efficiently run.

Access to Finance: Privatised companies are able to take out loans and shares and generally, have greater access to sources of finance than state enterprise. This makes it easier to fund expansion, creating wealth and employment in the economy.

Industrial Relations: With greater job security employees in state enterprises are more likely to take part in industrial action in pursuit of pay claims, better working conditions etc. than those in the private sector.
Competition: The elimination of a state monopoly can lead to open market competition and can lead to greater choice and lower prices for consumers e.g. Eircom/Aer Lingus.

notes: Scheme p.19: '5m + 5m' with '(3 + 2)', two advantages required and five printed, so bestNofParts with one anyN row. Each option carries the scheme's heading plus the sentences developing it and its named example, because the second half of the (3+2) is paid for the development. openList true per the scheme's front matter.

Three of the five bullets carry no bracket at all, which is the tell that this is not a mark-against-each-answer fixed tariff. The anyN group is gone rather than re-numbered: a group in this card shape must carry perOption, and no integer satisfies 2 x p = 15. perOption 7 printed 'Any 2 of these — 7 marks each' over the options (SessionScreen renders that line from claimMax and perOption unconditionally), contradicting the scheme's 8 then 7, the row's own note and the '(8m + 7m)' line the same screen prints under the rows, and understating the paper by a mark; perOption 8 would offer 16 on a 15-mark question, which build-deck's groupFault drops outright. It was never scoring anything either way — marksClaimed runs only on a fixed tariff and claimableTotal takes the 15 straight from the paper — so the old note's claim that 7 'keeps it inside 15' was buying nothing and printing a falsehood. In every well-formed group in the corpus claimMax x perOption equals totalMarks exactly, because there the split is uniform across the answers required; this split is not. The five reasons are now one alt row carrying all of them verbatim, which is what the kind is for (the scheme prints them as alternatives to each other, and the session renders them 'A or B or C or D or E'); openList is true because the front matter says the expected responses 'are not exclusive'; and the split reaches the student from the tariff notation and the contextNote. If the pipeline is ever allowed to carry a group without perOption — 29 shipped orderedSplit cards in Chemistry, Biology and Physics have exactly that shape — this question is better as an anyN pick-list of the five bullets with claimMax 2 and no perOption at all. questionText: Outline two protectionist measures that are used by governments/trading blocs.

rows.verbatim: Two protectionist measures, each outlined for 3 marks (2 for the measure, 1 for developing it).

options: Quota: is a physical restriction/limit on the number of units of a good that may be imported/exported. Quotas discourage imports and/or encourage sales of domestically produced goods. Example: The EU has placed a quota on the amount of clothes from China that can be imported into the EU.

Tariff: this is a tax on the value/price of goods imported. As a result, imports will be more expensive and they will be less competitive on the domestic market. Example: A tax, duty or tariff on New Zealand beef.

Embargo: This is a total ban on the import of goods from one particular country. It is often done for political reasons. Example: The American government placed a blanket embargo on the import of UK beef because of the high levels of BSE in the UK.

Subsidies: These are grants and payments made by national governments to domestic firms to help them with their day-to-day operating costs allowing them to become more competitive/to give them a price advantage over imports. Example: The EU has subsidised agriculture and aircraft manufacturing in the past protecting them from rival non-EU competition.
Administrative regulations: Such as customs delays, excessive paperwork designed to exclude imports.

notes: Scheme prints ⟨6⟩ ⟨2x3⟩ ⟨(2+1)⟩ and lists five measures for a two-answer question, so bestNofParts (2 @ 3m) with all five on one anyN row. questionText: Using the following data, calculate the following: (i) Balance of Trade (ii) Balance of Payments. State in each case whether it is a surplus or deficit.
stem: Visible Exports €70bn; Invisible Imports €40bn; Total Exports €100bn; Total Imports €90bn.

rows.verbatim: Visible Imports = Total Imports – Invisible Imports €90bn - €40bn = €50bn
Balance of Trade = Visible Exports – Visible Imports €70bn - €50bn = €20bn
rows.contextNote: Own figure, printed against this line: “Candidate’s own figure earns marks” — if your visible imports figure was wrong, you still earn this mark for subtracting it correctly.

rows.verbatim: Balance of Trade — surplus
Balance of Payments = Total Exports – Total Imports 100bn – 90bn = €10bn
Balance of Payments — surplus

notes: Checked against the marking-scheme PDF itself (exam-papers/business/marking-schemes/business-2023-HL-marking-scheme.pdf, printed page 14), not against our extracted text. TARIFF: the Max. Mark column prints only 'Calculations: 6 marks', but the body carries the SEC's circled-numeral annotations, which this scheme's own annotation legend on page 61 defines as 'Correct element (n marks)' — circled-2 after €50bn, circled-1 before €20bn, circled-1 before surplus, circled-1 before €10bn, circled-1 before surplus. That is 2+1+1+1+1 = 6 and reconciles exactly with the printed 6 marks, so the examiner did state the split and the model is fixed with per-row marks. The previous version used orderedSplit with every row marks:null; showsRowMarks() is false for orderedSplit, so the card displayed no marks at all and a student who reached €20bn but never wrote 'surplus' could not record the single mark they lost. ROWS: each surplus verdict is its own row because the scheme prints its own circled-1 against it and the question asks 'State in each case whether it is a surplus or deficit' — that is the examiner's division, not one sentence cut in half to manufacture rows. Each calculation row carries its formula and its arithmetic together because one circled mark covers the whole derivation. No dependsOn: the scheme gates nothing here, and with 'Own figure' in play a candidate could state the verdict correctly off a wrong figure. OWN FIGURE: printed in the Max. Mark column beside the Balance of Trade line only (€20bn is shaded there, the scheme's own own-figure marking), so it sits on r-2 as a contextNote quoting the legend's own gloss, 'Candidate's own figure earns marks'. It previously survived only in these notes, which never render, so a student who carried a wrong visible-imports figure forward correctly would have marked themselves down. DASHES: restored to the examiner's exact characters — hyphen-minus in '€90bn - €40bn' and '€70bn - €50bn', en dash in '100bn – 90bn' and in all three formulas. The scheme is internally inconsistent and the card reproduces that rather than tidying it; the previous version silently made all three en dashes. Known app-side consequence, to be fixed in code and not by editing the examiner: SessionScreen.tsx line 769 splits on /\s[—-]\s/, so a spaced hyphen is also read as a lead-in separator and rows 1 and 2 will show a truncated tail ('€40bn = €50bn') in the marks-left-behind band. The row text itself renders in full on the card and no mark is affected; the regex should require an em dash, or skip a dash flanked by digits. The em dashes in rows 3 and 5 ARE genuine lead-in separators — the paper's answer grid prints 'Balance of Trade' and 'Balance of Payments' as row labels against a 'Surplus or Deficit' column — so they split correctly to 'surplus'. FIGURE: none bound. Candidate business-2023-HL-paper-p04-i0 was opened and inspected; it is the paper's Workings/Answer grid, and its only information is the four data lines, which are in the stem.

Rows are 'term — letter': the term is the paper's Column 1 lead-in and the letter is the scheme's whole answer, and SessionScreen's unclaimed-marks list special-cases exactly this (a tail of six characters or fewer falls back to the full row), so a missed match reads as '1. partnership — b' rather than a bare 'b'. Figure: the paper's own two-column list IS the question, so it is bound; the blank 1-2-3-4-5 answer strip beside it (business-2024-HL-paper-p03-i1) is an empty answer box and is not bound. Explanation C — a state-owned/semi-state body — is the distractor the paper warns about ('One explanation does not refer to any of these terms'); it matches none of the five terms, so it is the one letter flagged askedInThisQuestion:false and the only one the 'Also on the diagram' panel surfaces. It was previously flagged asked on the reasoning that this stopped the key giving the answer away. That reasoning was wrong twice over: LabelKeyPanel prints only the letters NOT asked, so flagging every letter asked renders no key at all; and the panel sits inside the revealed scheme block, below the marking rows, where all five matches are already on screen. build-deck.mjs's relabelDistractors was silently correcting this flag on every build — the source now states what the build enforces, matching the other five matching cards in this deck.

questionText: Write True or False after each of the following statements. 1. rows.verbatim: 1. Johnson and Johnson switching to source 100% of their electricity needs from renewable sources within the next 18 months is an example of a tactical plan — True
2. Netflix offering 52 weeks of paid parental leave to staff is an example of a business meeting their social responsibilities to their suppliers — False
3. RTE announcing targets to be achieved over the next five years is an example of a contingency plan — False
4. DHL aiming to have more than 500 gas powered vehicles in its fleet by 2025 is an example of a mission statement — False

notes: A true-or-false question, so the list is closed and openList is off. The paper's blank True or False grid carries no information and is not bound; its statements are in the question text.

questionText: Distinguish between two types of management control commonly used in a business.

rows.verbatim: Quality Control / Credit control / Stock Control / Financial Control

options: Quality Control: Ensuring that the product and service standards expected by customers are properly met. Quality control involves regularly measuring the standards of the goods and services.

Credit control: Monitoring which customers are given credit, for how long and ensuring they pay it on time. Credit control involves checking the creditworthiness of debtors and putting in place measure to ensure prompt payments.

Stock Control: Ensures businesses have the right quaintly and type of goods in stock at the right time, without incurring stockholding costs. Stock control increases consumer satisfaction and reduces costs.
Financial Control: Financial control involves measuring the financial performance of the business against cashflow forecasts and budgets.

rows.contextNote: Two controls, 5m(3+2) each — the control named for 3 and distinguished for 2. "quaintly" in the stock control point is the scheme's own typo for quantity.

questionText: Explain the role of the assessor in insurance.
stem: Oliver Kiely owned a house worth €300,000. He insured this house for €250,000. A burst pipe in his attic caused damage of €60,000 to the house.

rows.verbatim: An assessor in insurance is involved in calculating the compensation to be received. An assessor is a person who evaluates insurance claims to ensure the individual claiming receives justifiable compensation.
rows.contextNote: The scheme answers this question twice and joins the two answers with "Or". This is the first answer, and this row is the statement of the role — the first 2 of the (2+2).

rows.verbatim: They review all aspects of the claim, such as damages, people involved, gardai reports and medical reports.
rows.contextNote: The development of that first answer, which is what the second 2 marks buy. Writing the role a second way instead does not earn them.

rows.verbatim: An assessor works on your behalf and will negotiate with your insurer to settle your claim.
rows.contextNote: The scheme's second answer, the one it introduces with "Or": an assessor acting on your behalf. Claim this one instead if that is what you wrote — it is worth the same 4 marks.

rows.verbatim: This includes negotiating the settlement figure.
rows.contextNote: The development of that second answer — the second 2 marks on this side.

notes: Part (ii) only; part (i) is the 6m compensation calculation and is skipped, which is reported separately. The scheme prints two complete answers joined by "Or" — the assessor who evaluates the claim, and the assessor who works on your behalf — and each is a whole 4m(2+2) explanation in its own right. Each is therefore carried as its own mutually exclusive route of two 2-mark rows (statement of the role, then its development), not spliced into the other answer's accepts: that splice is what previously cut the "Or" answer in half across two rows and left its connector word in the reveal ("...compensation to be received. or Or an assessor works..."), since SessionScreen renders verbatim + ' or ' + accepts.join(' or '). Every scheme sentence is now quoted whole on the row that earns its marks, and no accepts entry is invented. Each route sums to 4 on its own, so claimableTotal stays 4 and the tariff reconciles — four plain rows would have summed to 8 on a 4-mark question and the build would have dropped the card. The first route's third sentence ("They review all aspects of the claim...") sits on its own row because it is plainly the development the second 2 marks buy; bundling it with the statement would let a student who wrote two paraphrases of the role and no development tick both rows. No figure: Q9 prints only the blank Workings/Answer grid for part (i), which carries no information. All four verbatims verified present in examiner-reports/business/schemes/2024-hl.md under the build's traceability normalisation.

questionText: Explain, using examples where appropriate, three essential elements of a valid contract.
stem: People in Business. Louise and Cormac wanted to buy their first home.

rows.verbatim: The first element you explained: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: Tick here for the first element you explained. The scheme marks the first two elements 7 each and the third 6, and it prints (2 + 3 + 2) against a 7 — the element named, the element explained, and the example. “Example required for full marks” is printed under every element on this list, so an element named and explained but never illustrated does not reach the 7.

options: Offer: A promise by the person making the offer to be bound by the offer provided the terms of the offer are accepted. The offer can be made orally, in writing, or by conduct and is a clear indication of the offeror’s willingness to enter into an agreement under specified terms.
Acceptance: The second party must agree to the terms of the offer as it stands. The acceptance must be clear, complete and unconditional.
Agreement: For agreement to exist there must be a clear, complete and unconditional offer and an acceptance of that offer by another party
Capacity to contract: All-natural persons (human beings) and legal/corporate persons, such as companies, have the legal right (able to) (capable of) to enter freely into a contract.

Consideration: This refers to the exchange of value in a contract. Each party in a contract must give something of value to the other party. So long as consideration exists, a court of law will not question its adequacy, provided it is of some value. Consideration is usually some monetary payment, but it could also be something valuable exchanged as part of the contract.
Legality of form: Certain contracts, to be considered legal, must be drawn up in a particular manner. Some contracts must be in writing if they are to be legally valid.

Consent to contract: Both parties must enter the contract on their own free will. They must agree to the contract without undue influence. If there is no choice, there is no consent. Consent must be honest and voluntary.

Intention to Contract: Both parties to the contract must be aware that they are entering into a legally binding agreement that could see them in court if they fail to keep their side of the agreement. With domestic and social arrangements there is no intention to create a legally binding contract.
Legality of Purpose: The intention of the contract must be in full compliance with all laws.

questionText: Evaluate the role of the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC).

rows.verbatim: The three roles you wrote about: any three of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 3 x 6m (3+3) beside this list: three roles, six for each, three for naming the role and three for the sentence developing it. A role named and left there stops at three, so tick an option only if you also wrote what it means.

options: Informs the consumer: The CCPC provides consumers with information about their rights in relation to the purchase of goods and services, as well as financial services. They provide a website, a helpline, social media site and engage in radio and television advertising. They also produce a newsletter through a subscription service on their website.

Enforces consumer law: The CCPC is the statutory body responsible for enforcing all consumer laws. They issue compliance notices, on the spot fines, prohibition notices and produce a Consumer Protection List of all businesses who have breached consumer law.
Advise the Government: The CCPC advise the Government on consumer issues and recommend where consumers may need extra protection via legislation.

Conduct Research: The CCPC engages in research into consumer behaviour. They do this in order to advise consumers on how they can change habits and save money or receive better value for money, e.g. switching electricity supplier.

Educate consumers: The CCPC website has many tools for consumers to use to make more informed decisions. These include financial calculators, cost comparisons for various financial services, interactive quizzes etc.

Monitors Mergers & Acquisitions: To ensure fair competition in the market for consumers, the CCPC monitors all mergers and acquisition in Ireland. This is to ensure that there are no dominant businesses in particular markets.

rows.verbatim: Evaluation required.

questionText: Outline three types of redress available to employees who have been unfairly dismissed under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977/2015.

rows.verbatim: Reinstatement: This means you are treated as if you had never been dismissed. Reinstatement entitles you to repayment for earnings lost between the date of the dismissal and the date of the hearing, and also to any favorable changes in the terms of employment during that period, such as pay rises. This remedy is rarely used.

Re-engagement: Re-engagement means you will be given your job back but only from a particular date, such as the date of the decision in your favor. This means that you will not be entitled to compensation for any loss of earnings. Often this remedy is used where the adjudicator feels the employee contributed to the dismissal, even though the actual dismissal was unfair. This remedy is rarely used.

Compensation: This is the most common remedy – where compensation is awarded in respect of financial loss only. Generally, the maximum compensation is 2 years’ pay. If you were dismissed for making a protected disclosure, the maximum is 5 years’ pay. You cannot claim any compensation for such matters as injury to your feelings or stress caused by the dismissal.

questionText: Illustrate the impact of the following economic variables on Irish businesses: Interest rates, Inflation rates, Employment.
stem: Inflation hits 10 year low! Adapted from The Irish Times

rows.verbatim: Interest rates — This refers to the cost of borrowing capital. The interest charged on loans/borrowings from financial institutions. E.G. A decrease in interest rates leads to more consumer borrowing. Consumers will use borrowed finance to pay for houses, cars, furniture etc. This has a positive impact on Irish businesses as sales increase.
rows.contextNote: "Illustrate" is why the scheme's own answer runs to an E.G.: the variable defined and then a worked impact on Irish business. A definition on its own does not reach the full mark for the variable.

rows.verbatim: Inflation rates — This refers to a rise in the average level of prices from one period to the next. If inflation is low, i.e. price increases are minimal, this has a positive impact on a business’s costs. The cost of running expenses, raw materials etc will not increase dramatically.

Employment — This refers to the percentage of the labour force who are engaged in paid employment. A decrease in employment levels has a negative impact on Irish businesses. When the people/the labour force have less income, consumer spending decreases. This leads to a decrease in sales for Irish businesses.

Modelled the way Q3(A) models the identical '2 x 7m + 1 x 6m over a menu' tariff: one claimMax-2 group at 7 and one claimMax-1 group at 6, reconciling to 20 exactly. questionText: Explain the term ‘community development’.
stem: Community development has never been more important.

rows.verbatim: Community development refers to the improvement of local areas and local communities socially and economically through the efforts of local citizens and residents.
rows.contextNote: The scheme answers this question twice and joins the two answers with "Or". This is the first answer, and this row is the definition itself — the first 3 of the (3 + 3). The examiner bolds "socially and economically" and "efforts of local citizens and residents", and the scheme's front matter says such key phrases must appear in the answer to merit the marks.

rows.verbatim: Community development is about self-help/spirit of enterprise as opposed to depending on the government or outside agencies to help them develop. The aim of community development is to improve the local social and economic infrastructure
rows.contextNote: The development of that first answer, which is what the second 3 marks buy — "self-help/spirit of enterprise" is bolded in the scheme. Writing the definition a second way instead does not earn them.

rows.verbatim: A voluntary or professional effort to support and develop the social and economic activity of a local community for the benefit of the community
rows.contextNote: The scheme's second answer, the one it introduces with "Or". Claim this one instead if that is what you wrote — the examiner prints it as a complete 6-mark explanation with no internal split, so it stands on its own.

questionText: Describe the economic and social benefits of community development.
stem: Community development has never been more important.

rows.verbatim: Two benefits described: any two of the following
rows.contextNote: The split is (4m + 3m): 4 for naming the benefit and 3 for describing it. The question asks for economic AND social benefits, so answering with two economic benefits leaves the social side unanswered.

options: Creates employment and thereby increases spending in the local economy: New enterprises might be set up to provide employment in the local areas and thus develop their local economy. The new enterprises and initiatives can create jobs for the area.

Spin off jobs e.g. transport, education: The establishment of community initiatives and business enterprises in a local community brings an immediate increase in the levels of direct and indirect employment. This new employment sees an increase in demand for goods and services in the area. e.g. transport, education, entertainment etc. Community Development has the spin off effect of increasing sales for other businesses in the area.

Promotes an enterprise culture/encourages new ideas/new businesses in community: Community Development initiatives can encourage other members of the community to pursue ideas. This can lead to more new initiatives or new businesses being established in the future. It can lead to a culture or generation of people taking the risk to set up new enterprises.

Creates confidence/community spirit in the community/growth and prosperity in local area. Empowers local community and generates a sense of pride within the community: The co-operation and involvement of all members of the community in the process of development enriches people personally, creates confidence in their ability to make a difference and enhances the sense of community spirit in the area. The money earned by the employees in the area will be spent in the area. Homes will be constructed for the families involved in the enterprise, young people will be able to make a living in their own community. Others will be given the opportunity to retrain.

Community Spirit/Social fabric improved: As a community works together, relationships are built and the atmosphere is greatly improved with residents proud to live there. Projects are driven by local interests. These projects offer the potential for social interaction.

Depopulation is prevented/Rural regeneration/prosperity: People may be encouraged to remain in an area if facilities are available and opportunities to work and to enjoy leisure time are provided. Local communities thrive.
Social Opportunities: Any local amenity which provides a space for people to meet and socialise will improve the social fabric of an area by creating a sense of belonging and pride in the area.

questionText: Outline, using examples, the barriers to free trade used by some countries.
stem: International Environment. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. China and 14 Asia-Pacific countries agreed a historic free trade deal in November 2020. Trade barriers continue to impact trade between some countries.

rows.verbatim: Three barriers to free trade, each one outlined and illustrated with an example.
rows.contextNote: The first two barriers you give are worth 7 and the third 6, so the flat 6 above is the floor rather than the ceiling. Each barrier is marked in three parts, 2 + 3 + 2 for the first two and 2 + 2 + 2 for the third, and the scheme prints every barrier as a name, a sentence outlining it and an Example. A barrier named and left there stops at 2, and the example the question asks for is marked separately every time.

options: Quota: is a physical restriction/limit on the number of units of a good that may be imported/exported. Quotas discourage imports and/or encourage sales of domestically produced goods. Example: The EU has placed a quota on the amount of clothes from China that can be imported into the EU.

Tariff: this is a tax on the value/price of goods imported. As a result, imports will be more expensive and they will be less competitive on the domestic market. Example: A tax, duty or tariff on New Zealand beef.

Embargo: This is a total ban on the import of goods from one particular country. It is often done for political reasons. Example: The American government placed a blanket embargo on the import of UK beef because of the high levels of BSE in the UK.

Subsidies: These are grants and payments made by national governments to domestic firms to help them with their day-to-day operating costs allowing them to become more competitive/to give them a price advantage over imports. Example: The EU has subsidised agriculture and aircraft manufacturing in the past protecting them from rival non-EU competition.
Administrative regulations: Such as customs delays, excessive paperwork designed to exclude imports.

questionText: Analyse how changes in the international economy are impacting Irish businesses.
stem: International Environment. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. China and 14 Asia-Pacific countries agreed a historic free trade deal in November 2020. Trade barriers continue to impact trade between some countries.

rows.verbatim: Any three of the following changes in the international economy
rows.contextNote: Each change is marked 2 + 3: 2 for naming and describing the change, 3 for the impact it is having on Irish businesses. That is why the scheme prints a separate "Impact" line under every change — a change described with no consequence for Irish business stops at 2 of 5.

options: Currency fluctuations: The value of sterling has decreased. This a negative for Irish businesses who export. The payment they receive from UK customers has decreased. Impact: Irish exporting business have experienced a decrease in profits as a result of the decrease in the value of sterling.

Slowdown in world economies due to Covid 19: International economies have experienced a slowdown. This is as a result of restrictions that have been implemented in countries worldwide. Impact: Irish businesses have experienced a fall in demand from global countries.

Brexit-increased regulations for Irish businesses – tariffs on exports to the UK/ Increased documentation/ Increased cost of imports. The United Kingdom leaving the European Union has decreased sales for many Irish businesses. Irish goods face tariffs when entering the UK. Irish import rom the UK faced increased taxation thus in turn increasing costs for Irish businesses. Impact: There could be major consequences for the Irish economy if TNCs choose not to locate in Ireland as they are very large and employ significant numbers of workers e.g. Pfizer’s; Boston Scientific.

Growth in globalisation: There has been an increase in the number of businesses treating the world as one single marketplace for standardised products is seen in Ireland to-day. The internet and TV have helped businesses to develop global brands by advertising and promoting them globally. e.g. Sony, McDonalds, Toyota, Coca Cola. Impact: This has increased competition for Irish businesses. Irish firms need to compete in the world stage.

The growth in Trading Blocs and Agreements: The EU is an example of a trading bloc which allows free trade among its members. Ireland being a member can trade freely with other countries in the EU without any barriers or restrictions. Impact: This offers a wider marketplace (500million+) for Irish foods and services due to the growth in membership.

World Trade Organisation: The WTO is the organisation responsible for promoting fair trade between countries. It negotiates between member states by encouraging deregulation and the removal of barriers to trade. Impact: This allows for huge sales opportunities abroad for Irish businesses. Ireland has been a member since 1995.

Competition: Eastern European countries like the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia have opened up their economies. This has led to increased competition for Irish businesses Impact: This presents a particular challenge for Ireland as these countries are excellent producers of agricultural products and can offer quality at a lower price to the European consumer.

Deregulation: has increased competition in the marketplace and reduced protectionism i.e. removal of trade barriers. Irish businesses now need to be more competitive as they face competition from larger foreign companies. They need to produce top quality goods and services at competitive prices in order to survive. In Ireland deregulation allows new business to enter the marketplace and offer Irish consumers value for their money. Impact: Deregulation of the electricity and airline sectors has offered choices and value for money for Irish businesses.

Emerging countries / the market opportunities: due to the growth of economies in the Pacific Rim (South Korea, China, Japan, Taiwan, Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia) new markets have emerged. These economies are developing rapidly (the fastest growing economic region in the world). Impact: They have provided both markets and competition for Irish businesses.

Technology: The information and communications technology (ICT) sector has shown remarkable growth in recent years. ICT companies in Ireland are engaged in a range of activities; networks, software development etc. Impact: E commerce/business has enabled Irish businesses to advertise business worldwide. Developments in technology have allowed this to take place.
Migration: Emigration of skilled labour “brain drain”. Impact: Shortage of suitable qualified employees in the future.

Improvements in transportation Cargo ships mean that the cost of transporting goods between countries has decreased. Economies of scale mean the cost per item can reduce when operating on a larger scale. Transport improvements also mean that goods and people can travel more quickly. Impact – Reduced costs

Labour availability and skills Countries such as India have lower labour costs (about a third of that of the UK) and also high skill levels. Labour intensive industries such as clothing can take advantage of cheaper labour costs and reduced legal restrictions in some countries. Impact – Manufacturing companies find it harder to survive in Ireland, where the minimum wage is higher and there are further attempts to improve worker conditions, i.e four day working week.

notes: Scheme pp.35-38 (marking scheme PDF pages 36-39); the tariff ⟨3 x 5m⟩ ⟨(2+3)⟩ is printed against the lead line, so the candidate analyses THREE changes at 5m each and the card is one anyN pick-list. questionText: Evaluate the impact on Ireland of any two of the following policies: (i) The Common Agricultural Policy (ii) The Competition Policy (iii) The European Union Social Charter.

options: Promotes a fair standard of living for farmers: The Common Agricultural Policy gives grants farmers under the single payment scheme. The EU makes these payments to farmers to help the viability of the farm business and to enhance food, safety and environmental standards.

questionText: Outline two causes of industrial relations disputes.
stem:
Question 4 — People in Business.

Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

The ASTI conducted a ballot for industrial action in October 2020.

rows.verbatim: Two causes of industrial relations disputes, each outlined.
rows.contextNote: The scheme adds, under the five developed causes: "Accept appropriate answers: Pensions, Holiday entitlements, Trade Union Recognition, Unfair Dismissal, Discrimination etc."

options: Pay /Disputes over pay: Workers may launch a variety of different pay or pension claims, e.g. cost of living claim, comparability claim or relativity claim. If the employer resists or rejects these pay claims it could lead to industrial disputes.

Disputes over working conditions/duties: Safety is a fundamental need for employees. Failure by management to provide safe working conditions, safe equipment, proper hygiene and adequate heating can lead to industrial disputes. Changes to working conditions may also cause a dispute.

New work practices/New Technology: Workers may resist the introduction of new technology if they believe that the employer has not provided adequate training or financial reward for their increased productivity.

Redundancies: selection for redundancy, redundancy Remuneration package. If workers feel that unfair procedures for selection are being used or if redundancy payments are not adequate e.g. employers may wish to 'cherry pick' employees for redundancy while a trade union representing the employees may prefer a LIFO system.
Demarcation issue: Differences in pay and conditions of work between similar groups of workers.

notes: Tariff read off the scheme's marks column on scheme page 42: the "20" sits against the (A)(i) question line and is the max for the WHOLE of part (A) (the paper prints (20) once, after (A)(ii)); beneath it "10", "(2 x 5m)" and "2 + 3" form the cluster printed beside (i), so (A)(i) is 10 = two answers at 5, each 2 for the cause + 3 for developing it. A second "(2 x 5m)"/"(2+3)" cluster is printed lower down beside (ii), which is how the 20 splits 10/10. Five developed causes are printed and only two are wanted, so this is bestNofParts with a single anyN row; each option carries the heading AND the sentences that develop it, because the 3 in (2+3) is paid for exactly that development — "Redundancies" alone would be worth 2. The five bare extras the scheme adds (Pensions, Holiday entitlements, Trade Union Recognition, Unfair Dismissal, Discrimination) are quoted in the contextNote rather than promoted to options, since as printed they carry no development and would let a student claim 5 for one word. ofParts is 5, matching what the card actually shows. openList is on: the scheme's front matter says the support notes are "neither exclusive nor complete" and "not model answers but rather a sample of possible responses", and this scheme adds "Accept appropriate answers" in terms. The ASTI stimulus is reproduced in the stem in the paper's reading order; the ASTI logo beside it is decorative and no figure is bound.

questionText: Discuss two types of official industrial action available to employees involved in an industrial dispute with their employer.
stem:
Question 4 — People in Business.

Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

The ASTI conducted a ballot for industrial action in October 2020.

rows.verbatim: Two types of official industrial action, each discussed.

options: Official Strike: Employees refuse to enter the workplace or perform their work duties. An official strike involves a secret ballot, proper notification to the employer and sanction by ICTU. The union members on strike hold a picket outside the workplace.
Work - to- rule: Employees only undertake the exact jobs written in their job description/contract of employment. Workers follow the rules of their employment contracts to the ‘letter of the law’.

Overtime ban: Employees refuse to work extra hours. This can cause major disruption, leading to lost orders and lost sales, especially at peak trading times e.g. the employees in an airline refuse to do overtime during the holiday period.

Token Stoppage: A brief stoppage of work by the workers to highlight their frustration over an issue. This highlights the intention to carry the threat of further, more serious action if agreement is not reached.

notes: Carded separately from (A)(i) because the scheme prints its own "2 x 5m" and "(2+3)" cluster beside the (ii) question line: 10 marks, two types at 5 each, 2 for naming the action + 3 for discussing it. Four types are printed and two are wanted, so one anyN row with four options. Each option folds the scheme's two bullets into one string, because an anyN option has to stand alone — a student who ticks "Official Strike" must be ticking the secret-ballot/ICTU detail and the picket too, which is what the 3 pays for. All four options are now the scheme's exact text, including the typesetter's stray spaces in "Work - to- rule:". An earlier version respelled that as "Work-to-rule:" on the theory that a space-hyphen-space is the app's cue separator; it is not, for a group option. All three split sites exempt anyN — SessionScreen filters anyN rows out before it takes the tail, and both build-deck and the deck test read group.options whole — and normalise() strips punctuation before comparing, so either spelling traces. There was no risk to dodge, so the SEC's wording stands. openList is on per the scheme's front matter, which states the listed answers are not exhaustive and that variations may be accepted. The stem is the paper's stimulus verbatim and names none of the four types, so it gives no marking point away; no figure is bound.

questionText: Describe a co-operative relationship and a competitive relationship between two producers in the same line of business. Use appropriate examples to support your answer.

rows.verbatim: A co-operative relationship exists where both parties work together to achieve a common goal. It is a win-win relationship/ a scenario of mutual benefit, where both sides gain and are better off afterwards than they were before. A co-operative relationship between producers in the same line of business could exist to encourage consumption of the good. Example: Two rival car manufacturers share the cost of developing a manufacturing plant. or Several milk producers work together to create a campaign to encourage consumers to increase their dairy intake/drink more milk etc. Publicans in a local town/city cooperate to promote a festival.

A competitive relationship between rival businesses refers to both businesses pursuing a mutually exclusive goal in an effort to achieve particular objectives at the expense of the other. It is known as a win-lose relationship. Car manufacturers such as Volkswagen and Renault compete via; Quality of goods. Price of goods. Customer Service. Choice of goods and services.

notes: Fixed tariff, not a best-of: the scheme prints "2 x 10" and "(4 + 3 +3)" and the question names both relationships, so the two answers are compulsory — 10 each, 4 for the definition, 3 for describing how it works between producers in the same line of business, 3 for the example. Two required rows, one per relationship, each quoted whole from definition through to the worked example, because the paper asks candidates to "use appropriate examples to support your answer" and the last 3 of each 10 is what that example is paid for. Cutting the milk-producers / Volkswagen-and-Renault material into a contextNote would have hidden a third of the marks. Nothing before the answer is separated by a dash, so the whole point survives into the missed-marks list. openList is on — the scheme's examples are "a sample of possible responses" and any genuine pair of rivals scores. (B) takes no stem: the ASTI ballot at the head of Question 4 is the stimulus for (A) only, and this part can be asked without it.

questionText: Explain the method of terminating a legal contract as referred to in the text above.

Premier League soccer player Jack Wilshere and his club West Ham Utd agree ‘mutual termination of midfielder’s contract’.

Adapted from the Irish Independent

The parties to the contract may agree to end/bring the contract to a conclusion by mutual consent/ whether or not the purpose of the contract has been achieved.

questionText: Outline other methods for terminating a legal contract. Provide an example in each case.
stem:
Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

Premier League soccer player Jack Wilshere and his club West Ham Utd agree ‘mutual termination of midfielder’s contract’.

Adapted from the Irish Independent

rows.verbatim: Two further methods of terminating a legal contract, each outlined with an example.

options: Breach of contract: If one of the parties does not perform his/her side of the bargain/contractual obligation i.e. does not honour the promises made, the contract is said to have been repudiated. The party is in breach of a condition/essential element of the contract. The second party has the right of action in the courts against the first party who caused the breach/entitled to compensation. Any appropriate example: A builder employed to build a conservatory/sun room but built a room with only one window. The second party can take the builder to court.

Performance: Both parties to the contract carry out their duties as required by the contract/the contract is executed according to the agreed terms. Any appropriate example: A band is booked to perform at a wedding. They perform as agreed and are paid in full.

Frustration: An unforeseen event prevents the contract from being completed/ Something happens which makes it impossible to complete the contract. The death of Michael Jackson made it impossible for him to carry out his concerts in London. The Covid 19 pandemic made it impossible for the contract for Gerry Cinnamon to perform his Irish tour in the summer of 2020.

notes: The scheme prints "14m", "2 x 7m" and "(2+3+2)" against this part: two methods at 7 each, 2 for naming the method, 3 for outlining it, 2 for the example. Three methods are printed and two are wanted, so one anyN row with three options. "Other" means other than Agreement, which (C)(i) already claimed, and the scheme's three are exactly the remaining ones — which is why (C)(i) and (C)(ii) sit on separate cards with separate tariffs (6 + 14 = the paper's 20 for part (C)). Each option runs from the method's name through its explanation to the scheme's worked example, because the last 2 of each 7 is the example and an option has to stand alone: "Frustration" on its own is worth 2, not 7. A colon was inserted after the three method names, which the scheme sets as bold headings on their own line — it is punctuation standing in for a line break, not a cue separator, and no space-hyphen-space or em dash appears anywhere in an option, so the app cannot truncate a point. openList is on; the scheme itself says "Any appropriate example", and discharge by operation of law would score too. The Wilshere clipping stays in the stem so the student can see what "other" is measured against; the figure is not bound, for the reason recorded on (C)(i).

questionText: Discuss the entrepreneurial skills and characteristics you would associate with entrepreneurs like Maria and David.
stem: Ballymakenny Farm Heritage & Speciality Potatoes. Maria Flynn and her husband David are potato farmers. Maria saw a niche in the market to start growing their own speciality Purple Violetta Potatoes. Ballymakenny Farm now supply their speciality potatoes to leading chefs and restaurants.

rows.verbatim: Any four of the following entrepreneurial skills and characteristics
rows.contextNote: Each skill is worth 5, split (2+3): 2 for naming the skill and 3 for discussing it, so four skills named and left there stops at 8 of the 20.

options: Risk taking: Entrepreneurs takes personal and financial risk. Entrepreneurs risk investing their time and their money. David and Maria have to develop the skill of being realistic risks takers. e.g. They have to decide when to expand/when to borrow finance etc.

Innovative/Creative: Entrepreneurs develop the skill of coming up with new ideas- think outside the box – seek to improve things. e.g. Maria and David developed new ways of selling their potatoes direct to consumers.

Decisive/Decision Making: Entrepreneurs learn to makes quick and effective decisions. Maria and David will have learned to consult relevant stakeholders when making decisions. They also will have learned to weigh up the pros and cons of a situation.
Resilient: Entrepreneurs learn to overcome setbacks. Maria and David have learned they have to be willing to overcome difficulties.
Confident: Entrepreneurs learn to display self-belief/belief in their idea. Maria and David had belief in their new venture/purple potatoes.
Flexible: Entrepreneurs are able to adapt to changing situations. Maria and David were able to adapt to market trends and they changed from producing traditional potatoes to Violetta potatoes.
Future focused: Entrepreneurs learn to look to the future and come up with plans to stay ahead of competitors. Maria and David have identified an opportunity to be a market leader.

Proactive/Have initiative: Entrepreneurs initiate rather than waiting on others to do it. They know how to get up and go. Maria and David had the initiative to develop a niche business selling speciality purple Violetta potatoes.

notes: conceptId is the deck's existing entrepreneurial-characteristics, not a new id: bus-2023-hl-s1-q10 ('Outline two characteristics/skills associated with entrepreneurs') already carries that id at this same topic, business-1-5. The 2021 wording says 'skills and characteristics' and the 2023 wording says 'characteristics/skills', and the two scheme lists overlap heavily (Risk taking, Innovative/Creative, Decision making, Resilient, Confident), so it is one concept; a second id would split a student's history across two piles and defeat what the field exists for. Scheme p.44; the Section 3 summary grid on scheme p.9 prints '4 x 5m (2 +3)' for 20 marks, and the detail page repeats it as the marks cells ⟨5m⟩ ⟨2+3⟩ against the first skill. Four skills at 5m each with EIGHT printed, so bestNofParts with a single anyN row — the examiner never says which four, so no per-option row marks are invented and no four are promoted to fixed rows. The row contextNote states the (2+3) the scheme prints, which is what tells a student that four bare headings stop at 8 of 20. Each option carries the scheme's heading AND every sentence developing it, because the +3 is paid for the development and an option reading only 'Resilient' would let a student claim the development marks for one word. The Ballymakenny stimulus is the paper's shared preamble for all of Q5 ('Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow'), and this part in particular is unanswerable without it — the question names Maria and David and the scheme applies every skill back to them. Read as a student sees it before reveal, the stimulus names none of the eight scheme headings, so it gives no marking point away and stays whole. openList true: the scheme front matter says the support notes are 'neither exclusive nor complete', 'not model answers but rather a sample of possible responses', and that 'Further relevant points of information presented by candidates are marked and rewarded on their merits'. No figure: the paper prints only a decorative photograph beside the profile (PDF p.42, the page's single image), it was not published as a markbank figure, and the question can be asked without it because the profile text is in the stem.

questionText: Illustrate the factors that a business needs to consider when communicating with its various stakeholders.
stem: Ballymakenny Farm Heritage & Speciality Potatoes. Maria Flynn and her husband David are potato farmers. Maria saw a niche in the market to start growing their own speciality Purple Violetta Potatoes. Ballymakenny Farm now supply their speciality potatoes to leading chefs and restaurants.

rows.verbatim: Any four of the following factors
rows.contextNote: After the five illustrated factors the scheme adds "Other relevant factors: Legal requirements; Availability of technology etc", and a sixth heading, "Communication Skills of the Receiver /ability to respond", under which it prints no illustration. The examiner accepts these as factors, but each 5 is (2+3): the factor named is the 2, and the 3 is for illustrating it.

options: Appropriate Language/Clarity: If the language is too technical or too difficult for the customers to understand then the message may be misinterpreted. The business needs to choose language appropriate to its audience. In the case of customers, short clear sentences and visual supports etc. may be suitable for product assembly e.g. flat packs.

Confidentiality/Safety: The medium chosen must be appropriate to the message been given. If the message is sensitive for the stakeholder e.g. terminating the employment contract of an employee, then a meeting would be more appropriate than a letter or an e-mail.

Cost: The expense of the communication process is a very important factor. A CEO communicating with his managers worldwide may choose to hold a virtual meeting to cut down on travel and subsistence costs.

Urgency/Speed/Destination: If a crucial piece of information has to be communicated instantly to a supplier, then a phone call, a text or e-mail may be appropriate e.g. to arrange a change in delivery times.

Feedback/Accuracy/Record: The business may be looking for feedback in order to take further action. Communication with the revenue commissioners may require regular correspondence and written records and in this case business letters and e-mail can provide formal evidence of the feedback process, eliminating misunderstandings.

notes: Scheme p.45, marks cells ⟨4 x 5⟩ ⟨(2+3)⟩ (summary grid p.9: '4 x 5m (2+3)'). Four factors at 5m each, so bestNofParts with one anyN row; each option carries the scheme's heading plus the whole worked illustration printed under it, because 'Illustrate' and the +3 are paid for that example. Checked line-by-line against the scheme PDF (page index 45) with positions: the five options are verbatim, the only editorial mark is a colon joining each bold heading to the paragraph the SEC set beneath it. REPAIRED (finding upheld): the card previously listed six options, the sixth being the bare line 'Communication Skills of the Receiver /ability to respond'. The scheme does set that in Calibri-Bold like the five real factor headings, so it is genuinely an accepted factor — but it prints NO development under it, so as an option it priced six words at the full 5 and handed over the +3 that 'Illustrate' is paid for. There is no honest way to promote it: writing an illustration for it would be inventing scheme text. It is therefore named in the row's contextNote instead, quoted exactly, alongside the scheme's catch-all line 'Other relevant factors: Legal requirements; Availability of technology etc' (which is set in plain type, not bold, and is the examiner's note on scope) — the same treatment this batch already gave the scheme's bare extras in q4ai. ofParts drops 6 → 5 to match the options actually shown, as in every sibling Q5 card. openList stays true because the scheme's front matter says the support notes are 'neither exclusive nor complete' and 'not model answers but rather a sample of possible responses'; note for a later pass, though, that openList is inert on an anyN row — SessionScreen renders the 'I had something like this' control only in the non-group branch (line 498), so a student who named a sixth factor AND illustrated it has no button to record it. The contextNote is the only place that reaches them, which is why it states what the 5 is actually paid for rather than promising a control. Stem: the Ballymakenny profile is the paper's shared preamble for all parts of Q5 and is carried on every Q5 card, but the scheme's answers for this part are entirely generic (customers, a CEO, a supplier, the revenue commissioners) — nothing in the stimulus gives a factor away or is needed to earn a mark here. No figure: the paper's Q5 page carries no stimulus image and none of the published 2021 HL figures belong to this question.

questionText: Define the term delegation.

rows.verbatim: Delegation involves the assignment of authority to another person. It is generally assigned from a manager to a subordinate, to undertake a specific work task or project. The accountability for the particular task/project is also assigned.

One definition worth five, so fixed with a single row of 5 — part (C) totals 20 marks, of which (i) takes this 5 and (ii) takes 15. The definition is quoted whole across the four printed lines it wraps over, accountability sentence included: the marks cells sit beside the prose but do not interrupt it, and the +3 is paid for exactly that development, so stopping after 'assignment of authority to another person' would let a student claim the development marks for the opening clause. No dash is used in the row, because the scheme prints no lead-in label here. Wording note: the paper and the scheme's detail page both say 'Define the term delegation'; the summary grid on p.9 says 'Explain' — the paper's wording is used. openList true per the scheme front matter ('a sample of possible responses').

questionText: Describe the benefits of delegation for: management; the employees.
stem: Ballymakenny Farm Heritage & Speciality Potatoes. Maria Flynn and her husband David are potato farmers. Maria saw a niche in the market to start growing their own speciality Purple Violetta Potatoes. Ballymakenny Farm now supply their speciality potatoes to leading chefs and restaurants.

rows.verbatim: Any three of the following benefits
rows.contextNote: The question asks for benefits for management AND for the employees, so three benefits that all sit on the management side leave half the question unanswered. The scheme runs both audiences together in one list instead of splitting it, so check that the three you claim cover both. Each is marked 5m (2+3), and the 3 is paid for the description, not for the heading.

options: Frees up time for management for strategic planning: Manager is not required to do all the work and has more time for strategic planning.
Increased efficiency: Task/project may be completed to a higher standard due to the level of personal accountability provided by delegation.
Increased motivation/staff morale: Increased employee motivation from job enrichment/ improved staff morale/more challenging work.
Effective time-management tool/ managers can prioritise tasks that need their attention.
Staff development: Higher skilled workforce will allow greater management flexibility. The tasks up-skill staff and develop their capabilities.
Work-life balance improves for the manager: Delegation may improve the work-life balance for the manager. Manager recognises the need to delegate and their workload can decrease.

notes: Scheme p.46, marks cells ⟨3 x⟩ ⟨5m⟩ ⟨(2+3)⟩ (summary grid p.9: '3 x 5m (2+3)'). Three benefits at 5m each = 15, which with (i)'s 5m makes the 20 the paper prints against part (C). Six benefits printed, so bestNofParts with one anyN row. Each option carries the scheme's heading and the sentence developing it, because the +3 is paid for the description. The paper asks for the benefits 'for: • management • the employees' (p.42), but the scheme does NOT split its list into management benefits and employee benefits, it runs them as one list. That split is therefore still not imposed on the options and no row is invented to enforce one, because three of the six ('Frees up time for management for strategic planning', 'Effective time-management tool', 'Work-life balance improves for the manager') are management-side while 'Increased motivation/staff morale' is employee-side and 'Increased efficiency' and 'Staff development' straddle both, so any hard classification would be the author's and not the examiner's. Instead the two-audience requirement is carried in a contextNote on the row, exactly as the sibling 2021 HL Q2(C)(ii) does for its economic-and-social pair, so a student who ticks three management-side benefits is warned rather than told they covered the question. 'Effective time-management tool/ managers can prioritise tasks that need their attention' is quoted as the scheme prints it, as a single line with no separate heading. Stem: the Ballymakenny profile is the paper's shared preamble for all parts of Q5; the scheme's answers here are generic and take nothing from it, and it leaks no delegation benefit, so it is kept whole. No figure: page 42 carries only the decorative farm photograph, and the question can be asked without it. openList true per the scheme front matter.

questionText: Distinguish between forming and norming as stages in team development.
stem: Kerry Group is a leading taste and nutrition company. Total Quality Management (TQM), reward schemes and teamwork are evident in many leading companies such as Kerry Group.

rows.verbatim: Forming refers to the team members coming together for the first time. A lack of trust can exist between team members. The team leader will attempt to build relationships and outline the objectives of the team

Norming is when norms/rules have been established for how the team will behave, what standards are expected etc. Conflicts that might have occurred in the storming stage have been overcome. Trust has developed between team members and roles have been established.

notes: Scheme p.47. The examiner prints 6 and 3 + 3 against this part and the summary grid on scheme p.10 repeats 6m (3m+3m), so it is a fixed tariff — one 3 for forming, one 3 for norming, two rows rather than a single 6-mark row. The scheme runs each stage as continuous prose with no heading, so each row quotes the whole paragraph unbroken and no dash is used. openList true: the support notes are 'a sample of possible responses', so a candidate who distinguished the two stages in their own words scored.

questionText: Outline two benefits of teamwork for the employees in a business.
stem: Kerry Group is a leading taste and nutrition company. Total Quality Management (TQM), reward schemes and teamwork are evident in many leading companies such as Kerry Group.

rows.verbatim: Any two of these benefits of teamwork for employees

Reduced absenteeism: Employees recognise that others depend on them. This can reduce the level of absenteeism in the workforce.

Increased efficiencies/communications: Teamwork can improve communication with the organization. It can lead to staff developing greater interpersonal skills. This can lead to the sharing of ideas and improved efficiencies.
Improved decision making: Team members have knowledge and experience that they share with each other. This in turn can lead to more effective decisions and faster task completion

questionText: Discuss the benefits of adopting a Total Quality Management (TQM) system for a company such as Kerry Group.
stem: Kerry Group is a leading taste and nutrition company. Total Quality Management (TQM), reward schemes and teamwork are evident in many leading companies such as Kerry Group.

rows.verbatim: Any three of these benefits of adopting TQM
rows.contextNote: Each benefit is worth 5m (2+3): naming it earns 2 and developing it for Kerry Group earns the other 3. They must be three different benefits. The scheme prints employee empowerment twice, once headed 'Increased employee motivation/Increased job satisfaction' and once headed 'Teamwork/Employee empowerment/Increased job satisfaction', with the same two sentences beneath both, so it is one benefit the examiner pays for once and it is listed here once. Tick it once even if you wrote it under both headings.

options: Increased Sales/Enhanced Reputation: TQM involves the business focusing on the needs of the customer. The benefit is that sales for Kerry Group will increase as consumer satisfaction is improved and the business will develop a reputation for developing high quality goods and services.

The scheme prints five possible benefits but only four distinct ones: its second entry ('Increased employee motivation/ Increased job satisfaction') and its fourth ('Teamwork/Employee empowerment/Increased job satisfaction') carry the identical two empowerment sentences under different headings, and the fourth's whole body is a substring of the second's, which additionally ends 'This can boost productivity at Kerry Group.' Offering both let a student who made that one point tick two options and bank 10 of the 15 for it, which the examiner would not pay, so the fourth entry is no longer a separate tickable benefit; the contextNote names its heading in full so a student who wrote it that way still finds and claims the point once. ofParts is 4 to match the four options the card shows. Nothing markable was lost: the removed entry contains no wording the kept one does not. Each option joins the scheme's heading to the discussion printed beneath it with a colon, so no heading is left as a bare claim and the development the second half of the (2+3) pays for is on the card; every word of both halves is the scheme's. The scheme's contents page spells it 'adapting' where the paper and the scheme body both say 'adopting' — questionText follows the paper. The stem is the paper's stimulus verbatim; it names TQM, reward schemes and teamwork as practices at Kerry Group but states none of the five benefits, so it is kept whole. No figure: the question is text-only and the published figure list has nothing on this page.

questionText: Explain the following types of financial and non-financial rewards: Commission, Employee Share Purchase Plan, Flexitime.
stem: Kerry Group is a leading taste and nutrition company. Total Quality Management (TQM), reward schemes and teamwork are evident in many leading companies such as Kerry Group. Businesses offer a range of rewards to attract high calibre staff.

rows.verbatim: Commission: Employees earn a percentage of the total sales that they achieve. Commission can increase the motivation of sales staff to sell goods and services to consumers.
rows.contextNote: 6m (3+3): 3 for what commission is, 3 for the sentence developing it. The scheme prints both, so one sentence reaches half.

rows.verbatim: Employee share purchase plan: Employees can buy shares in the company at a discounted price. This can increase the motivation of employees as it is in their interest to work hard and make the business successful.
rows.contextNote: 6m (3+3): 3 for what the plan is, 3 for the sentence developing it.

rows.verbatim: Flexi-time: Employees are empowered to choose their own working hours within a time-frame. Employees must fulfil their contracted hours. i.e. Employees must work a 40-hour week but can choose to start at 10am and finish at 6pm rather than work the traditional 9am to 5pm.
rows.contextNote: 6m (3+3): 3 for what flexi-time is, 3 for developing it. The scheme's own 'i.e.' example is part of the answer, not an aside.

notes: Scheme p.49 (marking-scheme PDF p.50): the Max Mark cell prints 3@6m and (3+3) against 18 of part (C)'s 25 marks, the other 7 being (ii). The scheme prints each reward's name on its own line and then the sentences explaining it, and marks the three separately, so this is three fixed rows of 6 rather than one 18-mark row. Colons, not dashes, separate the name from the explanation on purpose: the app strips everything before a spaced dash when it lists the marks a student left behind, and with dashes this card listed three nameless paragraphs with Commission, Employee share purchase plan and Flexi-time deleted. questionText: Outline the internal and external sources of new product ideas for businesses.
stem: Moon Moods. The entrepreneurs behind Moon Moods set up a business that produces soft, comfortable and beautiful bedding for children and babies.

rows.verbatim: Any four sources of new product ideas

options: Skills and knowledge: An entrepreneur can possess a particular skill or knowledge that can be used to develop a business. For example a musician might start to offer music lessons.
Interests and hobbies: Entrepreneurs might use what they enjoy doing do identify an opportunity. Roz Purcell successfully launched a cookbook
Travel abroad: Entrepreneurs get ideas from products/services they have seen work in other destinations. They then adapt these ideas/products to meet the needs of their market.
Copy existing businesses/Competitors: Entrepreneurs get ideas from what they see existing businesses are doing. Competitors can give the entrepreneurs an idea for new product/service of their own.
Friends/Family suggestions: Entrepreneurs get ideas from friends or family who might make suggestions or highlight a problem with an existing product/service.
Internet: Entrepreneurs get ideas from the internet. An event, video, trend, problem they witness online might trigger an idea for a new product/service that they can offer.
Brainstorming: have a brainstorming session to come up with an idea.
Media – Entrepreneurs can get ideas from newspapers, TV, radio etc.
Fashion/Consumer Trends – listening to what is “in vogue”/customer trends and make a product to suit their needs.
Import substitution: Make a product that is currently being imported.

notes: Scheme p.51 of the PDF (printed footer 50). Tariff printed 4@5(2+3): four sources at 5m each, 2m for naming the source and 3m for developing it, so the paper's (20) is four answers, not one — bestNofParts, four of the ten the scheme lists. All ten of the scheme's sources are now on the menu, in the order the scheme prints them; Brainstorming and Import substitution were previously left off, which left a student who wrote either with nothing to tick. The Import substitution point is quoted whole, up to "imported." (2) "doing do identify an opportunity" in the Interests and hobbies point is the SEC's own typo, kept verbatim. Punctuation on the two additions normalised to the card's existing "Heading: development" form (the scheme prints "Brainstorming:" and "Import substitution-"); provenance is punctuation-insensitive and all ten options trace under both the current comparison and the stricter pre-LABEL_ONLY one. questionText: Illustrate the following by means of a breakeven chart: (i) Breakeven point.
stem: Moon Moods. The entrepreneurs behind Moon Moods set up a business that produces soft, comfortable and beautiful bedding for children and babies. Moon Moods has provided the following information for their new product line: Forecast Output (Sales) 30,000 units; Selling Price per unit €15; Fixed Costs €200,000; Variable Costs per unit €5.

rows.verbatim: Break-even Point = F.C. (i) S.P – V.C = 200,000 15 – 5 = 20,000 units
rows.contextNote: The scheme sets this working as two stacked fractions: F.C. is written, underlined, over S.P – V.C, and 200,000 over 15 – 5, so read each pair as the line above divided by the line below — fixed costs over selling price less variable cost per unit. The '(i)' is the scheme's part label, printed in the narrow left-hand column beside the formula rather than being part of it. The circled 4 is printed beside 20,000 units: the mark is one tick on the whole calculation.

notes:
Scheme p.51 (the model chart) and p.52 (the calculations), which are PDF pages 52 and 53. Part (B) is worth 25m on the paper and the scheme marks it with circled figures printed on its model chart: title 1, y-axis label 1, x-axis label 1, TR line 4, TC line 4, FC line 2, BEP 4, Margin of Safety 4, Profit at forecast output 4 = 25. The breakeven point element is 4m on the chart and 4m again in the scheme's alternative 'Calculations only' route on p.52, which is what this card marks, as its siblings (B)(ii) and (B)(iii) do. The 13m for drawing and labelling the chart itself cannot be self-marked from text and is not carded.

REPAIR. The row previously read 'Break-even Point = F.C. ÷ (S.P – V.C) — 200,000 ÷ (15 – 5) = 20,000 units'. Read off the scheme page itself, the 2021 scheme prints no division sign and no brackets: it sets the working as two stacked fractions — F.C. underlined over S.P – V.C, then 200,000 underlined over 15 – 5, then = 20,000 units with the circled 4 beside it. The ÷ notation is real but belongs to a different year: the 2025 HL scheme prints 'Break Even Point = 600,000 ÷ (10-5)', and that is where it was copied from. Nothing caught it because the build checks only the text after the dash and normalise() strips ÷ and brackets before comparing, so the old row passed provenance while carrying wording the SEC never printed. The row is now the scheme's own lines quoted in order and the dash is gone: the scheme prints no label-and-its-answer pair here, only one continuous calculation, and the 4 is for the whole of it.

The '(i)' inside the quote is deliberate. It is the part label from the scheme's narrow left-hand column, and the converted scheme merges it onto the 'S.P – V.C' line instead of giving it a line of its own, so the LABEL_ONLY filter in scripts/markbank/schemeText.mjs does not strip it and it survives in the comparison text between 'F.C.' and 'S.P'. Quoting the formula without it makes the point untraceable and the build would drop the card, so it is kept and the row note says what it is.

Two things about the scheme are left exactly as the SEC published them. Its Question column heads this answer page '6 B' although this is Question 7 — scheme p.51 heads the section 'Question 7' and the paper prints Moon Moods as Q7. And the fraction bars are drawn as underlines, which the text layer loses; that is why the flattened line needs its row note.

No figure. The paper's four values are a small data table on paper p.44 which the figure extractor did not publish (nothing for that page is in the published figure set), and they are carried in the stem the way bus-2022-hl-s1-q9 carries its break-even data. The stem gives nothing away: the bedding sentence is stimulus and the four values are what the calculation cannot be attempted without.

questionText: Define the term margin of safety.
stem: Moon Moods. The entrepreneurs behind Moon Moods set up a business that produces soft, comfortable and beautiful bedding for children and babies.

rows.verbatim: The Margin of Safety is the amount of sales (in units) that a business can afford to lose before it reaches Break-even Point. It identifies the point at which businesses will start to make a loss and acts as a buffer for business to ensure that this point is not reached.

questionText: Discuss one limitation of a breakeven analysis when making business decisions.
stem: Moon Moods. The entrepreneurs behind Moon Moods set up a business that produces soft, comfortable and beautiful bedding for children and babies.

rows.verbatim: Any one of these limitations of a breakeven analysis

options: Economies of scale: The breakeven chart does not account for the variable cost per unit decreasing as output increases.
Selling price: A limitation of the breakeven chart is that it assumes the selling price remains the same. It does not allow/factor that selling price might be reduced for bulk orders.
Faulty stock: The breakeven chart does not allow for the costs of products that are faulty/production errors.
Profits are a function of not only output, but also of other factors like technological change, improvement in management, etc., which are overlooked in this analysis.

notes: Tariff read from the scheme, not computed. Joining the grid cell to its split follows the same convention as Q6(A)(ii), whose grid cell wraps as '2@7m' / '(4m+3m)'. questionText: Discuss the three challenges below that a new business start-up must address: Ownership structure, Production, Finance.

Choosing a method of production: The method of production will be influence; Economies of scale, type of workers required (low skilled or high skilled) etc. Job, Batch or Mass production.
