questionText: Outline three provisions of the Industrial Relations Act 1990.
stem: The Taoiseach says 6.5% public sector pay offer is fair. Adapted from rte.ie

rows.verbatim: Any three of these provisions of the Industrial Relations Act 1990
rows.contextNote: Each provision is worth 5m (2+3) — naming the provision earns 2 and outlining what it actually requires earns the other 3, so a bare heading is only two-fifths of the answer.

options: Trade Disputes -Trade Dispute as defined by the Industrial Relations Act 1990 is ‘any dispute between employers and workers, which is connected with the employment or non-employment or the terms or conditions of employment of any person’.
Legitimate Trade Dispute – Grounds for legitimate trade disputes include disputes concerning pay, changes to conditions, demarcation disputes etc.

Secret Ballots- Under the provisions of the Industrial Relations Act 1990 no strike or other industrial action can take place without a secret ballot. All members are given a fair opportunity of voting. The act also provides that the union should not organise or participate in industrial action without a majority of votes having being cast in favour of industrial action. The union must make known to the members (entitled to vote) the results of a secret ballot as soon as practicable after the vote.
Notice of industrial action One week’s notice of action must be given to the employer involved in a dispute.

Official disputes unofficial disputes and Injunctions-Official dispute is one where a union has received approval from workers in a secret ballot and is confirmed by ICTU. Unofficial disputes have no ICTU or union approval and workers receive no strike pay.

Picketing - Primary picketing- According to the Industrial Relations Act 1990 it is lawful for workers to picket peacefully at a place where their employer works or carries on business provided the picketing is for the purpose of peacefully communicating information.

Secondary picketing- The act provides that secondary picketing (i.e. picketing of an employer other than the primary employer involved in the dispute) is lawful only in situations where it is reasonable for those workers picketing to believe that the second employer was acting to frustrate the industrial action by directly assisting their employer.
Immunity-The Industrial Relations Act 1990 states the trade unions and workers are immune from legal action/prosecution for damages or losses suffered by the employer as a result of a trade dispute.

notes: Paper p.6, scheme pp.43-44. The Max Mark cell prints 3@5(2+3) against (ii), which with the 5 on (i) makes part (A)'s 20. Eight provisions are printed and only three are marked, so one anyN row with claimMax 3 rather than eight rows — eight rows would display 40 marks on a 15-mark part and would also breach the five-row cap. Each option carries the scheme's heading joined to the sentences printed under it, because the 2 is for naming the provision and the 3 for outlining it; an option reading only Secret Ballots would let a student who wrote two words award themselves the outline marks. Primary and secondary picketing are kept as two options because the scheme prints them as two separate blocks with their own explanations. Immunity is quoted across the scheme's page break (pp.43-44) as one continuous run, which is how it is printed. openList true: the front matter states model answers are not intended to be exhaustive and that variations and alternatives may also be acceptable, so a candidate who outlined, say, the Act's establishment of the Labour Relations Commission scored too.

questionText: Under the terms of the Unfair Dismissals Act 1997 to 2021, explain the grounds for dismissal that are deemed to be fair.
stem: The Taoiseach says 6.5% public sector pay offer is fair. Adapted from rte.ie

rows.verbatim: Any four of these grounds on which a dismissal is deemed to be fair
rows.contextNote: Each ground is worth 5m (2+3) — naming the ground earns 2 and explaining what it means in practice earns the other 3. The question asks for grounds that are FAIR, so listing the discriminatory grounds on which a dismissal is automatically unfair answers the opposite question.

options: Incompetence refers to an inability to do the job (poor work performance/failure to meet sales targets). In the first place, the employee needs to be made aware of the standards that are expected.

Incapable The ‘capability’ includes issues such as lateness, absenteeism, and persistent absence through illness or injury, either short-term or long-term. If lateness or absenteeism is an issue, the employer should have proof of this allegation, such as: Clocking-in records and Documented absences on file that are not medically certified.

Qualifications Fair dismissal on grounds of qualifications can happen in two ways. One situation is where the employer is misled about qualifications during recruitment. The other is where the employer made continued employment conditional upon further qualifications which have not been obtained.

Misconduct Gross misconduct may give rise to instant (summary) dismissal without notice or pay in lieu of notice. Examples of gross misconduct include assault, drunkenness, theft, bullying or serious breach of the employer’s policies and practices.

Redundancy In this case the employer needs to show that a redundancy situation exists as your job is no longer required and therefore the dismissal is fair. This means that there is an economic justification for the redundancy; that the employee will not be replaced. Fair procedures must be applied (e.g. last in and first out).

Contravening the law The employer may dismiss an employee if their continued employment would contravene the law. However, your employer might be expected to look at alternatives depending on all the facts of the case.

notes: Paper p.6, scheme pp.44-45. The Max Mark cell prints 4@5(2+3), so four grounds are marked out of the six the scheme lists — one anyN row with claimMax 4, not six rows, which would show 30 marks on a 20-mark part and breach the five-row cap. Each option carries the heading joined to the sentences printed beneath it: the 3 is paid for the explanation, so an option reading only Redundancy would let a student claim marks the examiner pays for showing the job is genuinely gone and fair procedures were applied. The question wording follows the paper (1997 to 2021); the scheme's contents page abbreviates it to 1997. openList true: the front matter states model answers are not intended to be exhaustive and that variations and alternatives may also be acceptable.

questionText: Discuss the services provided by the Workplace Relations Commission.
stem: The Taoiseach says 6.5% public sector pay offer is fair. Adapted from rte.ie

rows.verbatim: Any four of these services provided by the Workplace Relations Commission
rows.contextNote: Each service is worth 5m (2+3) — naming the service earns 2 and discussing how the WRC actually delivers it earns the other 3. Conciliation and mediation are separate services here and are scored separately, so a discussion that treats them as one name is one service, not two.

options: Advisory Service The Workplace Relations Commission’s Advisory Service promotes good practice in the workplace by assisting and advising organisations in all aspects of industrial relations in the workplace. It engages with employers, employees and their representatives to help them to develop effective industrial relations practices, procedures and structures. Such assistance could include reviewing or developing effective workplace procedures in areas such as grievance, discipline, communications and consultation.

Conciliation Conciliation is a voluntary process in which the parties to a dispute agree to avail of a neutral and impartial third party to assist them in resolving their industrial relations differences. The Workplace Relations Commission provides a conciliation service by making available Industrial Relations Officers (IRO or Conciliation Officer) of the Commission to chair ‘conciliation conferences’. Conciliation conferences are basically an extension of the process of direct negotiations, with an independent chairperson present to steer the discussions and explore possible avenues of settlement in a nonprejudicial fashion.

Compliance/Inspection Service Inspectors visit places of employment and carry out investigations on behalf of the WRC in order to ensure compliance with equality and employment-related legislation. Such investigations involve examining books, records and documents related to the employment, and conducting interviews with current and former employees and employers. Where breaches of legislation have been found, an Inspector may issue either a Compliance Notice or a Fixed Payment Notice to an employer.

Mediation Mediation seeks to arrive at a solution through an agreement between the parties, rather than through an investigation or hearing or formal decision. The WRC offers a mediation service in certain cases to facilitate the resolution of complaints/disputes where possible at an early stage and without recourse to adjudication. The Mediation Officer empowers the parties to negotiate their own agreement on a clear and informed basis. The process is voluntary and either party may terminate it at any stage.

Adjudication Adjudication Officers of the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) are statutorily independent in their decision-making duties. The Adjudication Officer’s role is to hold a hearing where both parties are given an opportunity to be heard by the Adjudication Officer and to present any evidence relevant to the complaint. The Adjudication Officer will not attempt to mediate or conciliate the case. Parties may be accompanied and represented at hearings by a trade union official, a practicing barrister or practicing solicitor for example. questionText: Explain three implications for a manager of adopting a Theory Y approach to management.
stem: Jim Gavin, Director of People and Operations in the Irish Aviation Authority, is a speaker on leadership and motivation. He references motivational theorists such as Douglas McGregor and Abraham Maslow.

rows.verbatim: Any three of the following

options: High levels of trust-Industrial Relations are improved when the manager places trust and authority in their staff. Morale is improved. Less time is spent in resolving conflict.
Innovation -The improved communication may result in employees being more likely to innovate or come up with an idea for a new product, way of reducing costs etc.

Improved communications -The atmosphere in the workplace is improved as the manager uses a two way system of communication. This reduces resistance to change and helps the organisation manage change effectively.

Delegation- By giving employees more authority motivation improves as employees feel more in control of their environment. This may lead to better customer relations, as a happy workforce enjoys engaging with the consumer. In service industries, this can result in increased sales and profitability.

An open style of Management -Management are open to employee suggestions and welcome an opportunity to discuss rather than give directions. This improved knowledge base can lead to more effective decision making and higher productivity in design/manufacturing businesses.

Delegation requires training / Delegation may result in a pay claim:-Training may be required if employees are use to an autocratic style of leadership. They may resist the theory Y approach to management concerning delegation. This could lead to poor industrial relations and the notion that new management is ‘distributing extra work without pay’ to employees.

New Communication Style could result in resistance to change The new approach to communication and discussion of ideas may not be successful if the manager is newly appointed. Internal factors such as reactions to promotions or resistance to outside appointments may stagger the perceived benefits of a theory y approach to managing.

rows.contextNote: The scheme's tariff is 3@5(2+3): 2 marks for naming the implication and 3 for the explanation that develops it. The scheme prints seven implications for the three required, and heads the last two 'Implications can be negative, such as:' — a negative implication is marked from the same list.

questionText: Discuss two benefits of planning as a management activity.

questionText: Discuss two types of business insurance that you recommend a hotel business should have.
stem: Due to major increases in utility bills, business owners may cancel insurance premiums or under insure their risks.

rows.verbatim: Public Liability Insurance // Employer’s Liability Insurance // Premises/Buildings Insurance // Contents Insurance // Motor Insurance
rows.contextNote: Each type is worth 5, split 2 + 3 — naming it earns 2, discussing it earns the other 3. The scheme closes the list with "Any relevant type of insurance for a hotel accepted."

options: Public Liability Insurance-Public liability insurance protects the business against financial loss as a result claims made by members of the public such as consumers who are injured or hurt on the business premises.
Employer’s Liability Insurance-Employer’s liability protects the business against financial loss as a result claims made by employees as a result of injuries they have sustained in the workplace.

Premises/Buildings Insurance- This provides the business with protection against any loss caused by damage to the structure of the building caused by fire, flood or storm. You should ensure a smoke alarm is fitted and there are adequate fire extinguishers in the premises.
Contents Insurance-This provides the business with protection against any loss or damage to stock, raw materials, components etc. caused by burglary, fire or flood.

Motor Insurance-A compulsory type of insurance that must be paid by law if the business or individual own a motor vehicle. Protects the business from being at a financial loss as a result of a motor accident. Three types of motor insurance include; third party insurance, third party fire & theft and fully comprehensive insurance.

questionText: Outline the different types of financial and non-financial rewards that businesses use to attract employees.
stem: New employees will seek flexible working conditions if pay demands are not met. Adapted from Irish Examiner

tariffModel.notation: 3@5(2+3), at least one of each required

rows.verbatim: Financial Rewards: Time rate // Piece Rate // Commission // Salary // Bonus // Profit –sharing scheme // Employee share ownership scheme. Non – Financial Rewards: Benefit-in-kind // Promotion // Job sharing
rows.contextNote: Each five is 2 for naming the reward and 3 for outlining it. Time rate, Piece Rate, Commission, Salary, Bonus, Profit –sharing scheme and Employee share ownership scheme are the scheme’s Financial Rewards; Benefit-in-kind, Promotion and Job sharing are its Non – Financial Rewards. At least one of each required, so two financial and one non-financial, or one financial and two non-financial, both reach the full fifteen — three from a single heading does not. (Note: Benefit-in-kind can be considered financial or non-financial depending on whether it is taxable or not).

options: Time rate-The employee is rewarded a fixed amount per hour for a fixed number of hours.

Piece Rate-The employee is rewarded per item produced/job completed. This method may lead to quality control problems as employees may try to get as many items produced as possible to increase its earnings.
Commission-The employees are paid a percentage of the total sales they have achieved. This is normally paid in addition to a flat payment. It has the advantage of directly encouraging sales.
Salary-A salary is paid to the employees in equal amounts, either weekly, biweekly or monthly.
Bonus A sum of money raised for reaching a certain target e.g. producing units above an agreed limit.

Profit –sharing scheme-This is a scheme where some of the business profits are paid to employees on an agreed basis. The scheme is administered and profits are paid to employees to motivate them to become more productive.

Employee share ownership scheme-Shares may be given to staff instead of cash bonuses, maintaining employee interest in the job/share option schemes give employees an option to buy shares in a company at a specified price sometime in the future.

Benefit-in- kind: This is also known as a perk or a fringe benefit. It takes the form of goods or a service given to employees rather than money. Benefits-in-kind are often used to raise the status of a position in a firm and to boost morale. Examples include meal vouchers, company cars and health insurance.

Promotion: Movement to a more responsible senior level in the organisation. While this will also carry a higher wage it is often the job title, bigger office or the availability of a personal assistant that is the real reward as per Maslow’s self-esteem needs.

Job sharing: This involves employees sharing a position e.g. two employees have a job split between them. This is a flexible approach to employment and recognises that employees may wish to prioritise leisure time over work time.

questionText: Explain the following terms in the context of human resource management. Job Description and Person Specification. Internal and External Recruitment. Interview and Selection.
stem: In 2022 recruitment companies noticed that Human Resource forecasts were adapted as the economy struggled with a cost of living crisis.

rows.verbatim: Job Description – A job description sets out the purpose of a job, where the job fits into the organisation structure, the main accountabilities and responsibilities of the job and the key tasks to be performed. The job description defines where the job is positioned in the organisation structure and who reports to whom.
rows.contextNote: Five terms, 5 marks each, split 2 + 3 — naming what the term is earns 2 and explaining it earns the other 3.

rows.verbatim: Person Specification -A person specification sets out the kind of qualifications, skills, experience and personal attributes a successful candidate should possess. It refers to the person rather than the post and is useful in comparing and assessing the suitability of job applicants.

Internal recruitment- The employee is familiar with the culture, policies and work practices of the firm. Training and advertising costs are decreased. Motivation within the workplace improves as employees recognise that opportunities will occur as vacancies higher up the chain of command become available. No “new blood”, no new thinking. The best person for the job may not be the internal appointment. Promotion from within can have a negative effect on levels of co-operation between employees.

External recruitment – Fresh new perspective brought to the business by the external appointee. The new employee may have skills and experience that may be required by the business but is not present among existing staff. Training costs avoided as the external appointee may already have the skill set required. Links with colleges of education which provide staff with expertise to meet business needs.

Job Interview and selection - A job interview is a process in which a potential employee is evaluated by an employer for prospective employment in the company. The process attempts to determine the candidate’s ability to do the job, get along with other employees, work in teams and contribute to the business in an innovative and effective manner. Interviews generally take the form of interview panels where a number of interviewers interview one candidate. A variety of selection methods can be used.

notes: Three bullets on the paper but five explanations in the scheme and a 5@5(2+3) tariff, so the "Internal and External Recruitment" bullet becomes two rows and the "Interview and Selection" bullet is the scheme's single "Job Interview and selection" block. Five rows, exactly at the required-row cap, summing to 25. The scheme's own heading line "Internal and External Recruitment:" is a heading, not a marking point, so it is not a row.

questionText: Describe the benefits of employee empowerment for a business.
stem: Centre Parcs: Centre Parcs Longford features 400 acres of beautiful forest, swimming pool, a range of restaurants, activities and accommodation types.

rows.verbatim: Any three benefits of employee empowerment
rows.contextNote: Each benefit is worth 5, split 2 + 3 — naming the benefit earns 2, describing it earns the other 3. The question says "the benefits" without giving a number, and the tariff pays for three, so a student who stops at two leaves five marks on the table. The scheme prints "the manufacturing business" inside the third benefit; it is a leftover from another question and is quoted as printed rather than tidied to Centre Parcs.

options: Decision-making: Decision-making and control is in the hands of employees who use their greater skills and knowledge for the benefit of the business/decisions made quicker. Employees become more responsive to the needs of customers/come up with ideas to solve issues/more satisfied customers.

Prepares staff for Management roles/promotions: Empowerment trains staff to be decision makers. Empowerment means staff gain invaluable experience in having to make decisions and judgement calls. This prepares staff for promotions/ role of management which in turn can reduce the need for training.

Increased Motivation - Increased Staff Morale & Job Satisfaction: Employees will be empowered, allowing them to make decisions, increasing trust from management and allowing them to satisfy esteem needs (Maslow). The benefit for the manufacturing business is that there would be more energized and productive staff, and lower staff turnover.

notes: Repaired after review: the tariff was 2@5 and is now 3 x 5m (2+3) = 15. The scheme's Question 7 structure grid (PDF page 14) prints "(C) (i) Explain the term Employee Empowerment. 5m (2+3)" and "(ii) Describe the benefits of Employee Empowerment for a business. 3 x 5m (2+3)" against a part (C) Max Mark of 20 — 5 + 15 = the (20) the paper prints against part (C), and Q7 then makes 20 + 20 + 20 = the 60 the grid totals. The scheme's detail page (PDF page 57, numbered 54) prints "2@5(2+3)" beside this part, which cannot be right: it would leave part (C) worth 15 and Question 7 worth 55. Treated as an SEC typo in the detail cell, exactly as the sibling card q6aii treats the mirror-image error at 6(A)(ii), where the detail cell says "3@5(2+3)" and the grid and the paper both say two. The grid and the paper agree; the detail cell is the outlier, and it is the outlier in both directions, so the earlier note claiming a five-mark gap in the SEC's published scheme was wrong and is withdrawn. The scheme develops exactly three benefits and the tariff pays for three, so this is a fixed tariff with one anyN row capped at 3, not a best-of menu — bestNofParts would make the session print "Answer any 3 of these 3". openList true per the scheme's front matter ("these are not intended to be exhaustive. Variations and alternatives may also be acceptable"), so a fourth genuine benefit, described, scores too. Each option carries the scheme's bold heading AND the sentences that develop it, because the +3 is paid for the description; all three are quoted continuously and pass the provenance check unchanged. No figure: the only images on this page are the Centre Parcs stimulus box, which the stem carries, and Tommy's tax table, which belongs to part (B). Filed with (C)(i) under Management skills — leading & motivating: the benefits the scheme lists are decision-making, promotion readiness, motivation, morale and Maslow's esteem needs.

questionText: Illustrate the following by means of a breakeven chart: (i) Breakeven point (ii) Margin of safety at the forecast output (iii) Profit at forecast output.
stem: MJ Sports produce products aimed at Hurling and Camogie players. MJ Sports have provided the following information for their new product line: Forecast Output (Sales) 8,000 units; Selling Price per unit €20; Fixed Costs €40,000; Variable Costs per unit €10.

tariffModel.notation: Calculations only: (Max. 12m) — Break Even Point 4m, Profit at Forecast output 4m, Margin of Safety 4m

rows.verbatim: Break Even Point = Fixed Costs/Contribution per unit — 40,000/10 = 4,000 units
rows.contextNote: Contribution per unit is the €20 selling price less the €10 variable cost, so the €40,000 of fixed costs divided by €10 gives 4,000 units. The examiner's circled 4 is one tick on the whole calculation, formula and answer together.

rows.verbatim: Margin of Safety = Forecast output in units – BEP in units — 8,000-4,000 = 4,000 units
rows.contextNote: Forecast output is the 8,000 units given in the question and the breakeven point is the 4,000 units worked out above, so the margin of safety is 4,000 units of sales.

rows.verbatim: Profit at forecast output = TR-TC — €160,000 – €120,000 = €40,000
rows.contextNote: Total revenue is 8,000 x €20 and total cost is the €40,000 of fixed costs plus 8,000 x €10 of variable costs.

notes: Scheme p.57 (the Calculations block) with the tariff itemised in the structure table on scheme p.12. Part (C) is worth 25m on the paper and the scheme marks it two ways: the chart — X Axis 1m, Y Axis 1m, Title of Chart 1m, FC line 2m, TC line 4m, TR line 4m, BEP 4m, MOS 4m, Profit at Forecast output 4m = 25m — OR 'Calculations only: (Max. 12m)', which is Break Even Point 4m, Profit at Forecast output 4m, Margin of Safety 4m. This card is that second route, so all three rows carry route 'calculations' and the card's tariff is that route's 12m. The chart route cannot sit on this card as a second route: its nine required elements exceed the five-row cap, and every route on a card must reach that card's own tariff, which 25m and 12m cannot both do. The chart elements are carried by the two sibling Q8(C) cards, and a student takes one route or the other. On scheme p.57 the Max. Mark column's words are interleaved into the middle of answer (i) by the PDF-to-text conversion — the lines read 'Fixed Costs/Contribution per unit Calculations' and '= 40,000/10 = 4,000 units only:' — so r-1 quotes the examiner's answer across that intrusion, formula then substitution, with the dash on the line break the scheme itself prints between them. r-2 closes up the spaces around the scheme's minus sign so the worked answer survives whole in the app's list of marks left behind.

questionText: Illustrate the following by means of a breakeven chart: (i) Breakeven point (ii) Margin of safety at the forecast output (iii) Profit at forecast output.
stem: MJ Sports produce products aimed at Hurling and Camogie players. MJ Sports have provided the following information for their new product line: Forecast Output (Sales) 8,000 units; Selling Price per unit €20; Fixed Costs €40,000; Variable Costs per unit €10.

tariffModel.notation: TC line 4m, TR line 4m, BEP 4m, MOS 4m, Profit at Forecast output 4m

rows.verbatim: TC line — the total cost line, drawn from €40,000 at zero output and rising by the €10 variable cost per unit to €120,000 at the forecast output of 8,000 units
rows.contextNote: The €120,000 the line has to reach is the scheme's own figure: it is the TC in "Profit at forecast output = TR-TC = €160,000 – €120,000 = €40,000" on scheme p.57. The structure table on scheme p.12 itemises this as a single "TC line 4m", so the 4 is awarded on the line as a whole. At zero output the only cost is the €40,000 fixed cost, so the total cost line starts level with the fixed cost line rather than at the origin.

rows.verbatim: TR line — the total revenue line, drawn from the origin and rising by the €20 selling price per unit to €160,000 at the forecast output of 8,000 units
rows.contextNote: The €160,000 is the TR in the scheme's "Profit at forecast output = TR-TC = €160,000 – €120,000 = €40,000" (scheme p.57), and it is 8,000 units at the €20 selling price. Nothing sold means no revenue, so unlike the total cost line this one starts at the origin.

rows.verbatim: BEP — the breakeven point, Fixed Costs/Contribution per unit = 40,000/10 = 4,000 units, marked and labelled on the chart where the total revenue line cuts the total cost line
rows.contextNote: Scheme p.57 prints the calculation. Contribution per unit is the €20 selling price less the €10 variable cost, so 40,000/10 is 4,000 units. The same figure is paid for separately on the calculations route, which is the Q8(C) (calculations) card; here the 4 is for the point appearing on the chart.

rows.verbatim: MOS — the margin of safety, Forecast output in units – BEP in units, shown along the output axis as a gap of 4,000 units between the breakeven point and the forecast output of 8,000 units
rows.contextNote: Scheme p.57: "Margin of Safety = Forecast output in units – BEP in units = 8,000 - 4,000 = 4,000 units". On the chart this is a distance along the output axis, not a euro amount on the vertical axis.

rows.verbatim: Profit at Forecast output — the profit at the forecast output, TR-TC = €160,000 – €120,000 = €40,000, shown on the chart as the vertical gap between the total revenue and total cost lines at 8,000 units

notes: Scheme p.57 marks part (C) as a 25-mark chart and the structure table on scheme p.12 itemises the 25: X Axis 1m, Y Axis 1m, Title of Chart 1m, FC line 2m, TC line 4m, TR line 4m, BEP 4m, MOS 4m, Profit at Forecast output 4m. Nine required elements will not fit one card, so the chart is two: Q8(C) (chart labelling) carries the four presentation marks (5) and this card carries the five 4-mark elements (20) — the two plotted lines and the three readings the chart is drawn to show. The scheme's model chart is a picture that did not survive conversion to text (scheme p.57 shows only the word "Chart:", twice, where it sat), so each row states what has to be on the page using the scheme's own figures from that same page: "Break Even Point = Fixed Costs/Contribution per unit = 40,000/10 = 4,000 units", "Margin of Safety = Forecast output in units – BEP in units = 8,000 - 4,000 = 4,000 units" and "Profit at forecast output = TR-TC = €160,000 – €120,000 = €40,000", the last of which also fixes the total cost (€120,000) and total revenue (€160,000) the two lines must reach at the forecast output. The scheme's other route, "OR Calculations only: (Max. 12m)", is the separate Q8(C) (calculations) card; a student takes one route or the other, so nothing is double counted inside a card. Row r-4 quotes the margin of safety formula but gives the subtraction in words, because the scheme's "8,000 - 4,000" is a spaced hyphen and the session screen splits a row on the last spaced dash when it lists the marks a student left behind, which would reduce this point to the fragment "4,000 = 4,000 units". questionText: Outline three procedures an employer should follow when dismissing an employee, under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977/2015.

rows.verbatim: Any three of the following procedures
rows.contextNote: Fourteen marks for three procedures, printed 2@5m(2+3) plus 1@4m (2+2): two of the three you outline are worth 5 and the third 4, and the scheme never says which is which, so the panel shows the 4 that every one of them is guaranteed. Each procedure is paid 2 for naming it and the rest for outlining it, so a heading on its own takes 2. Where the dismissal is for gross misconduct the scheme accepts a different route: Suspension ("The employee is on paid leave pending the outcome an investigation."), Investigation ("A hearing or investigation is carried out. The employee is entitled to representation.") and Sanction and Appeal ("Following the hearing, an employee may be sanctioned and can appeal any decision. They can also take legal action to pause the process.").

options: Informal Counselling. This pre-disciplinary procedure should be carried out to ensure the employee knows the standards expected, and should be carried out by a supervisor/manager. They are made aware of the consequences if they do not meet these standards. If this informal counselling does not bring about the required improvement the formal disciplinary procedure will be invoked.

Formal Verbal Warning This would involve a meeting with the employee at which the employee could bring a colleague or other representative. At the meeting the employee should be advised of what the problem is and invited to respond and explain his actions. Following the meeting a confirmatory letter should be given to the employee. This letter confirms that the employee has been given a verbal/oral warning. It should also contain the improvements required of the employee in respect of the behaviour which led to the warning and the timeframe within which the improvement must be made.

First Written Warning If there is no change to the situation, a formal written warning follows the oral warning. A copy will be given to the employee’s representative. This may be followed by a final written warning, suspension without pay, transfer to another task, or section of the enterprise, demotion, some other appropriate disciplinary action short of dismissal and finally dismissal.

Second Written Warning If the required improvement is not forthcoming within the 3-month period after the 1st written warning then a 2nd written warning may be issued. This is entirely a matter for the employer and it is common for many employers to only issue a 1st and final written warning

Final Written Warning This warning letter will be the final one prior to dismissal so it is important that it is well drafted as it will be scrutinised closely by the employee and probably his legal advisor. This letter should only refer to the matters which have been the subject of the disciplinary procedure to date, not other matters which have never been put to the employee.
Suspension The employee is asked not to attend work or engage in any work but will be paid pending a further investigation

Right of Appeal The employee has the right to a fair and impartial determination of the issues concerned, taking into account any representations made by, or on behalf of, the employee and any other relevant or appropriate evidence, factors or circumstances.

notes: Pick any three from a printed list, so the card is one bounded anyN group and not five required rows. The five rows were the defect: the session lists every unticked required row as marks left behind and excludes an anyN group from that list, so a student who wrote three correct procedures was shown two more they were never asked for. The tariff model stays orderedSplit because 2@5m(2+3) + 1@4m (2+2) makes 14 across three answers with no per-row value defined, and bestNofParts cannot express it (3 x perPart never makes 14). perOption is 4, the largest figure three answers can share inside a 14-mark tariff — 3 x 5 would print 15 marks on a 14-mark question — and the real 5/5/4 rides on the notation the session prints under the rows and on the contextNote. The seven options are the scheme's ordinary disciplinary route quoted whole, heading and development together, because the (2+3) pays for the outline and "First Written Warning" on its own is 2 of 5. openList is kept and the scheme's three-step gross-misconduct route (Suspension, Investigation, Sanction and Appeal) is quoted in the contextNote, so nothing the examiner accepts is lost. "3- month", split across a line break in the PDF, is closed up to "3-month"; no colon or dash is inserted after a heading the scheme prints without one. Part (C) carries no stimulus — the newspaper clipping on this question belongs to (A) and is about a construction contract — so the stem stays empty.

questionText: Explain the importance for Ireland of any one of the following policies of the European Union: Common Agricultural Policy, EU Social Policy, EU Competition Policy.

rows.verbatim: Promotes a fair standard of living for farmers: The Common Agricultural Policy gives grants farmers under the single payment scheme. The EU makes these payments to farmers to help the viability of the farm business and to enhance food, safety and environmental standards. // Free trade/No barriers or restrictions EU farmers are allowed to sell their produce to other EU member states without any barriers or restrictions. This allows Irish farmers to export to a large market. // Improved Produce The CAP gives EU farmers grants to spend on improving their land and animals. questionText: Describe three types of official industrial action.
stem: Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. Firefighters to escalate industrial action. (Adapted from RTE News August 2023)

rows.verbatim: Any three of the following types of official industrial action

options: Official Strike: Employees refuse to enter the workplace or perform their work duties. An official strike involves a secret ballot, proper notification to the employer and sanction by ICTU. The union members on strike hold a picket outside the workplace.
Work - to- rule: Employees only undertake the exact jobs written in their job description/contract of employment. Workers follow the rules of their employment contracts to the ‘letter of the law’.

Overtime ban: Employees refuse to work extra hours. This can cause major disruption, leading to lost orders and lost sales, especially at peak trading times e.g. the employees in an airline refuse to do overtime during the holiday period.

Token Stoppage: A brief stoppage of work by the workers to highlight their frustration over an issue. This highlights the intention to carry the threat of further, more serious action if agreement is not reached.
Go Slow: Employees complete their duties but minimise productivity. This is designed to frustrate their employer.

questionText: Explain, using examples, the following three principles of insurance; Utmost Good Faith Indemnity Insurable Interest
stem: Insurance premiums in Ireland continue to rise.

rows.verbatim: Utmost good faith: A person must reveal all material facts when applying for insurance and be truthful in their application for insurance. Proposal forms must be completed accurately.
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints "Example required" under this principle, so the question's using examples is marked, not optional — an explanation with no example cannot reach the full 5m(2+3).

rows.verbatim: Indemnity: An insured person cannot make a profit from an insurance claim i.e. insurance can at best put an insured person in the same financial position as they were prior to a loss occurring. If a car is written off in an accident the insured receives its replacement value and not the original sum paid for it.
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints "Example required" under this principle. The written-off car is the scheme's own worked example of putting the insured back in the same financial position.

rows.verbatim: Insurable Interest: The insured must gain from the existence of the exposure unit and suffer from its loss. You can insure your own car but not your neighbours. In essence you can't insure something unless you have a vested interest in it.
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints "Example required" under this principle. Your own car against your neighbour's is the scheme's own worked example of a vested interest.

notes: Scheme p.52, paper p.8. The question names all three principles, so none of them is a choice — this is a fixed tariff of three rows at 5m(2+3), summing to the 15 of part (C)'s 20 marks that the Max Mark summary leaves to (i). Each row carries the principle and the whole explanation printed under it, because the 3 in (2+3) is paid for that explanation. Example required is printed under each principle and is carried on the row as a context note rather than as answer content, since it states a requirement rather than a marking point. openList true: the front matter states the support notes are a sample of possible responses, so a candidate's own accurate wording of the same principle scored. Stem is the boxed line the paper prints immediately above part (C). No figure: the box is plain text and carries no image.

The scheme closes the list with "Accept relevant explained example.", so any other policy type scored provided the reason was explained.

options: House/Home insurance: For house insurance if the applicant lives on a flood plain the insurance company might deem the policy an uninsurable risk.
Motor insurance: if they have previous driving disqualifications the applicant might be deemed to great a risk.

notes: Scheme p.52, paper p.8. The Max Mark summary prints 5m(2+3) against (C)(ii), the remaining 5 of part (C)'s 20 marks. The question asks for one type of policy and the scheme prints two worked examples, so one anyN row with claimMax 1 — two rows of 5 would display 10 marks on a 5-mark part. Motor insurance is quoted as printed, including the scheme's own 'to great a risk'. Stem is the boxed line the paper prints above part (C). No figure.

questionText: Explain the term batch production.
stem: 4TH ARQ is an Irish clothing brand that produce unisex everyday streetwear. 4TH ARQ offer a range of clothing including tops, bottoms, jackets and fleeces. Their popular half-zip fleeces are available in a range of colours.

rows.verbatim: A certain amount or limited quantity of identical goods is produced at the same time and then production switches to a different batch or group. Work is completed on each stage of the production before a new batch is started. e.g. in a bakery, a batch of loaves followed by a batch of scones.
rows.contextNote: 5m (2+3): two marks for the opening statement and three for developing it. The scheme prints the block continuously and does not say which sentence carries the 2 and which the 3, so treat the whole point as required for five — a limited quantity of identical goods made at the same time, production then switching to a different batch or group, and work completed on each stage before a new batch is started. The question asks only to explain the term, so the bakery example illustrates the answer rather than being a separately demanded element.

notes: Paper p.9 (PDF p.49), scheme p.53. topicId corrected from business-5-13 (6.1 Categories of Industry, Unit 6 Domestic Environment) to business-4-15 (5.2 Getting Started in Business, Unit 5 Business in Action): batch production is a method of production, not a sector of industry. The paper heads Q7 "Managing/Business in Action" and the scheme heads it "Business in Action", and the deck already files the 2025 OL methods-of-production question (bus-2025-ol-s1-q6) under business-4-15. The Max Mark cell prints 5m(2+3) against (i) and 3@5m(2+2+1) against (ii), which together make part (A)'s 20 — carding the whole of (A) as one 20-mark card would put a discuss tariff against a definition. One row, because the scheme prints one continuous block here and does not label which sentence carries the 2 and which the 3; the example is quoted inside the same row because it is printed inside the same answer, not as a separate marking point. openList true: the front matter states model answers "are not intended to be exhaustive" and that "Variations and alternatives may also be acceptable." No figure: the only image on the page is the 4TH ARQ wordmark inside the stimulus box (opened and checked — black lettering on white, no data), and no figure was published for this page; nothing the question depends on is carried by it.

questionText: Discuss the implications for 4th ARQ of changing from batch production to mass production process.
stem: 4TH ARQ is an Irish clothing brand that produce unisex everyday streetwear. 4TH ARQ offer a range of clothing including tops, bottoms, jackets and fleeces. Their popular half-zip fleeces are available in a range of colours.

rows.verbatim: Any three of these implications for 4th ARQ of changing from batch production to mass production
rows.contextNote: Each implication is worth 5m (2+2+1), so naming it earns only the opening 2 — the rest is paid for discussing what the switch would actually do to 4th ARQ. The command word is discuss, so an implication listed as a heading with nothing worked out under it stops at two of the five.

options: Economies of scale: The change to mass production will increase the economies of scale achieved. By reducing the cost of producing each unit this will increase profits.
Capital required for machinery: Mass production is heavily automated and may require investment in machinery, equipment and a premises.
Wages/Type of employee: The move to mass production might increase the number or factory operatives that the business needs. OR wages may decrease as less employees are required due to automation
Access to finance: Additional sources of long-term finance might be required.
Stock Control: An efficient stock control system will be required if changing to mass production.
Marketing Plan: a revised marketing plan might be required if switching to mass production

notes: Paper p.9 (PDF p.49), scheme p.53. TOPIC CORRECTED from business-5-13 (6.1 Categories of Industry) to business-4-15 (5.2 Getting Started in Business). This is a production-method question and three independent sources put it in Unit 5 Business in Action: the paper heads the question 'Question 7 — Managing/Business in Action', the scheme's own contents page for Question 7 is headed 'Business in Action', and the repo's Paper Trail tagger already records 2024 HL Q7 as primary business-4-15 with secondary business-5-14 (which is where sibling card q7b's ownership contrast correctly sits). Categories of Industry is primary/secondary/tertiary sectors, not job/batch/mass production; curriculum.ts places production under Unit 5's 'Finance, Ownership, Production'. Tariff: the Max Mark cell prints 3@5m(2+2+1), so three implications are marked out of the six the scheme lists — one anyN row with claimMax 3, not six rows, which would show 30 marks on a 15-mark part and would also breach the five-row cap. Each option carries the scheme's heading joined to the sentence printed under it, because the heading alone is only the first 2 of the 5; an option reading only Stock Control would let a student who wrote two words award themselves the discussion marks. The headings keep the scheme's colon rather than a dash: the session splits a row's verbatim on ' — ' and keeps only the tail when it names the marks a student left behind, and here the heading is itself a scored element. Wages/Type of employee keeps the examiner's OR branch inside the one option, because the scheme prints both directions of the wage effect as alternatives within a single implication, and it keeps the scheme's own 'the number or factory operatives' typo rather than silently correcting it. openList true: the front matter states model answers are not intended to be exhaustive and that variations and alternatives may also be acceptable, so a relevant implication the scheme did not print was still considered on its merits. No figure: the page's only image is the 4TH ARQ wordmark inside the stimulus box, which the question does not depend on, and no p49 figure was published for this paper. All six options were re-checked verbatim against the build's provenance gate and all six are found in the 2024 HL scheme.

questionText: Contrast a Sole Trader and a Private Limited Company as forms of business ownership, using the following headings: Formation, Liability, Finance, Control.
stem: 4TH ARQ is an Irish clothing brand that produce unisex everyday streetwear. 4TH ARQ offer a range of clothing including tops, bottoms, jackets and fleeces. Their popular half-zip fleeces are available in a range of colours.

rows.verbatim: Formation — You must register as a self-employed person with Revenue. If you want to use a business name, you must register your business name with the Companies Registration Office (CRO). Whereas a limited company -, you must register with the Companies Registration Office (CRO), your company must then return reports and accounts to the CRO each year. Register your business name and file your company returns online using the CRO’s CORE (Companies Online Registration Environment). Under the Companies Act 2014, private companies limited by shares can be registered as either: An LTD (private company limited by shares) or a DAC (Designated Activity Company)
rows.contextNote: 5m (2+3) for this heading. The question word is Contrast, and the scheme's answer runs both ways under it: how a sole trader registers, then how a limited company registers and keeps filing with the CRO. One side written on its own is half the heading answered.

rows.verbatim: Liability — In a sole trader ownership structure the owner has unlimited liability whereas the shareholders of a limited company have limited liability.
rows.contextNote: 5m (2+3) for this heading. What is printed here is a single sentence, and it is the whole answer the scheme gives: unlimited liability for the sole trader set against limited liability for the company's shareholders. There is no further sentence to find under this heading — write both sides of that contrast and it is answered.

rows.verbatim: Finance — Limited companies can have more than one owner and therefore find it easier to raise capital whereas a sole trader has only one owner to provide equity capital. The Sole trader might also find it more difficult to access credit.
rows.contextNote: 5m (2+3) for this heading. The scheme's sentence carries its own reason inside it — more than one owner to supply equity capital — rather than stopping at the claim that a company finds capital easier to raise, and it prints a second line on the sole trader's difficulty accessing credit.

rows.verbatim: Control — The Sole trader has full control over decision making whereas in a limited company control is based on the percentage of share ownership. The shareholders appoint a board of directors who appoint a Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer to run the business.
rows.contextNote: 5m (2+3) for this heading. The contrast is full control against control based on the percentage of share ownership, and the scheme prints a second sentence beneath it: shareholders appoint a board of directors, who appoint a Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer to run the business.

notes: Paper p.9 (PDF p.49), scheme p.54. The Max Mark cell prints 4@5m (2+3) — four stated headings, all four named in the question, so this is a fixed tariff of four rows of 5, not a best-of choice: a candidate cannot substitute a fifth heading of their own. Four rows sits inside the five-row cap. Each row is the scheme's own printed label (Formation; Liability; Finance; Control) as the cue, then everything the scheme prints beneath that label, quoted whole and unbroken. The four headings are not printed at equal length — Formation runs to four sentences, Liability to one — and the card no longer pads the short one: an earlier version of the Liability row told the student the development was 'what each actually means for the owner's personal assets if the business cannot pay its debts', wording that appears nowhere in this scheme (searched across the whole file, no hit for personal assets, personal possessions or debts of the business), so a student who had written the scheme's own sentence was being told they had missed the 3. All four contextNotes now describe only what is printed and no longer assert where inside the 2+3 the examiner placed the marks. The paper says Private Limited Company and the scheme abbreviates it to Limited company; the question text follows the paper. openList true: the front matter (line 30) states these are not intended to be exhaustive and that variations and alternatives may also be acceptable — that is the route by which an extra elaboration such as personal assets would be credited if a student wrote it, not something the printed answer demands. No figure: the only image on the page is the 4TH ARQ wordmark in the stimulus box, no figure was published for PDF p.49, and this part is generic — it never mentions 4TH ARQ, so the stem leaks nothing about ownership forms.

questionText: Explain any three of the following financial business terms: Liquidity; Profit and Loss Account; Debtors; Dividends.
stem: 4TH ARQ is an Irish clothing brand that produce unisex everyday streetwear. 4TH ARQ offer a range of clothing including tops, bottoms, jackets and fleeces. Their popular half-zip fleeces are available in a range of colours. The Companies Act 2014 requires directors of all companies to present a profit and loss account and a balance sheet annually.

rows.verbatim: Any three of these four financial business terms explained
rows.contextNote: Each term is worth 5m (2+3), so a one-line definition that stops at the first idea is short of the full five — the development is the second sentence the scheme prints. Explaining all four does not earn more; only three are marked.

options: Liquidity refers to the ability of a business to pay its short-term liabilities as they fall due.
Profit and Loss account records the sales less all the costs and expenses of the organisation for the financial year. It identifies the Gross and Net profit of the organisation.
Debtors are individuals or businesses that owe the business money after buying goods or services on credit.

Dividend is the portion of profits paid to shareholders at the end of the year. Dividends are decided and announced at the AGM annually. The board of directors will establish the company’s dividend policy.

notes: Paper p.9 (PDF p.49), scheme p.55. The Max Mark cell prints 3@5m(2+3) against (i) and 5m(2+3) against (ii), which together make part (C)'s 20. One anyN row with claimMax 3 of the four terms, because the paper prints four bullets and marks three. openList is false here — the only card in this question where it is — because the four terms are named in the question itself, so there is no fifth term a candidate could have explained and been paid for; a differently worded but correct explanation of one of the four is still claimed against that term's option. Each option carries the scheme's whole explanation, including the AGM and dividend-policy sentences under Dividend, because that is where the 3 of the (2+3) is paid. Stem carries the question's opening stimulus and then the Companies Act box printed above part (C), in the order the candidate reads them. No figure: the page's only image is the 4TH ARQ wordmark.

questionText: Outline one financial ratio used to measure the profitability of a business.
stem: 4TH ARQ is an Irish clothing brand that produce unisex everyday streetwear. 4TH ARQ offer a range of clothing including tops, bottoms, jackets and fleeces. Their popular half-zip fleeces are available in a range of colours. The Companies Act 2014 requires directors of all companies to present a profit and loss account and a balance sheet annually.

rows.verbatim: Any one of these financial ratios used to measure profitability
rows.contextNote: 5m (2+3). Naming the ratio earns the 2; the 3 is for outlining what it actually tells you about the business, so a bare name or a formula on its own does not reach five. Only one ratio is marked, so a second one written out earns nothing. A liquidity ratio such as the current ratio answers a different question — the ask is profitability.

options: The Gross Profit percentage: The percentage of sales that is profit before expenses are deducted. It can be used to assess the profitability of manufacturing activities. It can also be used to value stock if it is damaged by fire or accident.

The Net Profit percentage: The percentage of sales that is profit after expenses have been deducted. It assesses overall profitability. It helps investors assess if a business is generating enough profit from its sales. IF there is a large difference between gross and net profit margin, it could suggest that expenses are too high.

The Return on Capital Employed: Return on capital employed is a financial ratio that measures a company's profitability in terms of all of its capital. It shows the percentage return on each €1 invested. Investors often compare the ROI to the rate offered in deposit accounts. This allows them to see if they are getting a worthwhile return on their investment.

notes: Paper p.9 (PDF p.49), scheme p.55. The Max Mark cell prints 5m(2+3) against (ii), so only one ratio is marked while the scheme prints three — one anyN row with claimMax 1, not three rows, which would show 15 marks on a 5-mark part. Each option is the scheme's ratio name joined to everything printed under it, because the outline is what the 3 pays for. openList true: the front matter states model answers are not intended to be exhaustive and that variations and alternatives may also be acceptable, so a candidate who outlined another profitability ratio scored on its merits. Stem carries the question's opening stimulus and then the Companies Act box printed above part (C), in reading order. No figure: the page's only image is the 4TH ARQ wordmark.

questionText: Explain the term premium pricing.

rows.verbatim: Premium pricing refers to a business charging a high price to create the image of superior quality. Premium pricing can create an image of prestige for a product and can influence demand.
rows.contextNote: 5m(2+3). Stating that the business charges a high price is only the first element; the marks that follow are paid for developing it — the image of superior quality and prestige it builds, and the effect on demand. The scheme prints both sentences as one answer and never says which half takes the 2, so a bare one-line definition is short of the full five.

notes: Scheme p.56; paper p.10 (PDF p.50). REPAIR: the previous version split this into rows of 2 and 3 and asserted which sentence carried which half. The scheme prints ⟨5m(2+3)⟩ once, on the question line, against a single continuous two-sentence block, and never labels the halves — so the split was invented. Now one row worth the whole five, quoted across the line wraps exactly as printed, which is how q2bi, q2ci and q7ai in this same batch already model 5m(2+3). openList true per the scheme's front matter (model answers "are not intended to be exhaustive" and "variations and alternatives may also be acceptable"). No figure: the part (A) stimulus box holds three decorative brand marks (Rolex wordmark, Adare Manor wordmark, a photograph of Prime bottles); the sentence beneath names all three businesses, so the question can be asked without them, and none is in the published figure list for this paper. questionText: Outline the factors businesses may consider before deciding on a price for their product or service. Provide examples to support your answer.
stem: Rolex watches, Adare Manor Hotel and Golf Resort and Prime Hydration Drinks are examples of businesses who use premium pricing.

rows.verbatim: Any three of the following factors

options: Cost of production / research & development: A business must consider the cost of manufacturing each item before deciding on the price of each item. E.g. If a drink costs €1 to manufacture, the business will decide on a percentage to add the cost price.

The target market – Businesses must consider the group of people that each product is aimed at. E.g. Newspapers such as The Daily Mail and The Irish Times would consider the income levels of their target market before deciding on a price point to enter the market. Prime might have products especially aimed at young people who want to feel like they are drinking the best energy drink on the market.

Competition: A business must consider the prices of their competitors’ products. E.g. Prime must decide whether to charge the same, a higher or a lower price than her competitors such as Gatorade, Monster etc.

Economic conditions/demand – higher prices can be charged in a booming economy. Businesses such as hotels etc may decide to charge a higher price for her products if the economy continues to grow or alternatively the business might lower prices during a period of economic recession.

rows.contextNote: Each factor is worth 5m(2+2+1): the factor, the sentence outlining it, and the example. The scheme adds that it will also "Accept points that are fully explained with an example relevant to" demand in the marketplace, consumer expectations/image of product, taxation (tariffs, import charges), product positioning, stage of product life cycle, legal restrictions, and target market — but only where the point is fully explained with an example, so a bare heading scores nothing.

notes: Three factors wanted and four printed with a full outline and an example each, so this is best-three-of-four at 5 marks apiece. Every option carries the factor, the sentence that outlines it and the E.g., because the 2+1 of each (2+2+1) is paid for exactly those. The scheme's seven extra bullets are named in the contextNote rather than offered as options: they are bare headings with no outline attached, and as claimable options they would hand a student the outline and example marks for three words.

questionText: Distinguish between generic advertising and persuasive advertising.
stem: The ASAI published fresh guidance for Irish influencers on the clear labelling of ads on social media. For the avoidance of confusion, all commercial content should now be labelled #Ad (or #Fógra for Irish‐language posts). October 2023

rows.verbatim: Generic advertising is used to prompt the consumer to think about a type of product rather than a specific brand. E.g. The National Dairy Council encouraging the consumption of milk.

Persuasive advertising: This advertising attempts to entice the consumer that they need the product. Persuasive advertising attempts to convey the message that this product/service will bring value to the consumers life. E.g. L’Oréal try to persuade the consumer they will have healthier/more attractive hair as a result of using their products.

notes: A distinguish, so both sides are required and neither is optional: 5m(2+3) for generic and 5m(2+3) for persuasive. The E.g. stays inside each row because the 3 of each (2+3) is paid for developing the point, and the scheme develops both with a named example.

The scheme does not label the halves, but the question asks for a medium and then a reason, so the first 3 of each pays for the medium and the rest for the reason — naming a medium and stopping loses about half of that answer. questionText: Describe different sales promotions techniques that a business could use to promote a new or existing product. Use examples to support your answer.

rows.verbatim: Any three of the following sales promotion techniques

options: Price reduction/discounts; Retailers could offer 20% reduction on slow trade days or to sell stock that will be out of season soon. E.G Retailers such as Woodies, Elevery’s having a 20 or 30% sale for Black Friday or after Christmas.

Buy one get one free/Special Offers/2 for price of 1 Businesses could offer buy one get one free on a wide variety of products to incentivise sales. E.G. A special offer of buy one get one free on Dove Deodorants could incentivise customers who weren’t planning on purchasing deodorant.

Discount codes/Money off coupon for next purchase – Retailers could offer vouchers which reduce the cost of the customers next purchase. Vouchers are received in the post or with newspapers or are offered as a reward for previous purchases. E.g. Nike.com sending a customer a 10% off your next purchase email discount code. Dunnes Stores offering €10 off when you spend €50.
Loyalty Cards – loyalty card can be used to encourage repeat sales. E.g. retailers such as Centra could offer a free coffee for every five coffees purchased.

Competitions – retailers could run competitions to win prizes via social media. e.g. Vodafone running a competition to win two tickets to an Ireland rugby match or Allianz running a competition to win tickets to the All-Ireland Final.

Free Samples Free samples of a product can expose the consumer to the product and encourage the consumer to buy the product. E.g. A crisp company giving samples of a new flavour crisps to consumers as they do their groceries.
Merchandising A business will display goods in a more attractive way to incentivise purchases. E.g. some protein bars may be sold in special stands close to checkouts in a supermarket

rows.contextNote: Each technique is worth 5m(2+2+1): the technique, the description of how it works, and the example. The question asks you to "Describe" and to "Use examples to support your answer", so a list of technique names on its own cannot reach 15.

notes: Three techniques wanted and seven printed, so best-three-of-seven at 5 marks each. Every option carries the technique, the sentence describing how it works and the E.g., because a technique named on its own earns only the first 2 of its 5. Seven options is inside the eight-option cap, and the scheme prints exactly seven. The row's verbatim is a neutral lead-in: the seven headings are already the options, and the session never renders an anyN row's verbatim, so repeating them there put unsourced text in the deck (and truncated "Buy one get one free/Special Offers/2 for price of 1") for no reader.

questionText: Illustrate your understanding of the following essential elements of a valid contract: Consideration, Capacity to Contract, Consent to Contract, Legality of form.
stem: Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

rows.verbatim: Consideration — This refers to the legal exchange of value in a contract. Each party in a contract must give something of value to the other party. So long as consideration exists, a court of law will not question its adequacy, provided it is of some value.
rows.contextNote: The scheme closes this element with one more sentence: "Consideration is usually some monetary payment, but it could also be something valuable exchanged as part of the contract." Money is the usual form, but anything of value counts, and the court will not ask whether the deal was a good one — only that something of value passed each way. "Example required." is printed after this element as it is after the other three, so an explanation with no illustration does not reach the 5.

rows.verbatim: Capacity to contract — All natural persons (human beings) and legal/corporate persons, such as companies, have the legal right /able to /ability to enter freely into a contract. Example required.
rows.contextNote: Capacity is not only about people — the scheme names legal/corporate persons such as companies alongside natural persons, and the entry has to be free. The example at the end is not decoration: it is what the +1 or +2 of the 5 pays for, so a definition on its own is short.

rows.verbatim: Consent to contract — Both parties must enter the contract on their own free will. They must agree to the contract without undue influence. If there is no choice, there is no consent. Consent must be honest and voluntary. Example required.
rows.contextNote: Free will is the whole point — agreement given under undue influence, or where a party had no choice, is not consent at all. Honest and voluntary are the scheme's own test words, and the illustration is still required on top of the explanation.

rows.verbatim: Legality of form — Certain contracts, to be considered legal, must be drawn up in a particular manner. Some contracts must be in writing if they are to be legally valid. Example required.
rows.contextNote: This element is about how a contract is drawn up, not about what it contains; the scheme's own instance is that some contracts must be in writing if they are to be legally valid. The example is required here too, so naming the rule without illustrating it leaves marks behind.

notes:
Paper p.43 (Section 3, Part 1, Question 1 'People in Business'); scheme p.25. Four named elements for 20m. The Max Mark cell prints 4@5 with the splits (4+1),(4+1),(3+2),(3+2), so every element is worth exactly 5 and the tariff is fixed at 5 a row, not an ordered split. In the printed scheme those three cells sit stacked at the TOP of the block (y=189/204/219 in the Marks column) while the four elements begin at y=189, 321, 409 and 497 — they summarise how the 5 divides between explanation and example across the four answers, not which element gets which. Which two elements take the (4+1) and which the (3+2) is therefore not stated by the examiner and is not invented here.

The four terms are supplied by the question, so each is a cue and sits before the dash; the marking point the student self-marks is the explanation after it, development included. questionText: Explain, using examples, the different types of industrial action.
stem: Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

rows.verbatim: Any four types of industrial action, each named, explained and illustrated with an example
rows.contextNote: Official Strike: the scheme's sentence ends "Employees refuse to enter the workplace or perform their work duties.", and it credits two further points, "An official strike involves a secret ballot, proper notification to the employer and sanction by ICTU." and "The union members on strike hold a picket outside the workplace." Tick that option if you gave any of them. Under all five types the scheme prints "Example required.", so a type named and explained but not illustrated stops short of the full 5.

options: Official Strike. Employees refuse to enter the workplace or perform their work…
Work-to-rule. Employees only undertake the exact jobs written in their job description/contract of employment. Workers follow the rules of their employment contracts to the ‘letter of the law’

Overtime ban. Employees refuse to work extra hours. This can cause major disruption, leading to lost orders and lost sales, especially at peak trading times e.g. the employees in an airline refuse to do overtime during the holiday period.

Go Slow. In a manufacturing business, one section of the workforce takes longer than normal to complete their part of the production process, thus delaying overall production.

REVIEWER FINDING CONFIRMED AT SOURCE, and it is caused by a defect in the converted scheme which I did NOT edit: the marks-column labels 'Name,', 'Explain,' and 'Example' are still embedded at the ends of three consecutive lines inside the Official Strike block, and nowhere else on that page (…perform their work [Name,] duties. [Example] The union members…). schemeText.mjs strips marks cells, page markers and bracketed part labels, but not a column label sitting at a line end, so the longest contiguous run there is 'Official Strike. Employees refuse to enter the workplace or perform their work'. Verified by running comparableScheme over the real file: restoring 'duties.' SessionScreen renders one contextNote under the whole anyN group and no per-option note exists, so scoping it in its first two words is the only channel available. STRUCTURE KEPT: five plain rows under bestNofParts would give each type its own note, but suggestGrade counts claimed rows against rows.length for non-fixed tariffs, so a student who answered four types correctly (full marks) would be graded 'shaky'; and the anyN group is what caps the claim at four so nobody banks 5x5=25 on a 20-mark question. questionText: Define discrimination as set out in the Employment Equality Act 1998/2015.

rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 8+4 against this one definition. notes: Paper p.43; scheme p.27. REPAIRED: the definition was split across two rows and row 2 rendered as a dangling lower-case fragment with no subject. It is now one row quoted whole, worth 12. questionText: Illustrate your understanding of the following types of business organisations. Partnership   Sole Trader   Franchise   Public Limited Company

rows.verbatim: Partnership — A partnership is a form of business where two or more people share ownership and responsibility for a company. Business partners receive profits and are liable for debts based on the terms of a partnership agreement.
accepts: Each partner is jointly responsible for running the business, and each partner must pay income tax, PRSI and USC on their share of the profits. If the business fails, all partners are jointly responsible for the debt. Your partnership agreement should be drawn up by a solicitor.
rows.contextNote: 5m. "Example required." — the Marks column splits the four fives (4+1),(4+1),(3+2),(3+2), so the explanation is worth at most four and an answer that names no actual partnership cannot take the whole five. Two or more people sharing ownership is the first element; the profits and the liability for debts are the development.

rows.verbatim: Sole Trader — A sole trader is a business that is owned and run by one person who is fully responsible for the debts of the business. The sole trader makes all the decisions/has complete control, keeps all the profits but is fully liable for any business debt.
rows.contextNote: 5m. "Example required." — one person owning and running it is the first element only; complete control, keeping all the profits and full liability for any business debt are the development the second half of the (4+1)/(3+2) pays for.

rows.verbatim: Franchise — A franchise is a type of business where a business owner(franchisor) grants permission to an individual( franchisee) to use the businesses owners business model. The franchisor allows the franchisee use their full business model, sell their goods and services under the franchise name in exchange for a fee and a percentage of profits.
rows.contextNote: 5m. "Example required." — permission to use the business model is the first element; selling under the franchise name in exchange for a fee and a percentage of profits is the development, and a named franchise is what the last of the five pays for.

rows.verbatim: Public Limited Company — A Public Limited Company (PLC) is a company that is publicly listed on the Stock Exchange. This is done so that the company can offer its shares out to the general public. A PLC must have a minimum of seven members but there is no maximum number of shareholders
rows.contextNote: 5m. "Example required." — listed on the Stock Exchange is the first element; why it lists (so it can offer shares to the general public) and the minimum of seven members with no maximum are the development.

notes:
Scheme p.28. The Marks column prints "4@5" with "(4+1),(4+1),(3+2),(3+2)" and "Explain, Example"; the summary table on scheme p.8 repeats it against Q2(A). The paper names all four organisation types, so all four are required and each is worth five: a fixed tariff of 4 x 5 = 20, not a best-of. Four rows, inside the five-row cap, so this stays one card.
