questionText: Discuss the benefits and challenges of increasing employment for Irish businesses.
stem: Recent Central Statistics Office figures show the country's unemployment rate stood at just 4.1% in November 2024 - signalling an economy which remains at full employment. Adapted from cso.ie

rows.verbatim: Benefits of increasing employment for Irish businesses
rows.contextNote: The benefits half. Two are required and each is worth 5 — 2 for naming the benefit, 3 for explaining it — so a benefit written as a heading with nothing worked out under it stops at 2 of the 5. The scheme's own heading for the first option is “Increase sales”; that heading could not be carried into the option text, so tick that option if increased sales was one of your two.

options: High employment leads to an increase in consumption and this has led to increased sales of everyday goods and services

Increase spending on premium products and services and price increases for consumers: As people have more discretionary income, people will spend more on luxury items leading to e.g. more new cars, foreign holidays being purchased. The Society of the Irish Motor Industry (SIMI ) official statistics show that new car registrations increase during periods of high employment

Business confidence/growth of enterprise: The demand for goods and services has increased and new businesses open or expand due to increased business profits. There is more enterprise in the economy as people’s self-esteem and confidence increases.

Increased sales/profits caused by increased government spending: The government has increased revenue from employment and consumption taxes. This could lead to an increase in capital expenditure which creates new opportunities for business, resulting in increased sales and profits.

Limits the brain drain: There will be more Government finance to invest in the Irish economy. High employment rates can minimise emigration levels and the ‘Brain drain’ (Exporting of skilled labour) should reverse. This means more access to skilled labour for the business. The business can also benefit from government spending facilitated by the increased tax take.

rows.verbatim: Challenges of increasing employment for Irish businesses
rows.contextNote: The challenges half. Two are required and each is worth 5 — 2 for naming the challenge, 3 for explaining it. The examiner marks two on each side, so four benefits and no challenge reaches 10 at most, no matter how well the four are written.

options: Shortage of staff: Shortage of the availability of the type of staff employers need. The overall employment numbers in tertiary sector have increased but the number of people employed in the services industry continues to grow. However, many businesses in the services industry are struggling to recruit staff

Price increases: High employment can lead to an increased demand on services. Discretionary services such as hospitality can experience a surge in demand and prices can rise. Hotel prices in Ireland increasing and or the demand for tradespeople outweighing the supply of tradespeople available.
High costs/wage demands/pay increases: High employment leads to a labour market where employees can seek pay increases more readily. This can increase employer costs and reduce profitability.

notes:
Paper p.4 (PDF p.44), scheme pp.29-30, summary table scheme p.8. The Marks cell prints 4@5(2+3) with "2 benefits and 2 challenges required" beside it; the p.8 summary adds "Name, Explain". Two pick-lists rather than one, because the scheme requires two from each side — a single any-four list would let a student claim four benefits and print a full 20 for half the question the paper asked (the paper bolds the "and" in "benefits and challenges").

TARIFF CHANGED, bestNofParts -> fixed. Not part of the reviewer's finding, but the old model was wrong twice over. The paper sets ONE question requiring four answers, two from each half; the eight items on the scheme page are sample responses, not parts of the paper, so "best 4 of 8" is not a convention the SEC printed here. And bestNofParts broke the card in the session: showsRowMarks is true only for `fixed` (SessionScreen.tsx:166), so the card rendered no mark chips and no mark-loss total; suggestGrade then fell through to counting CLAIMED rows, and anyN rows are scored from `picks` and never claimed, so a student who ticked all four was still graded "missed"; and the footer printed "Answer any 4 of these 8 — 5 marks each", which is exactly the licence to write four benefits that the two-row split exists to deny. Two groups of claimMax 2 at 5 reconcile to the printed 20. Same question shape and same model as bus-2025-hl-s3-q7a on this paper.

"Limits the brain drain" STAYS IN BENEFITS. This is a deliberate judgement against the page layout, so here is the evidence rather than an assertion. Scheme p.30 (PDF page index 29) reprints only "Question / Possible Responses / Marks", "2 (B)" and the same 4@5(2+3) cell — no section heading at all — so the point sits under nothing, and the reviewer is right that it follows a challenge. Its content is unambiguously a benefit for business: "This means more access to skilled labour for the business. The business can also benefit from government spending facilitated by the increased tax take." The typography agrees. Every heading on both pages is bold Calibri 12 at x=132, so weight and indent give no cue, but the vertical gaps do: on p.29 each item is separated from the next by 29pt, the "Challenges" heading itself included (516 -> 545 -> 574); on p.30 the gap from "and reduce profitability." (y=134) to "Limits the brain drain" (y=178) is 44pt — one whole blank line more than any other break on either page, a section break whose heading was not reprinted after the page turn. Filing it under Challenges would do two things a card must never do: tell a student who correctly wrote it as a benefit that they answered the wrong half, costing 5 marks they earned; and hand 5 marks to a student who ticked it as a challenge, which no examiner would credit.

EXTRACTION DEFECT — the reviewer's second finding, and it cannot be fixed from inside the card. Restore the heading into the option once the extraction separates the support-note column. Same defect, same paper and same handling as bus-2025-hl-s3-q7a's fourth advantage. THE SCHEME FILE WAS NOT EDITED.

questionText: Outline how the Irish government could create a positive climate for business. Use examples to support your answer.
stem: Hospitality, tourism and retail firms hold Dublin protest. Adapted from rte.ie

rows.verbatim: Tick the four you outlined
rows.contextNote: Example required. The Marks column asks for Name, Explain, Example and splits each five as 2+2+1, so the last mark of every five is the example.

options: To improve competitiveness for the tourism industry and other industries the government could reduce VAT.

National minimum wage increases: The government sets the minimum wage to protect workers on low pay. e.g. To create a suitable climate for businesses the government could minimise minimum wage increases to ensure that businesses costs are sustainable and businesses remain viable.

Government Grants: The government could offer financial supports and or low interest businesses supports loans to facilitate expansion. e.g. The government could increase the number of grants available via state agencies.
Increase capital expenditure: The government could increase capital expenditure on infrastructure, schools, hospitals etc.
Through a network of state agencies that give business advice, training and guidance, mentoring services and grant aid to facilitate growth and expansion.
Government investments in Education and Training: The government invests in 3rd level education for all students in Ireland exempt of tuition fees ensures a steady supply of highly skilled labour.

Taxation: By creating a low tax environment for business, entrepreneurs are encouraged to establish business as they can retain most of the gains they make. Low corporation tax ensures that the limited companies retain most of their profits.

notes:
Scheme pp.31-32. The Marks column prints '4@5(2+2+1)' with 'Name, Explain, Example' on both pages, and the summary table on scheme p.8 repeats it. Four answers of five each from a longer sample list, so bestNofParts: 4 x 5 = 20, one pick-list capped at four.

Seven of the scheme's eight sample points are carried. The eighth, 'Increased current expenditure on public sector wages/social welfare', is not, for the reason set out below: the only spans of it that survive intact are the bare heading and mid-sentence fragments. A bare heading is exactly the failure this deck guards against - it would let a student who wrote four words award themselves the explanation marks - so the point is left out rather than gutted, and openList true keeps it claimable by a student who made it.

What constrains the wording of two options. Measured off the scheme PDF (business-2025-HL-marking-scheme.pdf, pages 31 and 32), the Possible Responses prose sets at x=131.3 and the Marks column at x=486-549. On those two pages the Marks cell is not a number but three words - 'Name,' at x=500.3, 'Explain,' at x=497.3, 'Example' at x=495.6 - printed against the first three lines of the first point on each page. The converter brackets a Marks cell only when it is numeric, so '4@5(2+2+1)' was lifted out but those three words were run into the ends of the prose lines they sit beside. In the converted scheme the VAT point therefore reads '...E.g. Reduce Name, / VAT for the tourism/services industry. This would allow the Explain, / business to charge lower prices and or increase profitability thus Example / enabling businesses to offer better rates of pay.' The scheme file is evidence and was not touched.

So the VAT point cannot be quoted from its heading through its development without either carrying three words of the Marks column into the student's answer or skipping them, which the provenance check reads as wording the scheme does not contain. Of the spans that do survive whole, the fullest is the SEC's own restatement of the point two lines further down - 'To improve competitiveness for the tourism industry and other industries the government could reduce VAT.' - and that is what the option carries. It is a complete printed sentence and it holds both halves of the five: the measure (reduce VAT) and why it helps (competitiveness, tourism and other industries). The heading plus first sentence, 'Reduce Value Added Tax: The government could reduce VAT on good and service', would also have survived, but it only restates its own heading, so a student who wrote three words could claim the two explanation marks off it. Carried once, not as two options, because both are the same point and two options would let one idea claim ten marks. Lost either way: 'This would allow the business to charge lower prices and or increase profitability thus enabling businesses to offer better rates of pay.'

The state-agencies option carries the development sentence alone - 'Through a network of state agencies that give business advice, training and guidance, mentoring services and grant aid to facilitate growth and expansion.' questionText: Describe, with examples the difference between a directive and a regulation as forms of law in the European Union (EU).

rows.verbatim: EU Directive — They are used to bring different national laws into line with each other and are common in matters affecting the operation of the Single Market (e.g. product safety standards, WEEE (Waste, electrical, and electronic equipment directive, Health and Safety at work directive or the common charger directive.)
accepts: It obliges member states to change their national laws to allow for EU rules, within a certain time limit. It is binding only as to the results to be achieved, leaving member states to choose, within prescribed limits, the means by which the rules and targets are to be attained.
rows.contextNote: 7m (4+3): the feature of a directive earns 4 and the example earns 3, and the scheme prints "Example required" underneath, so a description with no named directive stops at four.

It takes precedence over national law. It is self-executing and does not require any implementing measures. EU institutions can enforce a regulation throughout the EU. Regulation (EU) No.261/2004 established common rules on compensation and assistance to airline passengers.
rows.contextNote: 7m (4+3): the feature earns 4 and the example earns 3. "Example required" is printed here too — the airline compensation regulation is the scheme's own illustration, not the only one accepted.

questionText: Outline the global marketing mix for a product of your choice.

Different tariffs, customs duties and VAT rates. Local price levels and prices charged by competitors in the market/exchange rate fluctuations.
rows.contextNote: 5m (2+2+1). "Reference to product of choice required" — one of the listed factors, tied to your own product, is enough.

Examples of the various channels available include: Selling directly to customers on line. When selling goods or services globally the business channel of distribution might have more layers e.g. a distribution agent.
rows.contextNote: 5m (2+2+1). "Reference to product of choice required" — the extra layer has to be one your own product would actually travel through.

rows.verbatim: Global Promotion — Differences in legislation, language and culture need to be recognised in the choice of promotion such as advertising and publicity campaigns. The language of television advertisements may have to be amended in different countries due to language barriers or the message could be considered offensive in some countries.
rows.contextNote: 5m (2+2+1). "Reference to product of choice required" — say what would have to change in the campaign for your own product.

questionText: Illustrate the following barriers to free trade that can exist between countries. Embargo   Quota   Subsidy   Tariff
stem: The goal of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) is to ensure that trade flows as smoothly and freely as possible. Adapted from wto.org

rows.verbatim: Embargo — Embargo is a total ban on the import of certain goods from certain countries. They are normally motivated by political, economic, moral or environmental reasons. They may be used as a form of protest against another country’s practices.
rows.contextNote: The Max Mark cell reads 4@5 with the splits (4+1), (4+1), (3+2), (3+2) beside the column labels "Explain," and "Example" — every barrier is worth exactly 5, divided between the explanation and an illustration. The examiner does not say which two barriers take the (4+1) and which take the (3+2), and it is not guessed here. "Example required." is printed under all four, so no barrier reaches its full 5 on a definition alone.

rows.verbatim: Quota — A quota is a limit on the number of items that can be imported from a certain country/of a certain product.
rows.contextNote: "Example required." — the definition is the explanation; naming a real quota is what the remaining mark or two is for, whichever of the scheme's splits this barrier fell under.

rows.verbatim: Subsidy — A subsidy is financial support given by the government to a domestic industry to reduce the cost of production so it can sell its products at lower prices than competition from imports/given directly to firms to encourage production.
rows.contextNote: "Example required." The scheme prints two routes either side of its slash: financial support that reduces the cost of production so the firm can undercut imports, or money given directly to firms to encourage production.

rows.verbatim: Tariff — A tariff is a tax on an import. The effect of the tax is to raise the price of the import and discourage consumption.
rows.contextNote: "Example required." The scheme's answer does not stop at "a tax on an import" — it goes on to what the tax does, raise the price of the import and discourage consumption. Both sentences are printed as the response, and the illustration is needed on top of them.

questionText: Explain, using an example, the grounds for dismissal that are deemed to be fair under the terms of the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977/2015.
stem: A tech firm that admitted unfairly dismissing its Irish founder has been ordered to pay him a record €464,000 awards package by the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC). Adapted from the Irish Times

rows.verbatim: Any four grounds on which a dismissal is deemed fair under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977/2015
rows.contextNote: Each ground is worth 5: 2 for naming the ground, 2 for explaining it and 1 for the example. Four grounds named as bare headings stop at 8 of the 20, and four grounds explained with no illustration stop at 16. The command word is Explain, using an example, so the example is a mark every time.

options: Incapability: This includes issues such as persistent lateness, and absenteeism

Incompetence refers to inability to do the job (poor work performance/failure to meet sales targets). In the first place, employees need to be made aware of the standards that are expected of them and these must refer to the job they were hired to do. Secondly, if they fall short of the required standard, this must be clearly explained to them. This should be done through a formal set of procedure. The employer should also specify what improvements are necessary. These should be achievable, and a reasonable timeframe must be allowed for the improvement. Ultimately, the employer should give the employee a final warning setting out the likelihood of dismissal.

Qualifications (misrepresentation by the employee): Fair dismissal on grounds of qualifications can happen in two ways. One situation is where the employer is misled about qualifications the employee had when applying for the job. The other is where the employer made continued employment conditional upon your obtaining further qualifications and the employee failed to achieve this, having been given a reasonable opportunity to do so.
Minor incidents, when taken together, constitute misconduct and are enough to warrant dismissal, although the employer is obliged to give notice or pay in lieu of notice in this type of situation.

Redundancy: The job no longer exists due to closure, competition, decline in demand) In this case your employer needs to show that a redundancy situation exists as your job is no longer required and therefore the dismissal is fair. This means that there is an economic justification for the redundancy; that you will not been replaced. Fair procedures must be applied (e.g. last in and first out).

Legal reasons/ Contravening the law: Your employer may dismiss you if your continued employment would contravene the law. The employee cannot continue to work without breaking the law and dismissal may be deemed fair. However, the employer might be expected to look at alternatives depending on all the facts of the case.

notes:
Paper p.6 (PDF p.46), scheme pp.37-38. The Max Mark cell prints 4@5(2+2+1) Ground, Explain, Example against (B) and the scheme prints SIX grounds — Incapability, Incompetence, Qualifications, Misconduct, Redundancy and Legal reasons — so four are marked out of six: bestNofParts, one anyN row with claimMax 4, not six rows, which would show 30 marks on a 20-mark part and breach the five-row cap.

It reports an UNFAIR dismissal and an award against the employer, which is the contrast the part is set against; it names none of the six fair grounds, so it gives no marking point away. Checking the other four, two of them were short as well: Incompetence stopped after “hired to do” and Legal reasons after “may be deemed fair”. Every ground on this card is now quoted whole except the two below.

The scheme prints Ground, / Explain, / Example down the right-hand Marks column beside the first three prose lines of the first ground on each of pp.37 and 38. extract-scheme.py decides a Marks-column cell by whether it contains a DIGIT (is_mark / MARK_CELL), so a word-only cell is never lifted into ⟨brackets⟩; render_row then emits it as the last body cell of the row it shares a y-band with, dropping those three words into the middle of the SEC's sentences. questionText: Explain the term a competitive relationship.

rows.verbatim: A competitive relationship exists where two or more parties work against each other to achieve a mutually exclusive goal.
rows.contextNote: Mutually exclusive is what makes the relationship competitive rather than merely busy: both parties want the same thing and only one of them can have it.

rows.verbatim: It is a win-lose situation; one party gains at the expense of the other.

questionText: Discuss the factors to consider when choosing an effective communication medium.
stem: Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. "The single biggest problem in communication is the illusion that it has taken place." — George Bernard Shaw

rows.verbatim: Factors to consider when choosing a communication medium
rows.contextNote: Each factor is marked Name (2) + Explain (3). Other relevant factors: Legal requirements; Availability of technology etc Communication Skills of the Receiver /ability to respond/information overload.

options: Appropriate Language/Clarity: If the language is too technical or too difficult for the customers to understand then the message may be misinterpreted. The business needs to choose language appropriate to its audience. In the case of customers, short clear sentences and visual supports etc. may be suitable for product assembly e.g. flat packs.

Confidentiality/Safety: The medium chosen must be appropriate to the message been given. If the message is sensitive for the stakeholder e.g. terminating the employment contract of an employee, then a meeting would be more appropriate than a letter or an e-mail.

Cost: The expense of the communication process is a very important factor. A CEO communicating with his managers worldwide may choose to hold a virtual meeting to cut down on travel and subsistence costs.
Urgency/Speed/Destination: If a crucial piece of information has to be communicated instantly to a supplier, then a phone call, a text or e-mail may be appropriate

Feedback/Accuracy/Record: The business may be looking for feedback in order to take further action. questionText: Discuss the strategies used to manage change in a business.

rows.verbatim: Any four strategies for managing change, named and explained

options: Training and Development • Staff must be provided with the skills needed for the use of new technologies so as to achieve efficiencies and provide a better service to its customers. • Training increases staff’s ability to cope and eases staff’s fears about new changes. Teamwork • When employees are arranged into teams it can lead to discussion, innovation and change. Teamwork increases staff’s familiarity to change. • This can ease reluctance to changes that management introduce.

Rewards • By providing rewards to employees, behaviour can be influenced as they try to achieve those awards. Rewards may include a profit-sharing scheme, so employees are encouraged to work as they will achieve a portion of those profits.

Communicate with staff about the changes. • Management should explain the need for the changes and the consequences of not taking any action to ensure the survival of the firm. Consultation with staff • Management can be seen to seek staff input regarding the changes. Staff are allowed give their opinions about the change. This eases reluctance as staff start to shape the changes. As a result, staff are more likely to be open to changes suggested by management.

Facilitator approach to management Helping employees perform the tasks rather than controlling the task. This may be achieved a democratic or theory Y approach to management. As a result, staff are more likely to be open to changes suggested by management.
Lead by example
Resource Provider
TQM/Empowerment

options: Economies of Scale: The larger business benefits from discounts from suppliers due to bulk buying. This reduces business costs.
New Products: The combined resources of the firms may result in faster development of new products. This can increase a firm’s sales and profits.

rows.verbatim: Disadvantages of an acquisition (takeover) as a method of business expansion

Industrial Relations: Some staff may be unhappy with the takeover and possible redundancies. This can increase the likelihood of industrial relations conflict at the firm.

notes:

The session does not render an anyN row's verbatim, so which half a group is has to live in its contextNote, and it does.

Each option carries the scheme's heading joined to the sentence printed under it, because the heading alone is only the opening 2 of the 5 — an option reading “Economies of Scale” would let a student who wrote three words claim the discussion marks.

questionText: Illustrate four stages, apart from launch, that Glanbia may use for developing a new product.
stem: Glanbia acquired The Optimum Nutrition brand in 2008. This was part of a shift in focus towards consumer nutrition products.

rows.verbatim: Stages, apart from launch, that Glanbia may use for developing a new product
rows.contextNote: Every stage is 5 — 2 for naming it, 2 for explaining it, and 1 for a reference or example to Glanbia. The scheme prints “Reference/Example to Glanbia required.” under all six stages, Idea Generation included, so four stages named and explained with no Glanbia reference anywhere stops at 16 of the 20. Launch itself is ruled out by the question. The Idea Generation option reads short only because the rest of that stage could not be quoted with it: the scheme finishes it “It may come from internal or external sources. An idea may come from brain-storming.” Either of those is the explaining the second 2 pays for.

options: Idea Generation: Initial ideas for the new product are created.

Product Screening: The ideas are vetted/sorted and the impractical and unworkable ideas are eliminated, leaving the most likely one for further examination and development. Reference/Example to Glanbia required.

Concept Development: This involves turning the idea into an actual product or service that will appeal to customers. This stage involves identifying features for the idea. A unique selling point (USP) is identified which will distinguish it from other products. Reference/Example to Glanbia required.

Feasibility Study: This is carried out to assess if a product is viable. It looks at whether it can be produced technically and will it be profitable. It answers question like: What demand is there? What will it cost etc? Reference/Example to Glanbia required.

Prototype Development: This is a sample or working model of a product. It is produced to see if a product can be made and what materials are required to make it. It can be used to test the product to see what improvements can be made. Reference/Example to Glanbia required Reference.
Test Marketing: The product is tested on a sample of consumers before going into full production. Reference/Example to Glanbia required Reference.

notes:

The stem repeats the box's text so the card still reads if the image does not load. Unlettered, so it rides on a question card with an empty labelKey rather than a diagram card.

Idea Generation quoted short — checked against the source and it cannot be fixed in the card. In the SEC PDF (2025-marking-scheme.pdf p.47) the Marks column's words "Name," "Explain," "Reference/" "Example" are printed as a block at the FOOT of the column, well clear of the answer text; the whole Idea Generation point reads continuously as "Initial ideas for the new product are created. questionText: Discuss how Anthem Transport Ltd could use different medium-term sources of finance for their medium-term needs.
stem: Anthem Transport Ltd is a large courier business with operations in Ireland. They purchased a small regional courier which has an aging fleet and outdated I.T. system.

rows.verbatim: Hire Purchase: Is a medium source of finance that involves a three party agreement
rows.contextNote: 3 of Hire Purchase's 6 — the marks the scheme prints "Source" against in the Marks column. Naming hire purchase and saying it is a three-party agreement is what these 3 buy. The other 3 are for how the agreement actually works, on the next row.

rows.verbatim: Hire Purchase — pay the retailer for the asset, the buyer gets the asset immediately and repays the finance company in regular instalments. Interest is included and a deposit and final payment are required. The buyer does not legally own the asset until the final instalment is paid.
rows.contextNote: The other 3, printed against "Explain" in the Marks column; the subject of "pay" is the finance company. Ownership passing only on the final instalment is what separates hire purchase from a term loan, and it is where the explanation marks are usually left behind.

rows.verbatim: Medium term loan: This is a medium source of finance that involves a financial institution providing capital to a borrower. The borrower repays the capital with interest over 1-5 years in regular repayments.
rows.contextNote: 6 — 3 for naming the source, 3 for explaining it. The 1-5 year term is the load-bearing detail: it is what makes this a medium-term source rather than the overdraft or the mortgage a candidate might reach for, and the question asks only about medium-term finance.

rows.verbatim: Leasing: Through leasing, the business acquires, but does not necessarily purchase, fixed assets over the medium term. This is a form of hiring whereby a contract is agreed between a leasing company (the lessor) and the business (the lessee). The lessee pays rental income to hire assets from the lessor.
rows.contextNote: 6 — 3 for naming the source, 3 for explaining it. The distinction the marks are paid for is that leasing acquires the use of an asset without buying it: the lessor keeps ownership and the lessee pays to hire. An answer that describes leasing as buying in instalments has described hire purchase instead.

rows.verbatim: Each of the following medium term needs

options: Aging fleet
Outdated IT system

rows.contextNote: These are Anthem's medium-term needs, not sources — the scheme heads them "Medium term needs:" and ticks each for 1 mark, separately from the three sources. The question says "for their medium-term needs", so both have to be lifted from the information supplied; three sources explained in the abstract leave these 2 marks behind. The scheme prints "Outdated IT system"; the paper writes it "outdated I.T. system".

notes:
Paper p.9 (PDF p.49), scheme p.48. Tariff is fixed as printed: the Marks cell shows 3@6(3+3) against the three sources and a separate 2@1m against "Medium term needs:". 3 x 6 + 2 x 1 = 20, matching the (20) on the paper. Not a best-of — the scheme names exactly three sources for three answers.

REPAIR — the reviewer was right. Hire Purchase used to stop at "a three party agreement" with the rest of the SEC's explanation parked in a contextNote, so the 6-mark row a student self-marks named none of the three parties and none of the mechanism. It is now two rows carrying the SEC's own (3+3): r-1 the source half, r-2 the explanation.

WHY TWO ROWS RATHER THAN ONE WHOLE QUOTE. The scheme .md cannot be quoted continuously across this point, and the SEC's own PDF says why. On marking-scheme p.48 the answer prose sits at x=131-483 and the Marks column at x=498-549; "Source," (y=150) and "Explain" (y=164) are Marks-column annotations printed against the first two lines of the answer, not words of the answer. extract-scheme.py only lifts a marks cell into angle brackets when is_mark() matches, and is_mark requires a numeric mark, so these two descriptive cells were emitted into the body — landing inside the SEC's sentence at scheme lines 1485-1486: "...a three party agreement Source, between a retailer, finance company and a buyer. The finance company Explain pay the retailer...". comparableScheme() strips angle-bracket marks, page markers, marks-only lines and part labels, but nothing removes a descriptive cell at a line end, so no quote can cross either splice. THE SCHEME WAS NOT EDITED. The defect is in extract-scheme.py's is_mark; the fix is to bracket non-numeric Marks-column cells too and regenerate. About forty lines in this one scheme end in such a descriptor ("Name,", "Explain", "Reference", "Method,"), so it will keep costing marking points until the extractor is fixed.

The seam is the SEC's own 3/3 boundary, not an arbitrary cut: "Source," is printed against the line r-1 quotes and "Explain" against what follows it. The thirteen words stranded between the two splices — "between a retailer, finance company and a buyer. The finance company" — cost the card no marking content, because r-2 names the retailer, the buyer and the finance company itself.

r-1 takes no dash: the naming marks live in the words "Hire Purchase", and the app strips everything before a dash in the marks-left-behind list, which would delete them. r-2 does take one, because there the source name is only a cue saying which source the explanation belongs to — the 3 marks are for the explanation after it, which is what the gate checks and what the left-behind list shows. Medium term loan and Leasing are quotable whole, so they stay one 6-mark row each with the (3+3) explained in their contextNotes; splitting them too would need seven rows.

The two needs are one anyN row at 2 x 1m rather than two 1-mark rows only because the 5-row cap is now spent on the Hire Purchase split. anyN keeps them independently claimable — a candidate who named only the aging fleet still ticks 1 — which an allOf row would have made all-or-nothing. The anyN header does not render the row's verbatim, so the "Medium term needs" framing is carried in its contextNote instead.

The stem does contain the two 1-mark answers. That is unavoidable and correct: the paper prints the Anthem box inside part (C), and the marks are for selecting the right two details out of the stimulus, so a card without it could not ask the question at all — no candidate could know Anthem's needs otherwise.

No figure: the Anthem box is plain text in the paper, and the only crops published for PDF p.49 are the Glanbia stimulus and its table, which belong to (B). openList true — the scheme's front matter states that model answers "are not intended to be exhaustive. Variations and alternatives may also be acceptable."

Verified against the gates in scripts/markbank/build-deck.mjs and test/markBankDeck.test.ts: all six claims trace to the 2025 HL scheme, rows sum to 20, 5 rows within MAX_ROWS, group worth within tariff, no content-free row.

'collection/range' stays intact inside row 1: that solidus is alternative wording of ONE element, not a second element, which is why the split falls after 'offers' rather than at the slash. questionText: Illustrate the different methods of market segmentation used by businesses such as Proctor and Gamble.
stem: Proctor and Gamble’s (P&G) brands include Pampers, Ariel, Gillette and Head & Shoulders.

rows.verbatim: Two methods of market segmentation, each named and explained

The Demographic list in the scheme runs one item further than it does here, ending 'age, gender, family size, income, occupation.', and it carries a second point: 'For mass marketing demographic is one of the best ways as everyone has an age, gender and income.'

options: Demographic segmentation: Analyses consumers according to age, gender, family size, income

Geographic segmentation: Analyses consumers according to location county/region/country etc. By using segments such as urban versus rural, north versus south, sea coasts versus interior, warm areas versus cold, the business can design a marketing strategy to satisfy the chosen target markets.
Psychological: Analyses consumers according to social status, lifestyle and personality type. Attitudes- concerns around production. Lifestyles – health conscious
Behavioural: Analyses consumer according to their knowledge of and attitude toward the use of the product, impulse buying/value for money (special prices), gift packs of him/her.

notes:
Scheme p.49 (page index 48 of examiner-reports/business/2025-marking-scheme.pdf). The Marks column prints ONE bracket, 2@7(2+3+2), against a block listing FOUR methods, so this is best two of four at 7: one anyN row, bestNofParts, 2 x 7 = 14, which with (A)(i)'s 6(3+3) makes the 20 the paper prints against part (A). Each option carries the method name (the 2) joined by a colon to the scheme's own explanation of it (the 3), because the scheme prints the name as a heading and the explanation as bullets beneath it. The remaining 2 is the Reference, the candidate's own example, which the scheme demands ('Example Required.') under all four methods but never prints, so it is stated in the row's contextNote rather than invented into an option. openList true: the scheme's front matter says the support notes 'are neither exclusive nor complete' and are 'a sample of possible responses'.

REVIEWER FINDING UPHELD, AND THE HALF OF IT THAT CAN BE FIXED IS FIXED. Explain,' / '...as everyone Reference'. questionText: Describe the reasons why a business conducts market research.
stem: Proctor and Gamble’s (P&G) brands include Pampers, Ariel, Gillette and Head & Shoulders.

rows.verbatim: Three reasons why a business conducts market research, each named and described
rows.contextNote: Each reason is worth 5, split (3+2) — the reason named earns 3 and the sentence developing it earns the other 2, so a heading written on its own stops at three of the five. The scheme's summary page prints "Name, Explain" beside the 3@5(3+2). Its support notes are "a sample of possible responses", so another genuine reason, explained, scores as well.

options: Indicates the size of the market: Market research indicates the size of the market and the number of potential customers. Research will show whether the market is increasing, decreasing or stagnant.
Reduces risks and can reduce costs: Market research identifies the potentials challenges a business will face and allows plans to be put in place about how to overcome obstacles.
Identifies competitors: Market research identifies who are a business’s competitors in a market and what their competitive advantage is.

Tests consumer reaction: Market research can help a business to ascertain what consumers want in a product and their views on prototypes or product ideas. This allows a business to get feedback on product packaging, branding, pricing, the features of the product or service.
Predicts sales: Market research can estimate the likely level of sales for a product and therefore estimate the level of production required.

notes: Scheme p.50; summary p.11 reads 3@5(3+2) with 'Name, Explain'. Five reasons printed and three claimable, so one anyN row with five options, bestNofParts 3 x 5 = 15. Every option keeps the reason heading (the 3) together with the paragraph developing it (the 2) — an option reading only 'Identifies competitors' would let three words claim the description marks. Headings are joined to their paragraphs with a colon; the scheme prints them on separate lines and this region of the scheme is free of the support-notes column, so each option is quoted whole. openList true per the scheme's front matter ('not intended to be exhaustive. Variations and alternatives may also be acceptable'). questionText: Explain, using examples, the following provision of the Sale of Goods and Supply of Services Act, 1980: If a consumer purchases a faulty product who is responsible?

rows.contextNote: Four of the six, and naming the retailer is only the start of them — the reason is that the contract exists between the retailer and the consumer, which is why the shop cannot send you to the manufacturer. An answer that stops at the one word has not earned the four.

'replacement/refund' keeps its single solidus — the SEC uses it for alternative wordings of ONE point, so splitting it would invent a mark. questionText: Outline two forms of remedy/redress that consumers are entitled to if any provisions of the Sale of Goods and Supply of Services Act, 1980 are broken.

Each option keeps whatever development the scheme printed with it (the wages bullet keeps 'They negotiate with the employers and government in seeking general pay rises'; the advice bullet keeps its clause after the dash) because Describe is marked (4 + 4) / (4 + 3) and the second figure is paid for the description. The list is quoted at seven options, which is inside the eight-option cap. openList true per the front matter — a candidate who wrote that a union negotiates on redundancy or represents a member at a disciplinary hearing was not wrong. Stem is the paper's second stimulus box, the Newstalk headline printed immediately above parts (D) and (E); the CONSUMER LAW panel belongs to (A)-(C) and is not repeated here. No figure: the headline box is one line of text with no image in it.

questionText: Explain the process employees must engage in to hold an ‘official strike’, as set out in the Industrial Relations Act, 1990.
stem: People in Business. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. 'Unofficial strike causes severe disruption to bus services in Limerick' — Newstalk, Oct 2020

rows.verbatim: The first stage of the process you explained: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints four stages of the process but only two mark cells, 8m (4 + 4) for the first answer and 7m (4 + 3) for the second. Four of the eight are for naming the stage and four for explaining it.

options: A secret ballot of union members must take place.
If strike action is voted in favour, the ICTU must approve the strike action.
One weeks’ notice must be given to the employer in advance of strike action.

The employees are allowed to picket outside their own employer’s premises (primary picketing) and/or outside another premises if the other business is frustrating their strike action (secondary picketing).

rows.verbatim: The second stage of the process you explained: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The second answer is priced 7m (4 + 3), and it has to be a different stage from the one above. The 8 and the 7 attach to the order you wrote in, not to particular stages, so writing all four stages cannot score more than 15 — but it does protect you if one of them is wrong.

options: A secret ballot of union members must take place.
If strike action is voted in favour, the ICTU must approve the strike action.
One weeks’ notice must be given to the employer in advance of strike action.

The employees are allowed to picket outside their own employer’s premises (primary picketing) and/or outside another premises if the other business is frustrating their strike action (secondary picketing).

notes: Section 2 Q1(E), scheme p.7 (marking-scheme PDF p.9). 15m over four bulleted stages with exactly two mark cells beside them, 8m (4 + 4) level with the ICTU bullet and 7m (4 + 3) level with the picketing bullet — two cells for four bullets, so they price answer positions and the tariff is an ordered split with marks null on every row. One anyN per answer, each carrying all four stages, following bus-2021-ol-s1-q9. The picketing option is quoted whole, primary and secondary together, because the scheme prints it as one bullet joined by 'and/or' — a single solidus in an SEC scheme separates alternative wordings of one point, so splitting it would invent a mark. openList true per the front matter: a candidate who wrote that the union must ballot all members entitled to vote, or that no strike may be held while a collective agreement is being honoured, has written something an examiner could reward. The stem is the Newstalk headline box printed above parts (D) and (E). It says UNOFFICIAL strike, which is the contrast the question turns on and gives away none of the four stages, so it is kept in full. No figure: the box holds one line of text and its source line, no image.

questionText: Explain the term franchise as a form of business ownership.
stem: Janet and Michael O'Donnell are considering using a franchise method to expand their business. They operate an artisan burger bar, where all food is made freshly by Michael every day.

rows.verbatim: A franchise is an agreement between an original company (franchisor) and a new business (franchisee) which allows/licences the franchisee to use the name, logo, products, and business idea of the franchisor in return for a fee and an annual percentage of sales/profits.
rows.contextNote: The 10 marks are paid 4 + 3 + 3, so the definition has to run past the word 'agreement': the franchisor/franchisee relationship, what the franchisee is licensed to use, and what is paid back for it are three separate earners.

notes: Scheme p.8 (converted scheme lines 278-282). One definition worth the whole 10, and the marks column prints 4 + 3 + 3 against it, so the tariff is fixed with a single row rather than an ordered split. The row is quoted whole across the four printed lines; the ⟨4 + 3 + 3⟩ cell sits at the end of the second line but does not interrupt the sentence. openList true per the scheme's front matter ('The expected responses presented are not exclusive. Marks may be awarded for any other correct answers'), so a correctly worded definition of the student's own scores. Stem: the paper's franchise stimulus box, trimmed to the two sentences the part is set against; its third sentence ('The business thrived during the last year and they can see potential in franchising the idea') carries no information the part needs. Checked for leakage: the stimulus names franchising but gives none of franchisor, franchisee, licence, fee or percentage of sales, which are what the 4 + 3 + 3 pays for. No figure: the only image on paper p.3 is a decorative plate-and-cutlery clipart. Verified against scripts/markbank/schemeText.mjs — every row traces to the 2021 OL scheme.

questionText: Name two other businesses in Ireland which operate as franchises.
stem: Janet and Michael O'Donnell are considering using a franchise method to expand their business.

rows.verbatim: Any two of the following businesses
rows.contextNote: The scheme closes the list with 'Any other acceptable answer (SuperValu etc. are not franchises).' So a genuine Irish franchise it did not print still scores, but a symbol group or voluntary group such as SuperValu does not.

options: McDonalds
Supermacs
Burger King
KFC
Eason
Subway

notes: Scheme p.8 (converted scheme lines 283-290). Six businesses are listed and the candidate names two, so this is bestNofParts with one anyN row rather than six rows of 5. The two ⟨5⟩ cells land level with Supermacs and KFC only because a marks cell is centred against the block it governs; the scheme is not saying those two are the scoring ones, so every option is priced at 5. openList true: the scheme prints 'Any other acceptable answer' immediately under the list, and that sentence is carried in the context note because it also names the exclusion the examiner warns about. Stem cut back to the one sentence that makes 'other' mean anything: the paper's next sentence calls the business an artisan burger bar, and with two burger chains among the six options that is a nudge the part does not need. questionText: Outline one advantage and one disadvantage for Janet and Michael if they decide to franchise out their business.
stem: Janet and Michael O'Donnell operate an artisan burger bar, where all food is made freshly by Michael every day.

rows.verbatim: Any one of the following advantages
rows.contextNote: The advantage is the 8-mark half of this question, paid 4 + 4: four for the advantage and four for developing it, which is why each option carries its explanation and not just its heading.

options: Quick method of expansion as franchisees from all over the country may wish to get involved.
Capital/Finance provided by the franchisee for new outlet.
New revenue stream as the brand name or logo becomes more established.

rows.verbatim: Any one of the following disadvantages
rows.contextNote: The disadvantage is the 7-mark half, paid 4 + 3: four for the disadvantage and three for developing it.

options: Damage to brand if franchise fails.
Janet and Michael will have to fund all the promotion and advertising/marketing.
USP could be lost if franchise grows too big.

notes: Scheme p.8 (converted scheme lines 291-303). The marks column prints 15m against the part, then 8m (4 + 4) centred on the three advantages and 7m (4 + 3) centred on the three disadvantages, so the two halves are unequal and each is a one-from-three menu: two capped anyN rows, 1 x 8 and 1 x 7, which reconcile to 15. A single group cannot express it, because 15 does not divide in two. openList true on both per the front matter. Stem trimmed on purpose: the paper's stimulus opens 'considering using a franchise method to expand their business', and the first advantage on the scheme is 'Quick method of expansion', so the sentence carrying the word expand is dropped and only the burger-bar sentence kept. The part's own wording already tells the student they are franchising out. No figure. topicId business-4-18 (5.5 Business expansion) rather than the ownership topic used for (A) and (B), because every marking point here (expansion, franchisee capital, new revenue stream, brand damage, promotion costs, USP) is about franchising as a method of growing the business.

questionText: Name the sector of the economy in which the hospitality and tourism industries operate.

rows.verbatim: Tertiary (also known as Services sector)
accepts: Services sector
rows.contextNote: Naming it either way scores the full 5, because the scheme prints the two names as one answer.

notes: Scheme p.9 (converted scheme lines 308-310). The 25m cell covers the whole of part (D); the ⟨5⟩ sits against the tertiary line, so (i) is worth 5 and (ii) the remaining 20. One right answer, named two ways by the scheme itself, so kind alt with 'Services sector' as the printed alternative, and openList false because no other sector earns it. No figure.

questionText: Explain the other two sectors of the economy and give one example of an industry in each sector.
stem: Part (ii) of a two-part question: part (i) asked you to name the sector of the economy in which the hospitality and tourism industries operate.

rows.verbatim: Primary Sector: Also known as the Extractive industries, it involves extracting raw materials from natural resources. It includes Farming, Fishing, Forestry and Mining.
rows.contextNote: The scheme prices this block 4 + 4 + 2 and notes in the marks column that the 2m is for the example, so the explanation carries 8 of the primary sector's 10, paid 4 + 4. Naming the sector is not enough: extracting raw materials from natural resources and the industries the sector covers are both earning.

rows.verbatim: Any one of the following businesses involved in the primary sector
rows.contextNote: The marks column note that the 2m is for the example fixes 2 of the primary sector's 10 marks on naming one. Any correct primary-sector business or industry scores, not only the three the scheme prints.

options: Bord na Mona
Bord Gáis
Coillte

rows.verbatim: Secondary Sector: This covers the manufacturing, construction, and agribusiness industries. Raw materials from the primary sector are turned into finished products.
rows.contextNote: The second 4 + 4 + 2 block, read the same way: 8 of the secondary sector's 10 for the explanation, paid 4 + 4. The industries the sector covers and what happens to the primary sector's raw materials are both earning.

rows.verbatim: Any one of the following businesses involved in the secondary sector
rows.contextNote: The other 2m for the example. Any correct secondary-sector business or industry scores, not only the four the scheme prints.

options: Glanbia
Kerry Group
Sisk
Boston Scientific

notes: STEM REPAIRED. The old stem, 'In part (i) the hospitality and tourism industries were placed in the tertiary (services) sector, so the other two sectors are the ones this part is asking about', is printed nowhere on the paper and handed over the entire 5-mark answer to sibling card bus-2021-ol-s2-q2di before that card is ever asked. Verified against paper Section 2 p.3 (PDF p.39): Question 2 (Domestic Environment) prints a franchise box above (A)-(C) and a 'Hospitality industry welcomes the reduction of VAT to 9%' clipping above (D) and (E), and nothing else. The replacement stem states only what part (i) ASKED - wording printed directly above this part, and already the questionText of the (i) card - so 'the other two' has an antecedent without a single sector being named. The VAT clipping is deliberately not carried: this part is pure recall of the three sectors and cannot be helped by it, the same reason the (i) card's stem is empty. Marks: scheme p.9 (converted scheme lines 311-324). Part (D) carries one 25m cell and the 5 sits on the Tertiary line, so (i) takes 5 and (ii) the remaining 20, printed as two 4 + 4 + 2 blocks, one against the Primary Sector block and one against the Secondary Sector block. The marks column also carries '(The 2m is for the example)', which is why each sector is split into an 8-mark explanation row and a 2-mark example row instead of one 10-mark row: a student who explained the sector but named no business can honestly record 8. The 4 + 4 inside each explanation is not attributed to particular sentences, so each explanation is quoted whole and not split further; each 'Sector:' heading stays joined to its sentence rather than being cut off behind a dash, because the sentence alone would not tell the student which sector it explains. Four rows, 8 + 2 + 8 + 2 = 20. In the converted file that marks-column note is interleaved line by line with the 'Business involved: Glanbia...' line ('(The 2m is' / 'for the' / 'example)'); it reads as one note in the printed scheme, so it is paraphrased in the context notes rather than quoted as a string. The scheme file was not edited. openList true on all four rows: the front matter states 'The expected responses presented are not exclusive. Marks may be awarded for any other correct answers', the explanations can be worded differently, and the part asks for an example of an INDUSTRY while the scheme lists businesses, so a correct primary or secondary industry that is not on the printed list still scores - this is not a closed set. No figure: the only image on the page is a decorative plate-and-cutlery doodle inside the franchise box, which belongs to (A)-(C) and carries no information.

questionText: Outline one impact the reduction in the VAT rate will have on each of the following: Tourism and hospitality industries; Government Current Income.
stem: Hospitality industry welcomes the reduction of VAT to 9%. Budget 2021 saw a decrease in the VAT rate for the hospitality and tourism industries from 13.5% to 9% until December 2021. (Adapted from the Irish Examiner.)

rows.verbatim: Impact on Tourism and Hospitality Industries
rows.contextNote: This half is worth 8, paid 5 + 3: five for the impact and three for following it through, which is why each option runs on past the first clause.

options: Reduction in prices due to lower VAT will attract more tourists and people on staycation, leading to increased income for hotels and restaurants.
Extra demand for services will help create more employment in the sector.

rows.verbatim: Impact on Government Current Income
rows.contextNote: This half is worth 7, paid 5 + 2: five for the impact on Government Current Income and two for developing it.

options: Less VAT revenue from this sector will reduce Government Current Income.
The Government will have less to spend on important areas such as health and social protection.

notes: Scheme p.9 (converted scheme lines 325-336). The part asks for one impact under each of two headings and the marks column prints 8m (5 + 3) against the tourism and hospitality block and 7m (5 + 2) against the Government Current Income block, so it is two capped one-from-two menus, 1 x 8 and 1 x 7, reconciling to 15, not a best-of-four. Each option is quoted with its development because the second number in each split pays for it. openList true on both per the front matter. Stem: the paper's VAT news box, which the part depends on entirely, because 'the reduction in the VAT rate' has no referent without it, and which gives away none of the four impacts the scheme marks. No figure: the box is set as text on paper p.3, not as an image. topicId business-5-15 (6.3 Business, government and the economy) because the marking points turn on Government Current Income and what the Government can then spend, rather than on how VAT is operated by a business.

questionText: Using the information above, calculate the Balance of Payments for Q2 2020. Show your workings.
stem: Question 3 is the International Environment question. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. The paper prints a table headed “International Accounts Q2 2020: Ireland’s economic interactions with the rest of the world”, giving Goods: Exports €56bn and Imports €23bn; Services: Exports €52bn and Imports €53bn.

rows.verbatim: Balance of Payments = Total Exports – Total Imports
Total Exports (Visible Exports + Invisible Exports) €56bn + €52bn = €108bn
rows.contextNote: The paper prints Goods and Services; the scheme adds them as Visible and Invisible Exports. These 5 are split 2 + 2 + 1, so writing the two figures down and adding them earns marks before the total is even reached.

rows.verbatim: Total Imports (Visible Imports + Invisible Imports) €23bn + €53bn = €76bn
rows.contextNote: Split 2 + 2 + 1 in the same way as the exports line.

rows.verbatim: Balance of Payments = 108bn – 76bn = €32bn

notes: The paper prints (20) against part (A) as a whole. The scheme divides that between (i) and (ii) itself — 2, (2+2+1), (2+2+1) and 4 against the four working lines of (i), and 4 against the one-word answer to (ii) — so this card carries 16 and its sibling bus-2021-ol-s2-q3aii carries 4, and together they reconcile to the paper's 20. Split into two cards because (i) and (ii) are separately lettered parts. The accounts extract is bound as the figure because it is a real data table the calculation cannot be attempted without; its four figures are repeated in the stem so the card still works while the image loads. The dashes in rows 1 and 4 are the scheme's own en dashes standing for minus, not the app's label separator (an em dash or a spaced hyphen), so nothing is stripped from these rows on the marks-left-behind line. Validated against build-deck's own gates: provenance, tariff arithmetic (2+5+5+4 = 16), figure manifest hash.

questionText: State whether it is a surplus or a deficit.
stem: Question 3 is the International Environment question. The paper prints a table headed “International Accounts Q2 2020: Ireland’s economic interactions with the rest of the world”, giving Goods: Exports €56bn and Imports €23bn; Services: Exports €52bn and Imports €53bn. Part (i) asked you to calculate the Balance of Payments for Q2 2020 from those figures. Part (ii) asks what that answer is.

rows.verbatim: Surplus
rows.contextNote: This follows from part (i): the scheme's totals are €108bn of exports against €76bn of imports, so €32bn more came in than went out and the balance is a surplus rather than a deficit. Four marks for the one word, which is why it is worth writing down rather than leaving the examiner to infer it from the calculation.

notes: A one-word part, carded separately because the paper letters it (ii) and the scheme prints its own 4 against it inside part (A)'s 20. The stem repeats the accounts figures because 'it' in the question refers to the Balance of Payments calculated in part (i), and the card is unanswerable without them; it stops short of giving the €32bn away. Same figure as bus-2021-ol-s2-q3ai — build-deck permits one crop across two cards when the figureKey is identical.

questionText: Explain two reasons why international trade is important for Ireland.

rows.verbatim: Access to raw materials not available in Ireland – Irish business can access essential raw materials to produce their goods
accepts: Increased sales (exports) due to small home market – sales are limited in Ireland due to size of population
Growth and survival of Irish businesses – many businesses must export to survive
More choice for consumers – imports of foreign produced goods give wider selection to consumers
Improved quality and competitive prices for consumers – increased competition results in better quality products and fair prices
Creates employment – business growth in export markets results in increased employment
Improves Balance of Trade and Balance of Payments – increased exports of goods and services improves the Irish economy
Helps Irish business to achieve economies of scale by selling in large quantities.
rows.contextNote: The paper asks for two of these eight. The 8 and the 7 go to the first and the second reason you gave, not to particular reasons on this list, so any two of them score 8 then 7. Each is 5 for naming the reason and then 3 (2 on the second) for the words after the dash that explain it, so a reason written as a heading with nothing developing it leaves about a third of its marks behind.

notes: orderedSplit rather than fixed or bestNofParts. The scheme prints eight sample bullets with 8m (5+3) and 7m (5+2) stacked down the marks column beside the first four; the last four carry no bracket at all, which is the tell that the values belong to answer POSITIONS and not to particular bullets. bestNofParts is arithmetically impossible here — build-deck requires answer x perPart to equal totalMarks and no integer satisfies 2 x p = 15 — and an anyN group would have to print a perOption the scheme never states, so the eight bullets ride as one alt row: the first verbatim, the other seven in accepts, which SessionScreen renders as 'A or B or C …'. Same shape as the shipped bus-2021-ol-s1-q6 on this paper, for the same 8m + 7m reason. Every bullet is quoted whole, heading and development, because the development is what the +3 and +2 pay for. openList true on the scheme's own front matter ('the expected responses presented are not exclusive'). All seven accepts were separately checked against the scheme text even though build-deck does not check that field. No stem or figure: (B) sits above the Brexit box on the paper and needs no stimulus.

questionText: A tariff is used as a barrier to trade. Explain the term tariff and name one other barrier to trade.

rows.verbatim: A tariff is a tax on imported goods coming into a country from a specific country. It makes imported goods more expensive. The EU operates a free trade area where no tariffs are charged between EU member states. Tariffs are charged on goods coming into the EU from countries outside of it. Tariffs are used to encourage consumers to purchase home produced goods by making imports more expensive.
rows.contextNote: Ten marks, split 5 + 5 by the scheme: 5 for saying what a tariff is, a tax on imported goods, and 5 for developing it — that it makes imports dearer, that the EU charges none between member states but does charge them on goods from outside, and that the purpose is to push consumers towards home produced goods. A one-line definition on its own takes half.

rows.verbatim: Other barriers to trade

options: Quotas
Subsidies
Embargoes/Ban
Regulations
Import/Export Licences

rows.contextNote: The question asks for one other barrier and the scheme pays 5 for naming it — no explanation is required here, unlike the tariff. The list is a sample, so another genuine barrier to trade the scheme did not print still scores.

notes: The scheme prints the 15 as 10m (5 + 5) against the tariff explanation and a single 5 against the bulleted list of other barriers, so this is a fixed tariff of 10 + 5. The explanation is quoted whole across all five printed lines rather than trimmed to its first sentence, because the second 5 is paid for precisely the material a trimmed version would delete. The five barriers are an anyN pick-list, claimMax 1 at 5 marks each, which is what the paper asks for and what the build's arithmetic accepts (10 + 1 x 5 = 15). The row's own verbatim is the scheme's heading 'Other barriers to trade', not a restatement of the tariff, so it clears build-deck's TARIFF_PROSE check. No stem and no figure: the part is self-contained, and the Brexit box printed above it adds nothing the question cannot be attempted without.

questionText: Explain the term multinational company (MNC).

rows.verbatim: A multinational company is a business with headquarters in one country but company offices/locations in other countries throughout the world.
e.g., Google is a business who has its headquarters it the Unites States of America but also has operations and offices in other locations such as Dublin.
rows.contextNote: The second 5 is for the illustration, not for a second definition. Any real multinational named and placed the same way — headquarters in one country, offices and operations here — does the same job; the scheme's front matter says its responses are not exclusive. This is the half of an 'Explain the term' answer that Ordinary candidates most often leave out.

notes: The scheme sets (5 + 5) against a two-part answer: the definition, then an 'e.g.' worked through Google. Carded as two rows so a student who wrote only the definition sees the five marks they left behind, which is the whole point of a (5+5). Row 2 reproduces two errors in the published scheme verbatim — 'headquarters it the Unites States' should read 'headquarters in the United States' — because the row must match the scheme text the build checks it against, and files under examiner-reports/ may not be edited. Flagged here rather than silently corrected.

questionText: Outline two reasons why multinational companies might relocate to Ireland, following Brexit.
stem: Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. The paper prints: “Brexit is having a major impact on Irish business. Consumers and business are now faced with tariffs when buying and selling goods. Some multinational companies, however, are relocating to Ireland because of Brexit.”

rows.verbatim: English Speaking nation – Ireland will be the only remaining English speaking nation in the EU.
accepts: Access to EU – many MNCs currently located in the UK are there to access EU markets – this will continue if they move to Ireland.
Low Corporation Tax – Ireland’s low corporation tax rate of 12.5% is the lowest in the EU making it a more attractive location than any other member state.
Educated workforce – many MNCs will move to Ireland as we have a workforce where over 50% have obtained a third level qualification.
rows.contextNote: The paper asks for two of these four. The 8 and the 7 go to the first and the second reason you gave, not to particular reasons on this list, so any two of them score 8 then 7. Each is 5 for naming the reason and 3 (2 on the second) for the sentence developing it, so 'low corporation tax' on its own banks the 5 and drops the rest — the 12.5% rate, and why being lowest in the EU matters, are what the development marks pay for.

notes: Same shape and same reasoning as bus-2021-ol-s2-q3b: 8m (5+3) then 7m (5+2) stacked down the marks column beside a four-bullet sample list, so the values are positional and the card is an orderedSplit with no per-row marks. The four bullets ride as one alt row — the first verbatim, the other three in accepts — each quoted whole with its development, because the +3 and +2 pay for the sentence after the dash. openList true on the scheme's front matter. The Brexit box is carried in the stem because the question's 'following Brexit' rests on it; it was read as a student sees it before the reveal and gives none of the four reasons away — it says only that some multinationals are relocating, never why.

questionText: Explain two benefits to an employee of being a member of a trade union.
stem: Question 4 is headed People in Business. Above the parts the paper prints one boxed line of stimulus: 'Debenhams workers participate in a national strike outside 11 stores in Ireland' (Adapted from the Irish Examiner).

rows.verbatim: The first benefit given: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prices the first answer 8m (4 + 4): four marks for naming the benefit and four for the sentence that develops it, so a benefit named and left there stops at four.

options: The employee will have increased bargaining power as the trade union will speak on behalf of all employees in any negotiations.
Trade Unions use skilled negotiators in all dealings with employers to get the best results possible for the employees.

Job security for members is enhanced as employers will be deterred from dismissing employees without particularly good cause. They would know that the trade union would have enough power to have the employee reinstated.
Employees rights are protected – trade unions strive to ensure all members rights are protected by their employer.
Better pay – one of the main objectives of a trade union is to seek the best possible wages for all its members.
Better working conditions – the trade union tries to improve employees’ working conditions.
Negotiations on redundancy settlements – the trade union negotiates redundancy packages for employees if jobs cannot be saved.
Provides advice – the employees can contact their union for advice on all employment related issues such as legal entitlements, holidays, conditions, conflict, contracts.

rows.verbatim: The second benefit given: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The second answer is priced 7m (4 + 3): four for naming the other benefit you gave and three for developing it. The 8 and the 7 follow the order the answers are given rather than attaching to particular benefits on this list, so any two of the eight are worth 8 then 7.

options: The employee will have increased bargaining power as the trade union will speak on behalf of all employees in any negotiations.
Trade Unions use skilled negotiators in all dealings with employers to get the best results possible for the employees.

Job security for members is enhanced as employers will be deterred from dismissing employees without particularly good cause. They would know that the trade union would have enough power to have the employee reinstated.
Employees rights are protected – trade unions strive to ensure all members rights are protected by their employer.
Better pay – one of the main objectives of a trade union is to seek the best possible wages for all its members.
Better working conditions – the trade union tries to improve employees’ working conditions.
Negotiations on redundancy settlements – the trade union negotiates redundancy packages for employees if jobs cannot be saved.
Provides advice – the employees can contact their union for advice on all employment related issues such as legal entitlements, holidays, conditions, conflict, contracts.

notes: Section 2 Part 1 Question 4, paper p.5 of the Section 2 booklet; scheme QUESTION 4 part A. STEM CORRECTED: the card previously said the question 'opens with a photograph captioned Debenhams workers participate in a national strike…'. There is no photograph. Page 5 draws the Debenhams line as text inside a plain rectangle (box at y 119.6–155.6), with 'Adapted from the Irish Examiner' right-aligned beneath it, and the single embedded image on the whole page is the crèche clipart at (348, 330)–(526, 427), inside part (E)'s advertisement box. The stem now describes the printed headline box. Trimmed against the siblings: the crèche advertisement is deliberately absent, because its text is what (E) marks (female applicants only → gender discrimination; must be Irish → racial discrimination), and the headline names no trade union (B), no effect of a dispute (C) and no shop-steward function (D). The scheme prints 15m for the part and runs its mark column down one bulleted sample list: ⟨8m⟩ and ⟨(4 + 4)⟩ level with the first two bullets, ⟨7m⟩ and ⟨(4 + 3)⟩ level with the third. Those cells price the FIRST and SECOND answer given, not two particular benefits, so the tariff is an ordered split and no benefit carries marks of its own — hence one anyN menu per answer position, 1 x 8 then 1 x 7, which is the paper's 15. Collapsing the two positions into a single claimMax-2 menu would have to pick one perOption and so would state 14 or 16 on a 15-mark part; the renderer already blocks the same option being banked in both menus ('Already claimed above — one answer earns marks once'), so per-position menus do not offer one answer twice. questionText: Outline two functions, other than manpower planning, which are part of a Human Resource Manager’s job.
stem: Dunmackey House Hotel has struggled to remain open over the past year. Aideen McNally, the Human Resource Manager, had to make seven staff redundant during this time. Aideen did not like this aspect of manpower planning.

rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 5 + 5 against each of the two functions: five for naming the function and five for the description that develops it, so a function named without the detail underneath it stops at half.

options: Recruitment & Selection: A Human Resource Manager is responsible for hiring new members of staff – this involves creating a job description, person specification and job advertisement. The HR Manager then screens applicants and selects suitable candidates following an interview/aptitude test/selection process.

Training & Development: All training for new and existing staff is organised by the HR Manager. This may be done in house (on the job) or at an external location (off the job) by another agency. Development involves providing staff with additional skills which will help them in future roles.

Performance Appraisal: This is usually undertaken on an annual basis where the HR Manager reviews an employee’s performance. This will involve an interview process where the employee and HR Manager discuss goals set and achieved, training needs etc. It is also used to identify suitable candidates for promotion.

options: Utmost Good Faith: A person taking out insurance must be truthful when completing proposal form – all material facts must be declared. questionText: Name and explain two other methods of production.
stem: Cadbury bars are manufactured using mass production.

rows.verbatim: Job Production: This is the manufacture of one-off goods to order. Labour is highly skilled and intensive. Goods produced are customised to customers specifications and are more expensive. The products are of high quality. The machinery/ equipment used is expensive, leading to a high cost of production per unit. Examples: hand-crafted furniture, tailored suits, wedding dresses, cruise liners.
rows.contextNote: The course has three methods of production (job, batch and mass) and the question rules mass out, so job and batch are the two answers and there is no choice to make. The scheme prints 7m (4 + 3) beside Job Production: four for naming it and three for the explanation, so the name on its own stops at four.

rows.verbatim: Batch Production: This is the production of goods in groups or batches. A certain amount or limited quantity of identical goods is produced at the same time and then production switches to a different batch or group. The goods are produced using semi automation and skilled labour. Work is completed on each stage of the production before a new batch is started. Machinery can be adjusted to produce different products. Batch production reduces costs and has better economies of scale than job production. Batch produced products tend to be less expensive for consumers than those that are job produced. Example: in a bakery, a batch of loaves followed by a batch of scones.
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 6m (3 + 3) beside Batch Production: three for naming it and three for the explanation. Naming both methods and explaining neither leaves six of the thirteen marks behind.
