questionText: The Government assists business in Ireland in many ways. Outline two impacts, other than taxation, the Government has on Irish businesses.
stem: Section 2, Question 2 (Domestic Environment). Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. The information supplied is a boxed news panel: a photograph from a Government press conference, showing a speaker at a bank of microphones in front of a Rialtas na hÉireann / Government of Ireland backdrop, with the caption "CABINET APPROVES CHANGE TO THE IRISH CORPORATION TAX RATE" printed beneath it.

rows.verbatim: Grant aid – Government provides grant aid to businesses for start-up, expansion, R&D etc.
accepts: Infrastructure – Government provide infrastructure which allow businesses to operate efficiently e.g., transport links, communication utilities etc.
Education & Training – Government funds education and training which benefit business, who can access a skilled workforce
Regulation – Government implement legislation which regulates how business can operate e.g., Companies Act, Employment law etc.
rows.contextNote: The paper asks for two impacts, and these four are the examiner's sample. The 8 and the 7 go to the first and second impact you gave, not to particular impacts on this list, so any two of them score 8 then 7. The 8 splits 4 + 4 and the 7 splits 4 + 3, so the explanation after the heading carries nearly half the marks — "Grant aid" on its own is worth four.

notes: Repaired: the stem ended with an invented editorial sentence — "(The tax item is what \"other than taxation\" rules out.)" — that the paper never prints. Removed. The stem now reports only what page 3 of the Section 2 booklet shows above parts (A) and (B): a boxed news panel with a press-conference photograph and, beneath it, the caption "CABINET APPROVES CHANGE TO THE IRISH CORPORATION TAX RATE". The old stem also had these the wrong way round, describing the photograph as sitting under the headline; on the page the photograph is on top and the caption underneath. Trimmed against every sibling built from this stimulus: the news panel hands over no marking point on (A)(i) (which is paid for the definition plus the 12.5%/15% rates), on (A)(ii), or on the Aldi parts (C)–(E), so it is safe to keep. The Aldi panel is not described here because it is printed below part (B) and this part cannot need it. orderedSplit, not fixed and not bestNofParts: the scheme prints ⟨8m⟩ ⟨(4 + 4)⟩ and ⟨7m⟩ ⟨(4 + 3)⟩ once each, flowing down the right-hand column beside a four-bullet sample from which the candidate gives any two, so the values are positional — whoever writes Regulation first and Grant aid second scores 8 then 7 just the same. No mark stands against each bullet, so the split is not fixed per impact. An anyN group is arithmetically impossible: no integer perOption satisfies 2 x p = 15 — perOption 7 would print "Any 2 of these — 7 marks each" and understate the question by a mark, perOption 8 would offer 16 on a 15-mark question and be dropped by the build. This is the shape bus-2021-ol-s1-q6 settled on for the identical 8m + 7m tariff, and the shape parts (C), (D) and (E) of this same question use. Each impact is quoted whole, heading and explanatory clause together, because that clause is what the +4 and the +3 pay for; the en dash inside each is the scheme's own punctuation, not an added cue. "start- up" wraps across a line break in the scheme and is rejoined as "start-up". The Education & Training bullet carries no full stop in the scheme and is quoted without one. openList true: the column is headed "Possible Responses", the published front matter says model answers "are not intended to be exhaustive", and the Government affects business in ways beyond these four (state agency supports, public procurement, minimum wage), so an examiner could pay for an impact not on the list. No figureKey: no figure was published for this page of the paper, so the panel is described in the stem instead.

questionText: Outline two ways that Aldi can behave ethically towards its employees.
stem: Section 2, Question 2 (Domestic Environment). Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. Beside the Aldi logo the paper prints: "Aldi's corporate responsibility plan is driven by 5 principles: customers, suppliers, environment, employees and community." (Adapted from aldi.ie)

rows.verbatim: No discrimination in the workplace – treat all employees fairly.
accepts: Obey all employment law such as the Unfair Dismissals Act.
Provide fair wages. At least minimum wage or living wage.
Provide safe and healthy work conditions.
Provide secure job/employment contracts.
rows.contextNote: The paper asks for two of these. The 8 and the 7 go to the first and second way you gave, not to particular ways on this list, so any two of them score 8 then 7 — the 8 as 4 + 4 and the 7 as 4 + 3, with naming the way earning the first 4 and saying what it means in practice earning the rest.

notes: orderedSplit for the same reason as (B): ⟨8m⟩ ⟨(4 + 4)⟩ and ⟨7m⟩ ⟨(4 + 3)⟩ sit against a five-bullet sample the candidate picks two from, so the marks attach to answer positions and no integer perPart makes 2 x p = 15. One alt row carries all five ways, quoted whole — "No discrimination in the workplace" keeps its "treat all employees fairly" clause and "Provide fair wages" keeps its minimum-wage sentence, because those are what the second half of each split pays for. The Aldi stimulus stays in the stem: it names the five principles Aldi's plan covers, which the question itself already names ("towards its employees"), and prints none of the scheme's marking points, so a student reading it before the reveal is handed nothing. openList: the front matter says the expected responses are not exclusive.

questionText: Describe two ways that a supermarket can be environmentally responsible.
stem: Section 2, Question 2 (Domestic Environment). Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. Beside the Aldi logo the paper prints: "Aldi's corporate responsibility plan is driven by 5 principles: customers, suppliers, environment, employees and community." (Adapted from aldi.ie)

rows.verbatim: Minimise waste/safe disposal of waste – reduce packaging and use environmentally friendly packaging.
accepts: Conduct regular environmental audits.
Use eco-friendly delivery vans such as electric or hybrid cars.
Awareness – promote awareness amongst staff of the importance of being environmentally friendly.
Reduce carbon footprint by sourcing materials locally.
rows.contextNote: The paper asks for two of these. The 8 and the 7 go to the first and second way you gave, not to particular ways on this list, so any two of them score 8 then 7. The command word is "describe", and the 4 + 4 and 4 + 3 splits are why: half the marks are for the detail after the heading.

notes: orderedSplit: ⟨8m⟩ ⟨(4 + 4)⟩ and ⟨7m⟩ ⟨(4 + 3)⟩ against a five-bullet sample from which two are given, so the values are positional and 2 x p = 15 has no integer solution for a best-of or anyN model. One alt row holds all five ways, each quoted whole — "Minimise waste/safe disposal of waste" keeps the packaging clause and "Awareness" keeps the sentence that explains it, since a bare heading would let a student claim the development marks for three words. Two of the scheme's bullets ("Conduct regular environmental audits.", "Reduce carbon footprint by sourcing materials locally.") are printed without a development clause; they are quoted exactly as they stand and nothing has been added. openList: the front matter says the expected responses are not exclusive.

questionText: Explain two benefits to a local community of a new business such as Aldi setting up in the area.
stem: Section 2, Question 2 (Domestic Environment). Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. Beside the Aldi logo the paper prints: "Aldi's corporate responsibility plan is driven by 5 principles: customers, suppliers, environment, employees and community." (Adapted from aldi.ie)

rows.verbatim: Creates jobs/employment for people in the area – improves quality of life.
accepts: Makes available a wider variety of goods at competitive prices to the local community.
Improves standard of living in area – staff wages spent locally.
Spin-off effect – other businesses supply services to the new business.
Sponsorship of local events/teams/clubs.
Generates sales/business in the area – more money spent in local shops, cafes.
Improved infrastructure – more investment in roads/services.
rows.contextNote: The paper asks for two of these. The 8 and the 7 go to the first and second benefit you gave, not to particular benefits on this list, so any two of them score 8 then 7. Each is split 4 + 4 and 4 + 3, so naming the benefit is only half the answer — "creates jobs" needs the effect on the community after it.

notes: orderedSplit: the scheme prints ⟨8m⟩ ⟨(4 + 4)⟩ and ⟨7m⟩ ⟨(4 + 3)⟩ against a seven-bullet sample the candidate takes two from, so the marks attach to answer positions rather than particular benefits, and 2 x p = 15 rules out bestNofParts and any anyN group. All seven benefits sit on one alt row, quoted whole so each one carries the effect clause the second half of the split pays for. Seven separate required rows would breach the five-row cap and would also misrepresent a question that asks for two. openList: the front matter says the expected responses are not exclusive, so a valid community benefit the examiner did not list still scores. Note the scheme heads this part "ALDI" in capitals where the paper prints "Aldi"; the questionText follows the paper, which is where questionText must come from.

questionText: Imports can be both visible and invisible. Explain the term visible import and give one example of a visible import for Ireland.
stem: Question 3 — International Environment. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. The information supplied is a Central Statistics Office pie chart (www.cso.ie) headed "Ireland's Imports for 2021", showing where Ireland's imports came from: EU 36%, UK 23%, USA 15%, China 7%, Other 19%.

rows.verbatim: A visible import is when Irish people puchase a pysical good from a business in another county. Money leaves Ireland and goes to another country.
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 6m (3m + 3m) against this explanation — three marks for the physical good bought from a business abroad and three for the money leaving Ireland — so an explanation that stops at the first half stops at three.

rows.verbatim: The example of a visible import given: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 4 against the example list and asks for one example, so one worked example is the whole four.

options: An Irish supermarket buying fruit from Spain.
Irish consumers buying wine fom and France.
An Irish department store buys clothes from America.
Irish consumers buying cars from the UK.

notes: Scheme p.17 for the expected responses; the SECTION 2 tariff grid on scheme p.5 states this part in full — "(A) Explanation: 6 marks (3m + 3m) / Example: 4 marks", total 10 — so the split is fixed and stated, not inferred, and 6 + 4 makes the 10 the paper prints. The (3m + 3m) is the internal split of the explanation (the point plus its development), which is why the explanation is one row of six rather than two rows of three. The example is an anyN group: the scheme lists four sample imports and the paper asks for one, so a single pick is worth the whole 4. Three SEC typos are reproduced exactly as published because the build checks every row against the scheme text: "puchase" for purchase, "pysical" for physical, "county" for country, and in the second example "wine fom and France" for wine from France. openList true on both rows — the scheme's front matter (p.3) says "The expected responses presented are not exclusive. Marks may be awarded for any other correct answers." No figure bound: the only image on the question is the CSO pie chart of import sources, and this part is answerable without it (the chart names regions, not goods), so its content is carried as context in the stem instead.

questionText: Outline two reasons why goods and services are imported into Ireland.
stem: Question 3 — International Environment.

rows.verbatim: The first reason given: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prices the first reason at 8m (4m + 4m): four for naming the reason and four for the sentence that develops it, so a reason named and left there stops at four.

options: Production - We do not produce certain products for example cars.
Climate - We do not have the climate to grow certain crops.
Natural resources - We do not have certain natural resources such as oil and gas which businesses and consumers need.
Consumer choice - consumers are provided with a wider variety of products.
Growth in e-commerce – It is now easier for consumers to buy goods from other countries. It has been simplified due to the internet and smart technology.

rows.verbatim: The second reason given: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prices the second reason at 7m (4m + 3m): four for naming it and three for developing it. It has to be a different reason from the one above — a reason given twice is a surplus answer and earns nothing the second time. The 8 and the 7 follow the order the two reasons are written, not particular reasons on this list.

options: Production - We do not produce certain products for example cars.
Climate - We do not have the climate to grow certain crops.
Natural resources - We do not have certain natural resources such as oil and gas which businesses and consumers need.
Consumer choice - consumers are provided with a wider variety of products.
Growth in e-commerce – It is now easier for consumers to buy goods from other countries. It has been simplified due to the internet and smart technology.

notes: Checked at source; the reviewer's finding is NOT upheld on its mechanism, so the row shape stands. Scheme p.17 prints five sample reasons with only two mark cells beside them — 8m (4 + 4) and 7m (4 + 3) — and the Section 2 tariff grid on p.5 prints "(B) Two reasons: 8 marks (4m + 4m) / 7 marks (4m + 3m)", total 15. Two cells cannot attach to five bullets, so the 8 and the 7 price the FIRST and SECOND answer given: an ordered split by answer position, and no individual reason carries marks of its own. That is why the card carries one anyN menu per answer position, each offering the whole sample list, priced 8 then 7 — the shape of the shipped 2021 OL Section 1 Q9 card and ~70 other Business cards. The reviewer's failure mode (one reason ticked on both rows scoring the whole 15) cannot occur: SessionScreen.tsx computes takenByRow and disables an option already picked in a sibling menu, showing "Already claimed above — one answer earns marks once"; test/markBankSession.test.tsx ("a menu option claimed once cannot be claimed again") locks that in, and the guard works precisely because both menus carry identical option strings. The suggested single claimMax-2 row is arithmetically impossible here: a group has one perOption and 15 does not halve — perOption 8 makes 16 and build-deck.mjs groupFault drops the card; perOption 7 makes the session print "Any 2 of these — 7 marks each", stating 14 on a 15-mark part and hiding the extra mark the first answer earns. The scheme distinguishes the two shapes itself: where two answers are worth the same it writes "@ 5m each" (Q5(B), Q5(E)); here it does not. WHAT DID CHANGE. tariffModel.answer and ofParts were carrying 2 and 5 — bestNofParts fields that an ordered split does not define; "ofParts: 5" also asserted a closed set of five parts, which contradicts openList and the bullets being a sample. Both are now null, matching every other shipped orderedSplit card. The notation drops its redundant "Two reasons:" prefix so the session sentence reads "The examiner marks the first correct answers higher than the rest (8 marks (4m + 4m) then 7 marks (4m + 3m))". The stem's pie-chart recital is cut: the CSO chart (business-2022-OL-paper-p40-i0.png, opened and checked) shows only WHERE imports came from — EU 36%, UK 23%, USA 15%, China 7%, Other 19% — and carries none of the scheme's five reasons, so this part is answerable without it, and quoting those country shares steers a student toward country-based answers the examiner does not pay for. r-2's contextNote now states outright that the second reason must be a different one, in the scheme's own annotation vocabulary (p.3, "Surplus answer or part of answer", worth nothing). openList stays true on both rows per the scheme's front matter (p.3): "The expected responses presented are not exclusive. Marks may be awarded for any other correct answers" — reasons for importing are genuinely open, not a closed statutory list. Options are quoted whole across their line wraps with the development sentences intact, because the second figure in each pair (the 4 and the 3) is what pays for the development; the hyphen/en-dash mix is the scheme's own. No figure bound.

questionText: Using the figures below calculate the Balance of Trade for April 2021. Show your workings.
stem: Question 3 — International Environment. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. The table supplied is headed "International Accounts April 2021" and gives Visible Exports €12,706m and Visible Imports €8,053m. (Source: www.cso.ie)

rows.verbatim: Balance of Trade = Visible Exports - Visible Imports
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 2 against this line on its own, so writing the formula down banks marks before any arithmetic happens.
The bracket printed against this line is 2 + 2 + 2, so six of the ten marks sit on the workings the question tells you to show — more than the formula and the final answer put together.

The scheme prints 1 + 1 here and never says what the two marks are for, so do not read an allocation into it. What it does show is placement: the final figure is worth 2 of the 10, and the other 8 are already banked by the formula and the workings above it.

notes: Scheme p.17. Each marks bracket sits on the line that earns it: 2 against the formula, 2 + 2 + 2 against the workings line and 1 + 1 against the answer line, which makes 10 for (i); the surplus/deficit statement carries the 5 that completes the paper's (15) for part (C) and is the sibling card bus-2022-ol-s2-q3cii. The scheme does not say what the two 1s on the answer line are for and this card no longer guesses — an earlier version told the student one was for the figure and one for the € sign or units, wording the scheme prints nowhere. The SECTION 2 tariff grid on scheme p.5 states the same total a different way — "Formula: 2m / Calculation: 2m + 2m + 2m + 2m / Surplus: 5 marks" — so the grid parcels the eight non-formula marks into a single Calculation bucket while the expected-responses page splits them 2 + 2 + 2 on the workings and 1 + 1 on the answer. Both readings agree (i) is worth 10; the per-line brackets are used because that is where the examiner attached each mark, and the notation records them as printed rather than borrowing the grid's labels. openList false on all three rows: a balance of trade calculation has one correct value (12,706 − 8,053 = 4,653, exactly as the scheme prints), so there is nothing outside the scheme to claim. Figure bound: the question says "using the figures below" and cannot be asked without the International Accounts extract; p40-i2 is that complete table, checked against the image. The other published figure on the page, p40-i0, is the "IRELAND'S IMPORTS FOR 2021" pie chart, which belongs to the question as a whole and is not needed for the calculation, so it is not bound. One display artefact worth knowing: the scheme writes the formula in row 1 with a spaced hyphen for minus, and the session's marks-left-behind list treats a spaced hyphen or em dash as a lead-in separator, so that row abbreviates to "visible imports" there; the row itself is quoted whole and unaltered. Row 2's dash is the scheme's en dash, which the separator does not match, so that row is left intact.

questionText: State whether it is a surplus or a deficit.
stem: Question 3 — International Environment. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. The table supplied is headed "International Accounts April 2021" and gives Visible Exports €12,706m and Visible Imports €8,053m. (Source: www.cso.ie)

rows.verbatim: Surplus
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints the whole 5 marks against this single word: exports of €12,706m exceed imports of €8,053m, so the balance of trade is positive.

notes: Scheme p.17 prints this as one continuous line under (C) — "State whether it is a surplus or deficit: Surplus" with 5 in the marks column — and the Section 2 tariff grid on scheme p.5 agrees ("Surplus: 5 marks"); 10 for the calculation on (C)(i) plus 5 here makes the 15 the paper prints against (C). REPAIR: the row previously read "State whether it is a surplus or deficit: — Surplus", which drove the deck's cue dash into a line the scheme prints continuously and rendered a colon and a dash back to back (SessionScreen prints row.verbatim raw). The deck's "Label: — answer" form belongs to genuine field labels the scheme prints as labels — To:, From:, Date:, Workings:, Answer: — whereas this lead-in is simply this card's own questionText restated, so it is dropped and the row is now the marking point the examiner pays for, the single word Surplus. The session's unclaimed-marks list splits on " — " and falls back to the whole string when there is no dash, and "Surplus" is 7 characters so it clears the six-character guard — the left-behind list still reads "surplus", which is what the old dash was there to achieve. openList false, now stated explicitly: the answer is one of two words and only one of them is right, so nothing off the list could have scored. Carded separately from (C)(i) because the paper numbers it (ii) and the scheme prices it separately. Figure bound: without the International Accounts extract there is nothing to judge a surplus from, and it is a real accounts table rather than a blank answer grid. The scheme's line drops the second article ("a surplus or deficit"); questionText follows the paper, which prints "a surplus or a deficit".

questionText: Describe two challenges for Irish businesses involved in international trade.
stem: Question 3 — International Environment. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. The information supplied is a Central Statistics Office pie chart (www.cso.ie) headed "Ireland's Imports for 2021", showing where Ireland's imports came from: EU 36%, UK 23%, USA 15%, China 7%, Other 19%.

rows.verbatim: The first challenge described: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prices the first challenge at 8m (4m + 4m): four for naming the challenge and four for describing it, so a challenge named and left there stops at four.

options: Language difficulties - difficulties when translating marketing/advertising materials.
Cultural differences – different customs/traditions, e.g., people in India do not eat beef.
Distribution costs – Increased transportation costs due to distance.
Currency fluctuations – Currency changes may affect competitiveness and can lead to a decline in the demand for Irish exports.
Competition – competition from domestic producers who produce high quality goods.
Taxes and duties charged by other countries outside the EU may increase selling price and reduce demand.

rows.verbatim: The second challenge described: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prices the second challenge at 7m (4m + 3m): four for naming it and three for describing it. The 8 and the 7 follow the order the two challenges are written, not particular challenges on this list.

options: Language difficulties - difficulties when translating marketing/advertising materials.
Cultural differences – different customs/traditions, e.g., people in India do not eat beef.
Distribution costs – Increased transportation costs due to distance.
Currency fluctuations – Currency changes may affect competitiveness and can lead to a decline in the demand for Irish exports.
Competition – competition from domestic producers who produce high quality goods.
Taxes and duties charged by other countries outside the EU may increase selling price and reduce demand.

notes: Scheme p.18 for the sample challenges; the SECTION 2 tariff grid on scheme p.5 prints "(D) Two challenges: 8 marks (4m + 4m) / 7 marks (4m + 3m)", total 15. Six challenges are printed and two are described, so the 8 and the 7 price the first and second answer given rather than particular challenges — an ordered split, and no challenge carries marks of its own. One anyN row per answer position, each offering all six, priced 8 then 7 = 15, which is the shape the shipped 2021 OL Section 1 Q9 and 2021 HL Section 3 Q2(B) cards already use for this tariff; it also keeps the card inside the deck's five-row limit, which six separate point rows would have broken. Every option keeps the scheme's describing clause as well as its heading, because "describe" is what the second figure in each pair pays for and a bare heading would let three words claim eight marks. openList true per the scheme's front matter (p.3). No figure: the CSO import pie chart is not needed to describe a trading challenge, so it stays in the stem as context.

questionText: Outline three benefits for Ireland of remaining part of the European Union.
stem: Question 3 — International Environment.

tariffModel.notation: Three benefits: 7 marks (4m + 3m), 7 marks (4m + 3m) then 6 marks (4m + 2m)

rows.verbatim: Single European Market/Free trade – free movement of goods and services between member states. There are no taxes on goods and services sold between EU countries.
accepts: Free movement of people – EU citizens can live and work in any EU country without the need for visas. This gives Irish business access to skilled labour.
Grant aid – the EU provides huge financial supports to EU countries and Ireland has received billions in structural funds from EU. e.g., CAP has benefited farmers.
Access to large market – the EU is one of the largest trading blocs in the world and Irish businesses have access to over 400 million people.
rows.contextNote: The paper asks for three of these four. The 7, 7 and 6 go to the first, second and third benefit you wrote, not to particular benefits on this list, so any three of them score 7, then 7, then 6. Each splits 4 marks for naming the benefit and 3, 3 then 2 for the sentence that outlines it, so a benefit named and left there stops at four.

notes:
The reviewer's finding is confirmed against the scheme. Scheme p.5 prints the Section 2 tariff grid as "(E) Three benefits: 7 marks (4m + 3m) / 7 marks (4m + 3m) / 6 marks (4m + 2m)" against a total of 20, and p.18 prints FOUR sample benefits with the 7m (4 + 3), 7m (4 + 3) and 6m (4 + 2) brackets in the marks column — three values for the three answers required, the fourth bullet carrying no bracket at all. So the split is positional: a candidate who writes Grant aid first scores 7 for it and 6 for it if they write it last. That is orderedSplit, and the same grid settles the point by contrast — the SEC writes a uniform split as "@ ... each" two questions above (Q1(D) "Three grounds: @ 5 marks each (4m + 1m)", Q5(A) "@ 5m each"), so any row that prints "N marks each" over these benefits contradicts the scheme's own notation.

The three anyN menus are gone. They put per-answer marks back on an orderedSplit through group.perOption (7, 7 and 6) — a tariff whose whole premise is that per-row values do not exist — and each menu repeated all four benefits, so one benefit was claimable in every one of them and a single answer could earn marks three times. Re-pricing was not available: one menu with claimMax 3 must carry a single perOption, and no integer fits. 3 x 7 = 21 overshoots the 20 the paper prints and build-deck's groupFault drops such a card outright; 3 x 6 would make the session print "Any 3 of these — 6 marks each" over two benefits the scheme prices at 7, and understate the paper by two marks. The four benefits therefore ride as one alt row carrying all of them verbatim, development sentence included, which is what the kind is for and the same call already documented on bus-2022-ol-s2-q8aii and bus-2021-ol-s1-q6. The split reaches the student from the tariff notation and the contextNote instead. marks: null on the row, as orderedSplit requires.

Every benefit keeps the scheme's outlining sentence as well as its heading, because that is exactly what the 3 or the 2 on the right of each split pays for. All four are traceable verbatim into the 2022 OL scheme, checked with the build's own normalise/comparableScheme; the en dash the scheme uses is not the em dash or hyphen the session strips a lead-in on, so each point renders whole.

openList true per the front matter on p.3 — "The expected responses presented are not exclusive. Marks may be awarded for any other correct answers." It is genuinely open here, not open by default: access to EU funding programmes, the single currency and EU consumer-protection law would all be paid for and none is printed.

Stem trimmed to the paper's own question heading. The CSO import pie chart is not needed to outline a benefit of EU membership, and reciting "EU 36%" to a student before they answer nudges the scheme's own "Access to large market – the EU is one of the largest trading blocs in the world". The three sibling cards built from the same stimulus (Q3(A), (B), (D)) still carry the full chart description and want the same trim. No figure, for the same reason.

Filed under 7.2 The European Union (business-6-14, verified in topicTags.ts) with the conceptId bus-2023-hl-s3-q3a already carries, so a student who drops from Higher in spring keeps the work.

questionText: Explain the term stakeholder.

rows.verbatim: A Stakeholder is anyone who is interested in or affected by what happens in a business.
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints the definition as 5m (3 + 2), so the five marks come in two pieces rather than one — a half-stated definition does not reach the full five.

notes: Section 2 of the Ordinary paper IS the long-question section (225 marks; three questions of 75 — one from Part 1, one from Part 2, one from either). There is no Applied Business Question and no Section 3. Q4 sits in Part 1 under the paper's heading 'People in Business'. The question carries TWO separate stimulus boxes: the Glenisk fire above parts (A) and (B), and the Malone house purchase above part (C). No stem is carried on this card — 'Explain the term stakeholder' is a standalone definition, and the Glenisk box says the fire 'has had a huge impact on the business' stakeholders', which would hand a student the 'affected by' half of the answer before the reveal. Page 5 of the paper prints a Glenisk logo and a photograph of the destroyed plant; neither is a published figure candidate for this paper and neither carries anything the stimulus text does not, so no figure is bound. Marks: the scheme prints 20m against (A) as a whole and 5m (3 + 2) against this definition, which leaves 15 for (A)(ii).

questionText: Outline the impact of the fire at Glenisk factory on two of its stakeholders.
stem: A fire at the Glenisk yoghurt manufacturing plant in Tullamore, Co. Offaly has had a huge impact on the business’ stakeholders. The fire destroyed the entire production facility.

rows.verbatim: The first stakeholder given: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: Tick here for the first stakeholder you gave. The scheme marks the first answer 8 (4 + 4) — four for naming the stakeholder and four for the impact that develops it — so a stakeholder named without an impact stops at four.

options: Investors/shareholders/owners – will not receive adequate dividend or any profit
Employees – potential temporary layoffs or job losses
Consumers – no access to Glenisk products that they usually purchase
Suppliers – no buyer for their raw materials e.g., farmers have no other buyers for their milk as the factory is not operational
Government – will not receive VAT and Corporation Tax returns due to closure
Management/Employer – high level of pressure to get business operational again
Local Community – local businesses may suffer as a result of employees being temporarily laid off.

rows.verbatim: The second stakeholder given: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: Tick here for the second stakeholder, which has to be a different one from the first. The scheme marks it 7 (4 + 3). The 8 and the 7 follow the order the two answers are given rather than attaching to particular stakeholders on this list, so any two of the seven are worth 8 then 7.

options: Investors/shareholders/owners – will not receive adequate dividend or any profit
Employees – potential temporary layoffs or job losses
Consumers – no access to Glenisk products that they usually purchase
Suppliers – no buyer for their raw materials e.g., farmers have no other buyers for their milk as the factory is not operational
Government – will not receive VAT and Corporation Tax returns due to closure

questionText: Explain, with reference to the text above, three of the following elements of a valid contract: (i) Offer and Acceptance (Agreement) (ii) Capacity to Contract (iii) Consideration (iv) Consent to Contract.
stem: Sinead and Patrick Malone finally found the home they were looking for after a 2 year search. They put in an offer of €320,000 for the house and this was accepted by the seller. Sinead and Patrick are both aged 31 and want to buy the house.

rows.verbatim: Any three of the four elements, each explained and then applied to the text
rows.contextNote: The paper prints these four elements and asks for three of the following, so the menu is closed: a fifth element of a valid contract, however correct in itself, earns nothing here. The scheme prices them 3 @ 5m (3 + 2) — three for explaining the element, two for the reference back to Sinead and Patrick that the question demands — so an explanation with nothing about the house purchase in it stops at three of the five.

options: Offer and Acceptance (Agreement) – one party makes an offer to another party. This offer is accepted unconditionally by the other party. Sinead and Patrick offered €320,000 for the house and Eamonn Lynch, the seller, accepted the offer. He agreed to transfer ownership of the house to Sinead and Patrick on receipt of the money offered.

Capacity to Contract – all parties entering into the contract must have the ability to do so. They be over 18, of sound mind, and not under the influence of alcohol/drugs. Sinead and Patrick are both aged 31.

Consideration – this is the item of value that must pass between both parties to a contract. Usually, one party exchanges an asset or service for the other party’s money. Sinead and Patrick will give €320,000 to Eamonn Lynch, who will sell them the house.
Consent to Contract – both parties must enter into the contract of their own free will, under no pressure. Sinead and Patrick want to buy the house, the seller had invited people to buy it.

notes: Repair: openList was true and is now false. The paper (p.5 of the OL long-question section) prints the menu itself — 'three of the following elements of a valid contract: (i) Offer and Acceptance (Agreement) (ii) Capacity to Contract (iii) Consideration (iv) Consent to Contract' — and the scheme's possible responses are those same four and nothing else, so no fifth element can be paid for. The front matter's 'The expected responses presented are not exclusive. Marks may be awarded for any other correct answers' does not reopen a list the question itself closed; its fourth bullet says the opposite, that 'the detail required in any answer is determined by the context and the manner in which the question is asked'. An element outside the four is not a correct answer to THIS question. The scheme's own heading for this part reads 'Explain, with reference to supplied text, three elements of a valid contract' and drops 'of the following'; questionText follows the paper, which is what the candidate read. The Malone house-purchase box is carried in the stem and has to be: the question says 'with reference to the text above', and the second figure of every (3 + 2) is paid for exactly that reference. It is not a stem leak — it hands over no element name and no explanation, only the facts the candidate must apply. The four Roman numerals are a CHOICE MENU, not four sub-parts: the paper asks for three of the four and the scheme prints 3 @ 5m (3 + 2) against 15, so this is one card with a bestNofParts group (3 of 4 at 5), not four cards. In the last two years, he has noticed an increased demand for his services as pet ownership in Ireland increases. To continue to meet demand Ryan is planning to expand his business. As part of this expansion, he is planning to purchase a van so he can launch a mobile dog grooming service.

rows.verbatim: Any three of the following types of insurance
rows.contextNote: Each type is marked 3 + 2: three for naming the insurance and two for saying what it covers. A list of three names with nothing after them stops at 9 of the 15.

options: Property insurance –to cover financial loss to the buildings in the event of burglary or damage.
Public Liability Insurance – protects the business from claims made by members of the public for accidents on the premises.
Employers Liability Insurance – protects the business from claims made by employees for accidents in the workplace or in the duty of their work
Contents Insurance – protects against theft or damage to stock and equipment in the event of flooding or theft.
Cash in transit – protects the business if cash is stolen while in transit to bank.
Plate Glass Window insurance – covers replacement of front window of business in the event of damage/breakage.
Motor Insurance (Comprehensive) will be required if he purchases the van – this covers everyone, including Ryan, if he is involved in an accident.

notes: Scheme p.26. ⟨15m⟩ for the part, ⟨3 x 5m⟩ ⟨(3 + 2)⟩ against the first type and governing all seven the scheme prints, so bestNofParts with one bounded pick-list: three ticks, 5 each, and the third tick hits the cap. Every option keeps the scheme's cover sentence as well as the name of the insurance, because that sentence is what the 2 in the 3 + 2 pays for; "Property insurance –to cover…" is transcribed with the scheme's own missing space after the dash. openList true per the front matter — the seven are a sample, and a valid seventh type (e.g. business interruption) still earns 5. No figure: paper p.7 prints only the stimulus box and a stock photograph of a dog in a grooming bath. Stem audit: the van sentence stays even though the scheme's Motor Insurance entry is written as conditional on it ("will be required if he purchases the van"). It is not a marking point handed over — the stem names no type of insurance — and part (A) is unaskable without it, so cutting it would break two other cards and make one of the SEC's own seven answers unreachable.

questionText: Explain, with reference to Ryan, the principle of Utmost Good Faith in relation to insurance.
stem: Managing. Ryan’s Dog Groomers. Ryan Murphy runs a successful dog grooming business. To continue to meet demand Ryan is planning to expand his business. As part of this expansion, he is planning to purchase a van so he can launch a mobile dog grooming service.

tariffModel.notation: 10m — expected responses p.26: 7m(4+3) + 3m; tariff grid p.5: “Explanation: 10m (5m + 5m)”

rows.verbatim: Utmost Good Faith refers to the declaration of all material facts when taking out insurance. A material fact is anything which affects the level of risk the insurer is being asked to cover and therefore the premium charged. A person taking out insurance must be honest and truthful in all dealings with an insurance company. This enables the insurer to calculate the correct premium.
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 4 + 3 against this paragraph: four for the principle itself and three for developing it, so a one-line definition does not reach the seven. Be aware the scheme contradicts itself here. Its front tariff grid (p.5) prices the same part as “Explanation: 10m (5m + 5m)”. Both come to ten; only these expected responses tie marks to actual sentences, which is why the card splits them seven and three.

rows.verbatim: Ryan must be truthful with his dealings with insurance company – he must declare all material facts relating to the business and the van he intends to buy.
rows.contextNote: These are the three marks the words “with reference to Ryan” are worth, so an answer that explains the principle perfectly but never mentions Ryan stops at seven. The p.5 grid does not break the reference out at all and prices the part 5m + 5m, so three is the least this sentence could be worth, not the most. Either way, applying it to Ryan is not optional.

notes: Scheme p.26 (expected responses). Two mark cells, ⟨4 + 3⟩ on the definition paragraph and ⟨3⟩ on the sentence applying it to Ryan, making the paper's ⟨10m⟩ — the split is stated, so fixed, not orderedSplit. SCHEME CONFLICT, flagged on the card and not silently resolved: the front tariff grid on p.5 prices this same part as “Explanation: 10m (5m + 5m)”, which does not agree with 7 + 3. Both reach the paper's ten, so totalMarks is unaffected; only the internal split is in dispute. The rows carry 7 and 3 because that is the only split anchored to text — the grid's parenthesis is its idiom for the internal breakdown of ONE answer (compare Q4(B) “Role: 10 marks (5m + 5m)” and Q4(E) “One function: 10 marks (5m + 5m)”, both of which the expected responses confirm as a single ⟨10m⟩ ⟨(5 + 5)⟩ answer), so 5 + 5 cannot be mapped onto the definition and the reference without inventing an allocation the scheme never states. Compare Q8(D), this paper's other “with reference to” ten-marker, where the grid DOES break the reference out (“Explanation: 6m (3m + 3m) / Reference: 4 marks”) and the expected responses agree exactly ⟨6m⟩ ⟨(3 + 3)⟩ + ⟨4⟩ — which is what makes the 6(C) grid line look like a failure to separate the reference rather than a real 5 + 5 intention. I have not edited the scheme file. The definition is quoted whole as one 7-mark row rather than cut at an invented boundary: the scheme prints it as continuous prose and the 4 + 3 pays for the definition plus its development. The scheme's heading misspells the question as “the principal of Utmost Good Faith”; questionText follows the paper, which reads “principle”. openList true on both rows per the front matter — there is no list to close here, and a student's own wording of the principle, or of the application to Ryan, still earns it. No figure: nothing published for this paper bears on 6(C) (the only Q6 figure is the net-profit table, which belongs to (D)). Stem trimmed against the siblings: the boilerplate instruction line and the “increased demand as pet ownership increases” sentence are gone, as they carry nothing for this part. The van is deliberately KEPT even though it hands 6(B) one of its seven insurance types (motor) — the scheme's own three-mark reference names “the van he intends to buy”, so cutting it would leave r-2 unanswerable as printed; 6(B) must manage that leak in its own stem. Nothing in the stem mentions insurance, honesty, declarations or material facts, so this card's own answer is not given away.

questionText: Explain the terms induction training and on-the-job training.
stem:
Managing. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

Value Insurance Ltd: Leah Corcoran recently began a new job as an insurance sales agent at Value Insurance Ltd in Limerick city. Value Insurance Ltd is a growing company that sells a variety of insurance policies to individuals, families, and businesses.

rows.verbatim: Induction training is training given to a new employee when they start in an organisation. It involves information on how the organisation operates, who to report to, payment details, code of ethics, health and safety etc. It aims to help new employees feel comfortable in their new job.
On-the-job training means learning the skills and knowledge required for the job in the workplace by working with and observing experienced employees do their job.

notes: Scheme p.28. The part total is 10m and the scheme prints 5m (3 + 2) against EACH of the two definitions, and the front summary agrees ('(A) Explanation: 3m + 2m / Explanation: 3m + 2m'), so this is a fixed 5/5 — both terms are named in the question, so neither is optional and there is nothing to choose between. Each definition is quoted whole across its line wraps: the sentences about what induction involves and what it aims to do, and the 'by working with and observing experienced employees' clause, are what the +2 development marks are paid for, so cutting to a one-line definition would let a student who wrote one line claim the lot. STEM TRIMMED: the paper's stimulus goes on 'To prepare Leah for her role, she received induction training and on-the-job training.' That sentence is cut here — the question already names both terms, so it adds nothing a student needs, and 'to prepare Leah for her role' after 'recently began a new job' edges towards the scheme's own 'training given to a new employee when they start in an organisation'. No figure: paper p.44 carries no images at all (18 vector drawings, all text-box rules), and the Question 7 stimulus is a text box. openList true per the scheme's front matter ('Variations and alternatives may also be acceptable').

questionText: Explain three sources of new product ideas for a business.

options: Personal interests/hobbies/skills – The entrepreneur may be able to turn a hobby into a successful business.
Research and Development – A specific R & D department is responsible for coming up with ideas.
Foreign Travel – An entrepreneur may spot a successful product/service abroad and set up similar in Ireland.
Family/Friends – family members, friends or colleagues might make a suggestion or highlight a problem with an existing product.
Internet/Media – ideas from newspapers, TV, radio, websites.
Trends – An entrepreneur will keep an eye on market trends to identify a new product/service.

questionText: Outline two reasons for fair dismissal.
stem: Dental implant firm ordered to pay manager €55,000 A UK dental implants company has been ordered to pay €55,000 to a former Irish sales manager who was unfairly dismissed. Adapted from rte.ie

rows.verbatim: Capability – not completing the duties of the job due to absenteeism or lateness which are not due to illness or disability.
Competency – unable to carry out the tasks involved despite being given training and afforded a reasonable time to improve.
Qualifications – if it turns out that the employee does not have the qualifications required in the job advertisement.
Misconduct – an employee can be dismissed if they have engaged in any behaviour that is offensive, illegal, outside of their job contract e.g., assault, bullying/harassment, stealing, drunk at work.
Redundancy – if the employer cannot afford to retain the position which the staff member holds.

questionText: A legal contract may be terminated by the following methods: Frustration, Breach, Agreement, Performance. Explain, using examples, three of these methods.

rows.verbatim: Frustration: An unforseen event makes it impossible for the contract to be completed. Example: Taylor Shift gets a throat infection and is unable to perform her concert in Dublin; concert is cancelled.
Breach: One party in the contract breaks a condition of the contract, the contract is invalidated. Example: Liverpool footballer is caught drink driving and has his contract ended with the club.
Agreement: Both parties agree to end the contract before its finish date. Example: Christiano Ronaldo and Manchester United agreed to end Ronaldo’s contract before its end date by mutual consent.

Performance: Both parties fulfil the terms of the contract and the contract comes to its natural end. Example: IT consultant is hired for a 6 month period for Cyber security firm. At the end of the 6 months, the contact expires.

Improvement in infrastructure – increased Govt revenue should result in better infrastructure in the economy.

notes: Repair of the reviewer's finding. The single claimMax-2 group priced every option at 5, so the session printed "Any 2 of these — 5 marks each": 10 marks stated on a 15-mark part, and a per-option value attached to answers an ordered split prices by POSITION. No whole number of marks per option makes 15 across two answers, so the card now carries one anyN row per ANSWER POSITION — 1 x 10 for the first benefit, 1 x 5 for the second, summing to the paper's 15. That is the shape bus-2021-ol-s1-q9 and bus-2021-ol-s2-q1c already use for the identical arithmetic, and SessionScreen's takenByRow guard supports it: an option ticked in the first menu is disabled in the second with "Already claimed above — one answer earns marks once", so no benefit can be banked twice. Both rows keep marks: null, as an ordered split requires. Tariff read from bracket position: the scheme prints ⟨7 + 3⟩ level with the first bullet and ⟨4 + 1⟩ level with the second, over a list of SEVEN benefits of which the candidate gives two, with nothing at all against the remaining five — the tell that the cells price answer positions rather than particular benefits. Part (E) on the same page puts its two cells against the second and third bullets, which settles it. Stem edit: "IDA Ireland has welcomed the news." is cut here as it already is on the (B) card, because the stimulus box is shared by every card made from Q2 and two of (B)'s five marking options are IDA incentives (Access to Govt. Grants; IDA buildings/zoned industrial land) — naming the agency before reveal hands that family over. Nothing else in the box states a marking point on any of the six cards: the TikTok jobs sentences are the context this part sits under and name none of the seven benefits. openList true — the scheme's front matter says the support notes "are neither exclusive nor complete" and that further relevant points are "marked and rewarded on their merits", and the Irish economy has benefits of employment beyond these seven (reduced national debt, reduced poverty), so a student who wrote one was not wrong. Seven options, within the 14 a Section 2 long question may show. The en dashes inside the options are the scheme's own printing (heading, then the sentence describing it) and each option is reproduced whole, because that sentence is what the 3 and the 1 pay for; anyN options are never cue-split, and the cue regex matches only em dash or hyphen in any case. notes: The paper prints (20) against part (D) as a whole, covering (i) and (ii) together. The scheme resolves it: ⟨3 + 2⟩ = 5 against the definition here, and 10 + 5 = 15 across the two effects in (ii), which is why this card is 5 and the (ii) card is 15. conceptId shared with HL 2025 Section 1 Q11(a), the identical explain-the-term question at Higher.

questionText: Outline two effects of a high inflation rate on Irish business.
stem: Domestic Environment. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. High inflation may persist for years. Adapted from The Irish Times

rows.verbatim: The first effect given: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prices the first effect at 10m (7 + 3): seven for the effect itself and three for the sentence outlining it. The effect you write first is the one worth developing in full — an effect named with nothing under it stops at 7. Whatever you name has to land on the BUSINESS, since the question asks about Irish business rather than about consumers or the economy generally, and every option below ends in something that happens to the firm.

options: Reduced sales/profits – as prices rise, consumers decrease their spending on non-essential items, reducing sales for business.
Increased costs – costs of raw materials, fuel etc. increase business costs and reduce profits.
Demand for wage increases – employees will demand a cost of living pay increase to keep up with level of inflation, which in turn increases costs again.
Reduced investment – businesses are less willing to expand when inflation is high.

rows.verbatim: The second effect given: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prices the second effect at 5m (4 + 1): four for the other effect you gave and one for outlining it. The 10 and the 5 follow the ORDER the two answers are written rather than attaching to particular effects, which is why both menus list the same four. The support notes are "a sample of possible responses" and further relevant points are "marked and rewarded on their merits", so another genuine effect on Irish business, outlined, scores too.

options: Reduced sales/profits – as prices rise, consumers decrease their spending on non-essential items, reducing sales for business.

notes: Part (D) is 20 marks on the paper: (i) takes 5 (the scheme's ⟨3 + 2⟩ on the definition) and (ii) the remaining 15, marked ⟨7 + 3⟩ then ⟨4 + 1⟩. Those two brackets price ANSWER POSITIONS, not particular bullets — on part (E) of the same scheme page the ⟨7 + 3⟩ sits on the second bullet's line and the ⟨4 + 1⟩ on the third's, which no reading of "this bullet is worth 10" survives; the marks column is laid out by vertical position. The card therefore carries one menu per answer position (10 then 5) instead of one two-pick menu at a flat 5, which rendered "Any 2 of these — 5 marks each" = 10 marks on a 15-mark question. notes: REPAIR (reviewer finding upheld). The card carried ONE menu at claimMax 3 x perOption 3, and SessionScreen prints that group header unconditionally as "Any 3 of these — 3 marks each" — 9 marks stated on a 10-mark part, with the 4 the first answer is worth never reaching the student, and a flat per-option value asserted on a split the scheme prices by position. Now three menus, one per answer position, at 4, 3 and 3, which reconciles to the printed 10 exactly. Scheme p.18 (marking-scheme PDF p.18), read as a rendered image and not only as extracted text: the Marks column prints 15m against part (A), then 5 on the "European Union" line for (A)(i), then a single 4 + 3 + 3 cell against the examples, so (A) splits 5/10 and this card is the 10. One bracket over five listed examples for three required answers cannot attach to particular exports, so it prices the FIRST, SECOND and THIRD answer a candidate gives — an ordered split, hence marks: null on every row and no per-row mark chips (showsRowMarks is false for orderedSplit). Modelled exactly like the shipped sibling on this same paper, bus-2023-ol-s2-q8c (8 + 4 + 3 over a menu of seven), which the reviewer cites; NOT like bus-2021-hl-s3-q3a, which was collapsed to a single menu when nothing deduped picks across rows. That has since been fixed in the app: takenByRow in SessionScreen.tsx builds the set of options claimed in sibling menus and disables them ("Already claimed above — one answer earns marks once"), and its comment names this "7 + 7 + 6 across three answers" shape as the case it exists for, so an export cannot be banked twice. Each menu repeats all five because the split follows answer order, not which export is picked. The scheme prints the five as one comma-separated sentence and each is quoted from it unchanged, lower-case "a" included; all five verify against the scheme through the build's own normalise(). openList true per the scheme's front matter ("not model answers but rather a sample of possible responses", "Further relevant points of information presented by candidates are marked and rewarded on their merits") and because Irish exports are genuinely open — whiskey, software or medical devices would have been marked on merit; this is not a closed statutory list. No figure: the only stimulus on paper p.4 is a bar chart of export REGIONS plus the 50th-anniversary line, and this part asks for goods and services, so it is fully askable without either. Stem unchanged and re-read as a student sees it before reveal, and trimmed against every sibling: it names no export, no barrier to trade, no EU benefit, challenge or institution, and omits the Balance of Payments figure that (C) supplies, so it gives no marking point away on any card built from this question.

questionText: Name two barriers to trade and explain one of them.
stem:
Question 3 — International Environment.

Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

rows.contextNote: Naming is all this half asks for, so a one-word answer scores here in full. The scheme prints its two 4s beside the block of four names, not beside particular ones, so any two of them earn the same.

options: Tariff
Embargo
Subsidy
Quota

rows.verbatim: One of those barriers explained.
rows.contextNote: The scheme heads this second list "One explanation:" and prints 4 + 3 against it, so the explanation is worth 7 in two halves. The answer it prints against that 4 + 3 says what a tariff is in one sentence and then what it does to prices and to domestic producers, which is what the 3 is paid for — a bare definition leaves it behind.

options: A tariff is a tax placed on foreign products. It increases the price of that product to encourage consumers to purchase goods from domestic producers.
An embargo is a government ban on all imports from a particular country.
A subsidy is money that a government or the EU gives to its own indigenous businesses to allow them to sell their products and services more cheaply.
A quota is a limit on the number of a certain good that can be imported into a country.

notes: Scheme page 18, read off the rendered PDF page rather than the extracted text alone. 15m for part (B), split by the Marks column into two 4s printed beside the four-name bullet block (two names at 4 = 8) and one 4 + 3 printed beside the four explanations (one explanation at 7 = 7). 8 + 7 = 15, which is why the tariff is fixed rather than an ordered split: the scheme states both halves. Two rows because the question genuinely asks two things, and a student who names Tariff in the first row and then explains a tariff in the second is entitled to both — unlike the 2021 HL case where two rows covered one task, here the double claim is the marking scheme's own arithmetic. The naming options are bare because naming is the whole of what that half asks; the explaining options each carry the scheme's complete sentence, definition and effect, because the 3 in (4 + 3) is paid for exactly that development. openList true per the scheme's front matter. No figure: the bar chart on the paper shows Ireland's export regions and no part of (B) reads anything off it. Stem checked as a student sees it before the reveal — it names no barrier.

questionText: Explain the term Balance of Payments.

Question 3 — International Environment.

Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

(C) Ireland's Balance of Payments was €15.8 billion from October – December 2022.

rows.verbatim: The Balance of payments is total exports (visible and invisible) minus total imports (visible and invisible).
rows.contextNote: Printed as 4 + 4, one half for the exports side of the sum and one for the imports side, so a definition that names only one of the two stops at 4. Visible and invisible are inside the scheme's own answer on both sides: goods and services both count.

notes: Scheme page 18. The Marks column prints 15m against part (C) as a whole and then 4 + 4 beside this definition and 4 + 3 beside (C)(ii), so (C) splits 8/7 and this card is the 8. One row, not two: the scheme sets the answer as a single sentence and splitting it at "minus" would quote half a marking point, so the 4 + 4 is carried in the contextNote instead. openList true per the scheme's front matter — a student who wrote that it is the difference between all the money coming into the country and all the money leaving it has defined the same thing and was marked on merit. conceptId matches bus-2024-hl-s3-q3ai, which asks this question in identical words at Higher Level, so a student who drops level keeps the history. The €15.8 billion line is part (C)'s own preamble on the paper, so it sits in the stem; it gives nothing away, since the answer wanted is the definition and not the figure. questionText: Does Jack have to accept the Credit Note? Explain your answer.
stem:
Question 4 — People in Business.

Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

Consumer problems: Jack McCarthy purchased a pair of hiking boots from Outdoor Life in Gateway Shopping Centre. After he tried them on again at home, he found the boots to be slightly uncomfortable and went back to the store to return them. The sales assistant told him he would have to accept a Credit Note if he wanted to return the boots.

rows.verbatim: Yes, he does.
rows.contextNote: Four of the ten marks are for the verdict on its own, before a word of reasoning. The scheme's marks column prints 4 against this line, and the Question 4 structure grid repeats it as "(i) Yes 4 marks".

rows.verbatim: As there is no fault with the product, the retailer is not obliged to provide a refund/replacement. The retailer must provide a refund/repair/replacement of the item if any of the provisions of the Sale of Goods & Supply of Services Act 1980 are broken. In this situation, Jack tried them on in the store and purchased the item. He changed his mind and returned the boots; there was no fault with the product.
rows.contextNote: The remaining six are printed as 3 + 3 — two awards inside one paragraph. The scheme's explanation does two things: it states the rule (no fault, so no obligation to refund or replace) and it applies that rule to Jack, though the SEC does not print which of the two earns which 3. A candidate who wrote only "Yes" and stopped has 4 of 10.

Stem is the paper's own "Consumer problems" stimulus box, checked against paper page 5 (PDF page 41): it states the facts the question turns on and gives no marking point away — that the boots were not faulty is the premise, and the rule the student must supply (no fault, so no obligation to refund) appears nowhere in it. stem:

After he tried them on again at home, he found the boots to be slightly uncomfortable and went back to the store to return them. rows.contextNote: Naming the agency is worth 5 and explaining it 10, and the ten are printed as 5m + 5m — two separate awards inside the explanation rather than one. options: Competition & Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) The CCPC is responsible for informing consumers about their rights in relation to the purchase of goods & services. It provides information via its website, a telephone service, and media advertisements. The website provides tools which help consumers make more informed choices.

notes:
Repaired after review. Two defects, both checked at source before acting.

STEM — the previous stem ("Greenlawn Golf Club has issued the Notice and Agenda shown for its AGM on 21st November 2023. The three underlined terms are AGM, Minutes and AOB.") was authored prose. Paper page 7 of Section 2 (PDF page 43) was extracted and rendered and prints exactly three things above the parts: the header bar "Question 6 | Managing", the line "Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.", and the Notice and Agenda box. There is no introductory sentence at all. The stem is now only the page's own framing, in the same form the sibling Q4 cards on this paper use, and the stimulus is left to the figure that actually carries it. The document is deliberately NOT transcribed into the stem as well: plain text cannot show an underline, so a transcription would leave a student guessing which three of Agenda, Chairperson, Treasurer, Minutes, AOB the question means, and it would repeat the agenda line "Minutes of the 2022 AGM" and the secretary's signature in front of Q6(B)(i), whose answers are the duties of a secretary.

openList — was false on all three rows, which is wrong and was costing a correct student the whole 15. openList drives the "I had something like this" claim in SessionScreen (canSynonym), so closed rows tell a student who explained AGM, Minutes and AOB accurately in their own words that they scored nothing. The scheme's front matter says the support notes "are not model answers but rather a sample of possible responses", are "neither exclusive nor complete", and that further relevant points are "marked and rewarded on their merits"; page 2 adds that "Variations and alternatives may also be acceptable". This matches the deck's own convention on the same paper: Q4(E), the identical shape (three named terms, three explanations at 5 each), marks all three open, and Q4(A)(i) marks the fixed verdict "Yes, he does." closed but its explanation open. questionText: Explain, using examples, commission and benefit-in-kind.
stem: FastParts Ltd offer several different rewards schemes as part of its package for attracting new employees.

rows.verbatim: Commission – refers to a method of rewarding employees working in sales. Employees are paid a basic wage/salary and are paid a commission on their sales – this is a percentage of the value of sales they have per week/month. It is used as an incentive for salespeople to work harder and sell more as the more they sell, the more they earn.
Example: Sales rep earns 5% commission on sales. In Week 3 he had €10,000 sales and earned €500 commission.

Benefit-in-Kind – this is a non-cash method of payment, also known as perks. Employees may receive different types of benefit-in-kind depending on the type of work they do. This is in addition to their wage/salary and is subject to income tax.
Example: company car, laptop/tablet, free health insurance.

questionText: Using the figures above, calculate the Balance of Payments for Q1 2023. Show your workings.
stem: Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

rows.verbatim: Total Exports = €89bn + €83bn = €172bn
rows.contextNote: The scheme sets the formula out first (Balance of Payments = Total Exports (visible + invisible) – Total Imports (visible + invisible)) and then prints 1 + 1 + 1 against this line: one mark for the goods exports figure, one for the services exports figure, one for the total. Services exports of €83bn are the invisible exports, which is why they are added to the €89bn of goods.

rows.verbatim: Total Imports = €33bn + €85bn = €118bn
rows.contextNote: 1 + 1 + 1 again: the goods imports figure, the services imports figure and the total. Services imports of €85bn are the invisible imports.

rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 4 (2 + 2) against this line. It also allows two alternative routes to the same €54bn for the same marks, one of which nets each side first: (€89bn - €33bn = €56bn) + (€83bn - €85bn = – € 2bn) = €54bn. Show your workings is part of the question, so a bare €54bn with nothing above it cannot pick up the six marks the two totals carry.

questionText: Outline one non-legislative method of solving an industrial relations dispute.

rows.verbatim: One non-legislative method, named and outlined: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The split is (7m + 3m): 7 for the method and 3 for outlining how it works, so naming it alone leaves three marks behind.

options: Meeting/Talk: The employee and the employer can meet to discuss the issue and try to resolve the problem. The shop steward might meet with the HR manager to discuss an issue affecting an employee or group of employees.

Negotiation: This involves both parties sitting down together to discuss the issue. Each side sets out their position and tries to find a solution that they can both accept. It involves bargaining where both sides must give up something.
Mediation: A third party becomes involved and tries to open communication between the parties involved in the conflict.

Conciliation: This is when an independent third party listens to both sides of a dispute and tries to get the parties to see each other's point of view and tries to help them negotiate a solution. The parties agree a solution themselves.

Arbitration: This is when an independent third party listens to both sides in a dispute and makes a recommendation to solve the problem. Normally, the parties agree in advance to accept the recommendation.

notes: Section 2 Q4(B), scheme p.21, tariff from the summary on scheme p.5: “One method: 7 marks + 3 marks”, 10 in all, with ⟨7 + 3⟩ printed beside the first sampled method on the answer page. questionText: Explain two of the following practices prohibited by the Consumer Protection Act 2007: (i) False or misleading advertising, (ii) False product descriptions, (iii) False pricing.
stem: The Consumer Protection Act 2007 protects consumers from unfair commercial practices.

rows.verbatim: The first practice you explained: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: Priced 7 + 3: the practice named, then the explanation the scheme prints under it. Naming the practice and stopping there leaves three marks behind, and any one of the three printed practices can be the one you write first.

options: False or misleading advertising: A business cannot give wrong information to customers when comparing its goods with its competitors’ goods. It must be clear on what is included in the purchase of a product and what consumers should expect.

False product descriptions: A business cannot mislead customers about the origin of a product, the previous usage of a product, sell fake/counterfeit items claiming they are real and cannot make false claims about an award/prize.

False pricing: A business must be truthful about the actual price, the previous price and the recommended retail price to consumers. A good advertised in a sale must have been at a higher price for 28 consecutive days in the previous three months.

rows.contextNote: Priced 4 + 1, so the second practice is worth 5 rather than 10. The 10 and the 5 follow the order the two practices were written in rather than attaching to particular practices. questionText: Explain three of the following elements of a legal contract: (i) Consideration, (ii) Capacity to Contract, (iii) Consent to Contract, (iv) Legality of Purpose.

rows.contextNote: The scheme prices the first element 7 marks (4m + 3m): 4 for the element and 3 for the sentence explaining it, so an element named and left there stops at 4. options: Consideration: This is the item of value that passes between both parties in a legal contract, e.g. a house is sold for €300,000 – the house and the money are the consideration.
Capacity to Contract: A person entering into a legal contract must have the legal capacity to do so: over 18, of sound mind, not under the influence of alcohol/drugs.
Consent to Contract: All parties entering a contract must do so of their own free will – they cannot be forced or coerced into the contract.
Legality of Purpose: Contracts must be within the law – a contract cannot be made for illegal/criminal activities.

questionText: Explain one risk and one reward for entrepreneurs who set up their own business.
stem: Enterprise / Managing. Blizzard Entertainment is a leading American developer of video games with an office in Cork city.

rows.verbatim: The risk you explained: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints (4 + 4) against the risk, so it carries 8 of the 15: four for naming the risk and four for the sentence explaining it. A risk named and left there stops at four, which is why every option below carries the whole point the examiner printed and not just its heading.

options: Financial problems / No guaranteed income / possible bankruptcy – a failed business can result in huge financial difficulties for an entrepreneur.
Hard to raise finance/acquire loans – might find it difficult to raise finance for the business.
Stress – must work long hours to get business going. Setting up a new business can cause a lot of stress and possible burnout.
Competition – may not be able to compete with existing businesses in terms of quality of service and price, thus reducing sales and profits.
Business failure – the business model might not be successful, forcing the business to close down. The entrepreneur risks their reputation if the business does not succeed.

rows.verbatim: The reward you explained: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The reward is marked (4 + 3), so it is worth 7 — one less than the risk, and three of those seven are for developing the point. The question asks for one of each, so two risks and no reward can only ever reach 8 of the 15.

options: Financial rewards – a successful business can generate good profit for the entrepreneur.
Independence – the entrepreneur has control over their own working life and makes decisions to suit themselves.
Satisfaction – the challenge of setting up a business is rewarded if the business is successful.
Generating wealth for others – providing employment, spin-off business creation etc.
Employment creation – creating jobs in an area can be very rewarding.
Flexibility – choosing own working hours, running their own business as they see fit.
Positive impact on society – supporting local community, job creation.

notes: Tariff read off the scheme's own brackets: (4 + 4) sits against the first Risk bullet and (4 + 3) against the first Reward bullet, under a (15m) part total — risk 8, reward 7. Fixed rather than orderedSplit, because risk and reward are two named categories, not two positions in one list: whichever order the candidate writes them in, the risk is worth 8 and the reward 7. Stem trimmed hard: the stimulus sentence about the healthcare/insurance package and company-wide team events is the answer to (B)(ii) and carries nothing this part needs, so only the company-identifying sentence is kept. Scheme's front matter states model answers 'are not intended to be exhaustive', hence openList on both rows.

questionText: Explain two of the following principles of insurance and give one example in each case: (i) Utmost good faith (ii) Insurable interest (iii) Indemnity.
stem: Managing. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. Banking and payments app Revolut is launching car insurance in Ireland in partnership with insurer AIG.

rows.verbatim: Any two of these three principles, each explained and illustrated with one example

options: Utmost good faith: A person taking out insurance must be truthful when completing proposal form – all material facts must be declared. A material fact is anything which affects the level of risk the insurer is being asked to cover and therefore the premium charged. Example: Thatched house, house near river, medical condition, smoker re health insurance. These material facts must be disclosed.

Insurable interest: The person taking out insurance must have a financial interest in the item being insured – must gain from its existence and suffer financially from its loss. Example: People can insure their own house but have no insurable interest in insuring their neighbour’s house.

Indemnity: A person cannot make a profit from insurance – the purpose of insurance is to leave the person in the same financial position as before the loss occurred. This protects the insurer from over-insurance. Example: Car insured for €30,000. Market value of €20,000. Insured will only receive €20,000 compensation in the event of a write-off due to an accident.

rows.contextNote: Each principle is worth 10, split 6 + 4: the explanation earns the 6 and the example earns the 4, so a principle explained with no example stops four marks short. The paper names the three principles itself, so there is no fourth answer here — and only two are marked, so a third scores nothing however good it is.

questionText: Explain any two of the following functions of a Human Resource Manager: (i) Manpower Planning (ii) Training and Development (iii) Performance Appraisal.
stem: Question 7 is the Managing long question on this Ordinary Level paper, 75 marks across parts (A) to (E), all sitting under one short news extract. This is part (B), worth 15 marks, and it names the three functions itself, so nothing in the extract is needed to answer it.

rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 7 + 3 against the first function and 4 + 1 against the second, but the question lets you pick any two of the three, so the brackets follow the order you answered in rather than attaching to a particular function. This row is the first position: ten marks, in a larger piece and a smaller one.

options: Manpower Planning: This is making sure the business has the right number of staff with the right skills in the right place at the right time. It involves forecasting future staffing needs. It involves auditing the present manpower levels, forecasting future staffing needs, and planning to increase or decrease the number of employees.

Training and Development: Training involves supplying the skills, knowledge and attitudes needed by employees to do their jobs better. Training can include induction, on-the-job training, and off-the-job training. Development refers to improving the whole person as opposed to just teaching the worker the skills of the job. Development provides additional skills that prepare employees for more challenging work and promotions.

Performance Appraisal: This is a review of an employee's progress over a specific period of time. Employees performance is measured in relation to the targets set and are rewarded accordingly. It is undertaken by Human Resource Management to identify the quality of the work, potential of the employee, training needs, rewards, etc. It usually takes the form of an interview.
