WHAT THE 10 + 5 IS. The scheme's own Section 2 summary on p.5 prints "(E) Explanation: 10m + 5m" against 15. Read against the rest of that summary — "Two reasons: 10 Marks (7m + 3m) / 5 Marks (4m + 1m)" for every two-answer part, and "One method: 7 marks + 3 marks", "One duty: 10 marks (7m + 3m)", "Explain role: 10 marks (5m + 5m)" (2023 OL Q6E) for the single-answer ones — a 15-mark part is never worth 15 for one bare point on these papers. Under either reading of the plus sign (a first point at 10 then a second at 5, or the role at 10 and its development at 5) ONE role statement is worth 10, which is what the card now says; the scheme does not split it further, so nothing finer is asserted. The old note's citation is withdrawn as wrong: 2023 OL (E) is "Name two institutions of the European Union" 10m (5 + 5) — two institutions NAMED at 5 each — not "Explain the role of one of them", and it says nothing about a statement-plus-development split.

SHAPE. Three anyN rows, one per institution, each claimMax 1 x perOption 10, each listing that institution's own printed roles as separate options. The alternatives were run through the build's gates rather than argued about: (1) one menu of all sixteen roles with two positional rows at 10 and 5 — the shape used on sibling (A) and on Q1(A) — is DROPPED, "row r-1 shows 16 options, past the 14 any question may show", and cutting two of the SEC's roles to fit is the one thing this tool exists not to do; (2) three institution rows under a fixed tariff is DROPPED, "rows sum to 30, tariff is 15"; (3) two rows at 10 and 5 over the same three institution blocks is not dropped but is actively wrong in the session — takenByRow in SessionScreen.tsx keys off the option STRING, so ticking "European Parliament" in the 10 menu disables the identical option in the 5 menu and tells the student "Already claimed above", i.e. the one institution they answered on is the one they cannot finish claiming; (4) bestNofParts needs answer x perPart === totalMarks, so 15 can only be 1 x 15 (which reprices one role at 15, the defect being repaired) or 3 x 5 (which claims three roles at 5 each, which the scheme does not say); (5) routes, one per institution, are deliberately absent because they are inert — committedRoute() reads `claims` and togglePick() only ever writes `picks`, so a route on an anyN row is never committed.

TARIFF orderedSplit, notation "10m + 5m", the SEC's own string from p.5. One bracket covers the part without saying which answer is which, which is what an ordered split is; it also makes the session print "The examiner marks the first correct answers higher than the rest (10m + 5m)" above the menus and suppresses per-row mark chips and the running total, so three parallel 10-mark menus can never add to a number on screen. Each menu still prints "Any 1 of these — 10 marks each", so the 10 shows exactly where the student claims it, and each row's note says where the other 5 goes.

OPTIONS are the scheme's bullets, one per option, quoted whole across their line wraps. No institution prefix on the options: the provenance gate compares normalised text, so only a run CONTIGUOUS in the scheme passes, and "European Parliament: Approves the annual EU budget." is not contiguous — four bullets sit between them. The institution is carried by the row instead, an anyN row's verbatim being the one string the build does not check against the scheme. All sixteen options were run through comparableScheme/normalise against examiner-reports/business/schemes/2025-ol.md and all sixteen are found.

openList true, and it now means the right thing. On the old card the OPTIONS were the three institutions, so an open list told the student a fourth institution might have scored — false, the paper names three. Here the options are one institution's roles, and the examiner would have paid for a real role the sample omits (the Parliament also elects the Commission President; the Commission is guardian of the treaties), which is what the front matter licenses: the notes are "neither exclusive nor complete" and "Further relevant points of information presented by candidates are marked and rewarded on their merits".

STEM unchanged and shared on purpose: it is the paper's EEC/EU panel, the same one carried by the sibling (D)(i) and (D)(ii) cards. Read before reveal it hands over no marking point on any of the seven cards from this question — it names no institution, no EU country, no benefit of exporting and no reason a multinational locates here. No figure: the two crops the extractor catalogued on paper p.40 are the Apple clipping (bound by (A) and (B)) and the inflation infographic (bound by (C)), and this part can be asked with nothing at all. Whole-question check unchanged: A 15, B 15, C 1 + 14, D 7 + 8, E 15 = the 75 the paper prints.

SCHEME TEXT DEFECT, reported not edited: the Council option carries "draŌed" for "drafted", a mis-extracted ligature — the scheme PDF prints "drafted" (confirmed on the rendered page). It is reproduced as the converted file has it because the provenance gate compares against that file and "drafted" FAILS it, which would drop the card outright; the fix belongs in scripts/markbank/extract-scheme.py, not in the scheme or the card. "internationally agreements" in the last Council bullet is the SEC's own typo and is quoted as printed.

questionText: Outline two types of industrial action available to employees involved in an industrial dispute with their employer.
stem: People in Business. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

rows.verbatim: The first type of industrial action you gave: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: Tick here for whichever type you wrote FIRST. The scheme prices the first answer 7 + 3 and the second 4 + 1, and it ties those figures to answer positions rather than to particular types, so any one of the five can take the 10 here. The scheme does not label the two halves, but it prints every type as a name followed by a sentence saying what the employees actually do, so the 7 is for the type and the 3 for that sentence — a type named and left there stops at 7.

options: Strike: where the employees do not enter their workplace and do not do their duties.
Work to rule: where employees only undertake the exact jobs written in their job description or contract of employment.
Overtime ban: where workers refuse to do overtime. This can cause major disruption, leading to lost orders and lost sales, especially at peak trading times, e.g., a toy shop at Christmas.
Token Stoppage: a brief stoppage of work by the workers to highlight their frustration. It highlights their intention to carry the threat of further, more serious action, if agreement is not reached.
Go slow: employees work more slowly and less effectively.

rows.verbatim: The second type of industrial action you gave: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: Tick here for the second type, which has to be a different one from the first: an option claimed above is closed here, because one answer earns marks once. The scheme prices this one 4 + 1 on the same split — 4 for the type and 1 for the sentence saying what the employees do. Only two types are marked, so a third scores nothing, and a student who gave only one type leaves this 5 behind.

options: Strike: where the employees do not enter their workplace and do not do their duties.
Work to rule: where employees only undertake the exact jobs written in their job description or contract of employment.
Overtime ban: where workers refuse to do overtime. This can cause major disruption, leading to lost orders and lost sales, especially at peak trading times, e.g., a toy shop at Christmas.
Token Stoppage: a brief stoppage of work by the workers to highlight their frustration. It highlights their intention to carry the threat of further, more serious action, if agreement is not reached.
Go slow: employees work more slowly and less effectively.

notes:
Paper p.5 of the Section 2 booklet (PDF p.41); scheme p.24, tariff repeated on the scheme's summary page 6. Section 2 IS the long-question section at Ordinary Level — there is no Applied Business Question and no Section 3 — so the ref carries the section to keep this apart from Section 1 Q4. Question 4 is 75 marks over five parts of 15; (A) has no (i)/(ii) split, so it is one smallest part and one card.

TARIFF — REPAIRED. The scheme STATES the split rather than leaving it open: the summary page prints '(A) Outline two: 10 Marks (7m + 3m) / 5 Marks (4m + 1m)' and the answer page repeats it as a marks cell of 7 + 3 against the first type and 4 + 1 against the second. The card previously carried that as ONE anyN row of claimMax 2 x perOption 7 under an orderedSplit tariff, which was wrong three ways. SessionScreen builds its group header straight from those two numbers, so it printed 'Any 2 of these — 7 marks each', a per-answer figure the examiner never awards. 2 x 7 is 14, one short of the part's 15, which is also what build-deck's groupFault measures a menu against. And orderedSplit makes showsRowMarks false, so marksClaimed returned 0 and suggestGrade fell through to its claimed-ROWS branch — ticking an option sets picks, never claims, so a student who ticked both correct types was still told 'Missed'.

It is now TWO menus, one per ANSWER POSITION — the first worth 10, the second 5 — on a fixed tariff. 1x10 + 1x5 reconciles to exactly 15, the session prints the examiner's own figures, and the bottom bar can finally say 10 of 15 to a student who gave one type and 15 of 15 to one who gave two. This is the deck's established shape for a stated positional split: bus-2022-ol-s1-q6 ('8 + 7'), bus-2021-hl-s3-q1a ('7 + 7 + 6'), bus-2023-hl-s3-q2aii.

The cells price the FIRST and SECOND type given, not Strike and Work to rule in particular — the candidate may take any two of the five — so each menu lists all five and neither row carries marks of its own (marks: null; the value rides on group.perOption, which is what tariffReconciles and the session both read). The old note that two menus would let a student bank the same type twice is STALE: SessionScreen's takenElsewhere set disables an option already ticked in a sibling menu and prints 'Already claimed above — one answer earns marks once.'

Every option carries the scheme's heading joined to the sentence printed under it, because that sentence is what the 3 (or the 1) pays for; an option reading only 'Overtime ban' would let a student award themselves a developed answer for two words. The 7/3 and 4/1 halves are NOT broken into rows — the scheme prints one marks cell against a whole option and labels no halves, so rows for them would be rows the scheme does not contain. That split lives in each row's contextNote instead, which is the one place the anyN branch actually renders.

FIGURE: business-2025-OL-paper-p41-i0, opened and checked — the rte.ie news clipping printed above (A) and (B), headline 'Health workers represented by the INMO vote in favour of industrial action over staff shortage' beside a greyscale photograph of a picket line holding SAFE STAFFING NOW placards. It is the 'information supplied' the stem's lead-in refers to, and it hands over no marking point on (A): it says industrial action generically and names none of the five types. Kept rather than dropped — the published figure map assigns this crop to Q4 (A)(B), (B) binds the same key, and the build's srcHash guard only refuses a repeated crop under a DIFFERENT key. The second clipping on the page (Employment Equality Acts / WRC) belongs to (D) and (E) and is not bound here. No labelKey — nothing lettered.

STEM: the paper's own lead-in, unchanged and checked against all five siblings. It names the topic and tells the student to read the panel; it hands over nothing on (A), (B), (C)(i), (C)(ii), (D) or (E). The McGrath/Buildings AFD contract paragraph that would give (C)(i) its whole answer, and the 'Race and sexual orientation discrimination complaints up sharply — WRC' headline behind (D) and (E), are on the same page of the paper and are deliberately absent here.

openList true on both menus: the scheme's front matter states the support notes are 'neither exclusive nor complete' and are 'a sample of possible responses', and that 'further relevant points of information presented by candidates are marked and rewarded on their merits' — so a sit-in, an unofficial or wildcat strike, a picket or 'blue flu' scored. This list is genuinely open, unlike the closed sets elsewhere on this paper (three types of motor insurance, one named statute). topicId business-0-14 (1.3 Conflict resolution — industrial relations); conceptId shared with the Higher sibling bus-2025-hl-s3-q1b, which asks the same thing at 4 x 5m.

questionText: Outline the effects industrial action would have on any two stakeholders in the health service.
stem: People in Business. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

rows.verbatim: The first stakeholder you wrote about, with the effect on them: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: Whichever stakeholder you wrote about first is priced 10, printed as 7m + 3m. The scheme does not label the two halves, but every entry on its list is a stakeholder followed by more than one sentence of effect, so the smaller figure is there for the second effect or for developing the first. The question asks for the effects, so naming the stakeholder and stopping — 'Patients' — does not reach the 10.

options: Employers (HSE): Reduced services lead to disruption and longer waiting periods for patients. Rescheduling of appointments would be required due to backlogs.
Employees (nurses): Face disruptions to their working lives and may feel anxious about job security. Lose wages/salary depending on the type of industrial action.
Patients: Frustration for patients. Health concerns due to delays.
Government: Under pressure from unions and the public to resolve the dispute. Increased funding may be required to resolve the dispute.
Private Hospital shareholders: Loss of revenue due to disruption.

rows.verbatim: The second stakeholder you wrote about, with the effect on them: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The second stakeholder is priced 5, printed as 4m + 1m, and it has to be a different stakeholder from the one you ticked above. The 7 + 3 sits beside Employers (HSE) and the 4 + 1 beside Employees (nurses) only because those two head the list — the paper says any two stakeholders, so the 10 and the 5 price the first and second answer you gave, not two particular stakeholders. Only two are marked; a third scores nothing.

options: Employers (HSE): Reduced services lead to disruption and longer waiting periods for patients. Rescheduling of appointments would be required due to backlogs.
Employees (nurses): Face disruptions to their working lives and may feel anxious about job security. Lose wages/salary depending on the type of industrial action.
Patients: Frustration for patients. Health concerns due to delays.
Government: Under pressure from unions and the public to resolve the dispute. Increased funding may be required to resolve the dispute.
Private Hospital shareholders: Loss of revenue due to disruption.

notes:
Paper p.5 of the Section 2 booklet (PDF p.41), which prints (15); scheme p.24, tariff also on the scheme's summary page 6, which prints '(B) Two effects: 10 Marks (7m + 3m) / 5 Marks (4m + 1m)'. One smallest part, one card.

REPAIR — TARIFF: the card previously held one anyN group of claimMax 2 at perOption 7. The session screen renders a group as 'Any 2 of these — 7 marks each' and scores picks x perOption, so it told the student both stakeholders were worth the same 7 and put only 14 of the 15 printed marks on the table. The scheme pays 10 (7 + 3) for the first answer and 5 (4 + 1) for the second, so the two answers are now two rows: claimMax 1 at 10 for the stakeholder written first, claimMax 1 at 5 for the second. 10 + 5 = 15, and the two figures the student sees are the two the examiner printed. This is the shape every other reconciling 10/5 Ordinary part in this deck already uses (2025 q1a-q1e, q2b, q3a, q5b, q5d, q6a, q6d, q6e, q7b, q7c, and the 2022-24 equivalents).

TARIFF KIND: still orderedSplit, and row marks stay null as that requires. The 7 + 3 cell sits level with Employers (HSE) and the 4 + 1 with Employees (nurses), but the paper says 'any two stakeholders', so the cells price the first and second answer GIVEN rather than those two stakeholders in particular.

ONE ANSWER, ONE PAYMENT: the two rows are two differently priced answer slots over one list, not two offers of the same answer. r-2's contextNote states it has to be a different stakeholder from r-1 and that a third scores nothing. The single claimMax 2 group is the only alternative and it cannot price two answers unequally, which is exactly what produced the defect.

Every option keeps the scheme's stakeholder heading joined to the effect sentences printed under it — 'Patients' alone is not an effect, and the question asks for the effects, which is what the rest of each answer pays for.

FIGURE: business-2025-OL-paper-p41-i0, the rte.ie INMO clipping printed above (A) and (B) — opened and checked: the headline 'Health workers represented by the INMO vote in favour of industrial action over staff shortage' beside a photograph of a picket line with a SAFE STAFFING NOW placard. It is what makes 'the health service' in the question a real setting rather than an abstraction, and the deck binds this panel to both parts it sits above. Weighed again as a possible give-away and kept: the clipping names no stakeholder as a stakeholder, the question's own words ('stakeholders in the health service') already imply nurses, patients and the HSE, and naming one is only part of an answer the scheme pays mainly for the effect. No labelKey.

openList true on both rows: the scheme's five are a sample under front matter (scheme p.3) that calls the support notes 'neither exclusive nor complete' and 'not model answers but rather a sample of possible responses', with further relevant points 'marked and rewarded on their merits'. 'Any two stakeholders' is an open set, so suppliers to the hospital, the local community, private health insurers or the union itself score on their merits.

topicId business-0-14; conceptId shared with the Higher sibling bus-2022-hl-s3-q1aii ('Illustrate the impact of trade disputes on any three stakeholders').

questionText: Explain with reference to the text above one way the McGrath family can terminate the contract.
stem: People in Business. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. On 6 January 2025, the McGrath family signed a contract with Buildings AFD Ltd to add a conservatory to their home for an agreed cost. A deposit was paid, and the project was scheduled to be completed by 1 May 2025. This was specified in the contract. However, it is now 1 June 2025, and the project is still not started.

rows.verbatim: The McGrath family can terminate on grounds of Breach as Buildings AFD Ltd did not have the conservatory completed on 1 May 2025 as outlined in the contract. They did not complete their part of the contract.
rows.contextNote: Ten marks, printed 10 Marks (7m + 3m). The scheme does not label the two halves, but its answer names the ground and then points at the facts, and the question says "with reference to the text above", so the word Breach on its own is not the whole answer: the dates matter. Buildings AFD Ltd did not have the conservatory completed on 1 May 2025 as the contract specified, and they did not complete their part of it.

notes:
Paper p.5 of the Section 2 booklet (PDF p.41); scheme p.25, tariff on the scheme's summary page 6: '(C) (i) One way: 10 Marks (7m + 3m)' and '(ii) One other way: 5 Marks (4m + 1m)'. Part (C) divides, so it is TWO cards — (i) here at 10 marks, (ii) separately at 5 — and the two together make the part's 15.

TARIFF: fixed, not an ordered split. Only one answer is asked for and the scheme states its value outright, so the single row carries its real 10.

The row is the scheme's answer quoted whole, in one run, heading and application together — the 3 is paid for tying the ground to the dates in the text, so stopping at 'Breach' would let a student claim the applied marks for one word. The scheme's line prints a stray space before the full stop after 'in the contract'; that is an extraction artefact of the converted PDF and not a word of the answer, and closing it up changes nothing the provenance check compares (verified: the row traces to the scheme). The scheme file itself was not edited.

STEM: the paper's own stimulus box (y320-377), which sits directly above (C) and is the 'text above' the question names — the one place a stem may run long, because the part cannot be attempted without it. Read as a student sees it before the reveal it gives nothing away: it supplies the dates and the fact that the completion date was specified in the contract, and leaves the student to name the ground, which is the whole of what is being marked. The word breach appears nowhere on the paper.

No figure: the two crops inspected on this page are the INMO clipping above (A)/(B) and the Employment Equality Acts / WRC clipping above (D)/(E); the McGrath stimulus is plain paper text and belongs in the stem.

openList false, unusually for this subject: the question restricts the answer to the text above, and those facts support one ground only. A student who wrote 'agreement' or 'performance' here has not answered what was asked, and (ii) is where the other methods are marked. topicId business-0-12 (1.1 People in business and contract law).

questionText: Explain one other way a contract can be terminated.
stem: People in Business. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. On 6 January 2025, the McGrath family signed a contract with Buildings AFD Ltd to add a conservatory to their home for an agreed cost. A deposit was paid, and the project was scheduled to be completed by 1 May 2025. This was specified in the contract. However, it is now 1 June 2025, and the project is still not started. (i) Explain with reference to the text above one way the McGrath family can terminate the contract.

rows.verbatim: Any one of the following other ways a contract can be terminated
rows.contextNote: Five marks for one method, printed 5 Marks (4m + 1m), and it has to be a method other than the one the text above illustrates. The scheme does not label the two halves, but it prints each method as a name followed by a sentence explaining it, so the 4 is for the method and the 1 for that explanation: a single word does not reach five.

options: Performance – both parties in the contract fulfil their part of the contract and it comes to its natural end.
Agreement – both parties agree to end the contract before it is completed.
Frustration – an unforeseen event makes it impossible to complete the contract.

notes:
Paper p.5 of the Section 2 booklet (PDF p.41); scheme p.25, tariff on the scheme's summary page 6: '(ii) One other way: 5 Marks (4m + 1m)'. The smaller half of a part that divides, so it is its own card; (i) carries the other 10.

TARIFF: bestNofParts, one answer of 5 chosen from the three the scheme prints (1 x 5 = the printed 5). Three plain rows would show 15 marks on a 5-mark part and would tell a student they had left two answers behind that the paper never asked for, so it is one bounded anyN group with claimMax 1.

Each option is the scheme's method name joined to its explanation, exactly as printed, en dash and all — that dash is the scheme's own punctuation between a method and its explanation, and options inside an anyN group are never split on it, so the method name cannot be stripped off the front of the point. The explanation is what the +1 buys.

STEM: the paper's own stimulus box plus part (i) exactly as the paper prints it, because 'one OTHER way' in (ii) refers back to (i) and is meaningless without it. Quoting (i) leaks no answer — (i) is a question, not a response, and it names no method — while it does tell the student which route is already spoken for, which is the difference between a fair card and a confusing one. Nothing here is our own wording.

No figure. openList true: the scheme's three are a sample under front matter that calls the support notes neither exclusive nor complete, so a candidate who wrote that a contract ends by lapse of time or by operation of law was marked on merit. topicId business-0-12; conceptId shared with the Higher sibling bus-2021-hl-s3-q4cii, the same 'other methods' follow-on.

questionText: Outline two grounds, other than race or sexual orientation, on which discrimination is outlawed under the Employment Equality Acts.
stem: People in Business. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

rows.verbatim: The first ground given: any one of the following

It does not label the two halves, but it prints every ground as a name followed by a sentence saying who it protects, and the question says outline — so a one-word ground is not the whole answer, and the sentence under it is what the rest of the ten is paid for.

options: Age: younger and older employees cannot be treated differently.

Membership of the Traveling Community: An employee cannot be dismissed because they are a member of the traveling community.

Disability: People with physical, intellectual, medical conditions.

rows.verbatim: The second ground given: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prices the second ground at 5 Marks, printed as 4m + 1m further down the same list. Race and sexual orientation are ruled out by the question, and the scheme does not print them.

questionText: Explain two functions of the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).
stem: People in Business. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow.

rows.verbatim: The first function given: any one of the following functions of the Workplace Relations Commission
rows.contextNote: Tick here for the first function you wrote. The scheme prints 10 Marks (7m + 3m) against the first of the two answers and 5 Marks (4m + 1m) against the second, and those figures follow the order the answers are given rather than attaching to particular services, so whichever function you wrote first takes the 10. The scheme does not label the two halves, but every entry is a service name followed by what the WRC actually does in it, and the command word is explain: a service named and left there does not reach ten. Conciliation, mediation and adjudication are three separate services on this list, so they are three different answers here, not one.

options: Information service: Promote good industrial relations and work practices by providing information to employees and employers on their rights and obligations under employment law.
Codes of Practice: Provide written rules on how to comply with employment regulations.
Advisory service: WRC works closely with employers, employees and trade unions to promote, develop and implement industrial relations policies, practices and procedures.

Conciliation service: Industrial Relations Officers (IRO) act as an intermediary to provide impartial conciliation services between employers and employees to help them to reach a solution to an industrial relations issue.
Mediation service: A third party helps parties in an industrial dispute to reach a voluntary resolution of a complaint or grievance.

Adjudication service: A hearing is held for both parties in a dispute to be heard and give evidence. The adjudicator makes a written decision on the case which both parties are free to accept or reject.
Inspection: WRC can visit the workplace and carry out investigations to ensure the organisation is compliant with employment legislation.

rows.verbatim: The second function given: any one of the following functions of the Workplace Relations Commission
rows.contextNote: Tick here for the second function, which has to be a different service from the first: one answer earns marks once. The scheme marks it 5 (4m + 1m), so most of it is for the service and the last mark for the sentence saying what the WRC does in it.

options: Information service: Promote good industrial relations and work practices by providing information to employees and employers on their rights and obligations under employment law.
Codes of Practice: Provide written rules on how to comply with employment regulations.
Advisory service: WRC works closely with employers, employees and trade unions to promote, develop and implement industrial relations policies, practices and procedures.

Conciliation service: Industrial Relations Officers (IRO) act as an intermediary to provide impartial conciliation services between employers and employees to help them to reach a solution to an industrial relations issue.
Mediation service: A third party helps parties in an industrial dispute to reach a voluntary resolution of a complaint or grievance.

Adjudication service: A hearing is held for both parties in a dispute to be heard and give evidence. The adjudicator makes a written decision on the case which both parties are free to accept or reject.
Inspection: WRC can visit the workplace and carry out investigations to ensure the organisation is compliant with employment legislation.

notes:
Paper p.5 of the Section 2 booklet (PDF p.41), which prints "(E) Explain two functions of the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC)." and "(15)"; scheme p.26, with the tariff repeated on the scheme's summary page 6: "(E) Explain two functions: 10 Marks (7m + 3m) / 5 Marks (4m + 1m)". The last of the five parts that make Question 4's 75 marks, and one smallest part, so one card.

TARIFF, REPAIRED. The card previously carried ONE anyN row of claimMax 2 at perOption 7. That is 2 x 7 = 14 of the 15 the paper awards, and the session renders those two numbers literally as "Any 2 of these - 7 marks each", which contradicts the scheme: the answer page prints a 7 + 3 cell level with the first entry and a 4 + 1 cell level with the second, i.e. 10 for the first answer and 5 for the second. Fifteen does not divide by two, so no single group can price this part; the only representation that reaches 15 is one menu per ANSWER POSITION, which is the shape SessionScreen's takenElsewhere guard exists for and the same repair already applied to bus-2021-ol-s1-q9 and shipped on bus-2022-ol-s1-q6. So: r-1 is the first function given at 1 x 10, r-2 the second at 1 x 5, each offering the whole seven-item list, and 10 + 5 is exactly the paper's 15. The cross-menu guard stops one service being ticked in both, so nobody banks a single answer twice.

Kind is fixed, not orderedSplit. The scheme states this split outright - it names which POSITION takes the 10 and which the 5 - and once each row IS a position, each row carries its own stated marks, which is what fixed means. It also matters to the student: showsRowMarks() is false for orderedSplit, so an orderedSplit card whose rows are all anyN scores marksClaimed 0, reports marksAvailable 0 and suggests "missed" however well it was answered, because picks never set a row claim. Under fixed the session totals 10 + 5 correctly. No row claims that any particular service is the ten-mark one.

Every option is the scheme's service name joined to the sentences printed under it, quoted whole and traced against the 2025 OL scheme (all fourteen strings match). "Advisory service" on its own is a name, not an explanation, and the smaller figure in each pair is what the explanation earns. The scheme's own colon separates the name from the explanation - there is no cue dash anywhere in these options, so nothing gets stripped to a fragment.

questionText: Outline one risk and one reward for Aimee of setting up her own business.
stem: Enterprise / Managing. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. Aimee Connolly is honoured as the Emerging Entrepreneur of the Year. Aimee Connolly, a makeup artist and beauty entrepreneur, founded Sculpted by Aimee in 2016. At the age of 23, she launched her own brand, driven by her desire to create products she felt were missing, all with a focus on making them more accessible. Today, Sculpted by Aimee is one of the fastest-growing brands in its field. It reported a 50% increase in revenue, reaching €22.23 million last year. It has 55 employees, over 500 stockists, and, together with its booming online shopping website, it exports to 68 countries. Adapted from thinkbusiness.ie

rows.verbatim: The risk you outlined: any one of the following

options: No guaranteed income – may not have enough money to run the business.
Hard to raise finance/acquire loans – Aimee might find it difficult to raise finance for the business as she is on her own.
Stress – must work long hours to get business going. Seƫng up a new business can cause a lot of stress.
Competition – may not be able to compete with existing businesses in terms of quality of service and price. Make up is a highly competitive market.
Business failure – the business model might not be successful, forcing the business to close. Aimee may lose her investment and possibly damage her reputation if the business is not a success.

rows.contextNote: The scheme prices the risk 10m (7 + 3): seven for naming the risk and three for the sentence developing it. Outline is the command word, so a risk named and left there stops three marks short.

rows.verbatim: The reward you outlined: any one of the following

options: Profit – a successful business can generate good profit for the entrepreneur. Revenue reached €22.23 million last year.
Independence – the entrepreneur has control over their own working life and makes decisions to suit themselves.
Satisfaction – the challenge of seƫng up a business is rewarded if the business is successful.
Generating wealth for others – providing employment, spin-off business creation etc. Aimee employs 55 staff.

rows.contextNote: The reward is priced 5m (4 + 1) — four for naming it, one for developing it. The scheme puts the larger 7 + 3 beside its Risks list and the smaller 4 + 1 beside its Rewards list, so the reward is worth five however well it is written. A second risk instead of a reward scores nothing, because the question names one of each.

notes: Section 2 Q5(A), scheme p.27. The Marks column prints 15m for the part, then 7 + 3 against the first entry of the Risks list and 4 + 1 against the first entry of the Rewards list. Those two brackets sit on DIFFERENT lists, and the question compels one answer from each, so the split is fixed by category — risk 10, reward 5 — rather than by the order the candidate wrote in. That is why this card is fixed and parts (B) and (D), where both brackets land inside one undifferentiated menu, are ordered splits. One row per category, each offering the whole of the scheme's list for that category (five risks, four rewards), and no individual risk or reward is given a value of its own. Every option carries the scheme's heading AND the sentence developing it, because the 3 and the 1 are paid for that sentence. Stem carries the paper's stimulus panel whole: it supplies the revenue figure and the employee count that the scheme's Profit and Generating wealth for others options apply, but it names no risk and no reward, so nothing had to be cut. No figure bound — the published crop for this question is the Sculpted wordmark, a portrait of Aimee, a product shot and the award headline, all of which is scene-setting the question can be asked without; the headline is reproduced in the stem instead. One transcription note: the scheme file on disk renders the ligature in "setting" as a single glyph, so the Stress and Satisfaction options read "Seƫng". That is how the SEC text extracts and the options are left byte-for-byte as the scheme has them — rewriting it to "setting" would make the marking point untraceable to its own scheme and the build would drop the card.

questionText: Outline three entrepreneurial characteristics/skills associated with entrepreneurs like Aimee.
stem: Enterprise / Managing. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. Aimee Connolly is honoured as the Emerging Entrepreneur of the Year. Aimee Connolly, a makeup artist and beauty entrepreneur, founded Sculpted by Aimee in 2016. At the age of 23, she launched her own brand, driven by her desire to create products she felt were missing, all with a focus on making them more accessible. Today, Sculpted by Aimee is one of the fastest-growing brands in its field. It reported a 50% increase in revenue, reaching €22.23 million last year. It has 55 employees, over 500 stockists, and, together with its booming online shopping website, it exports to 68 countries. Adapted from thinkbusiness.ie

rows.verbatim: Any three of these characteristics/skills, each outlined and linked to Aimee

options: Risk Taker: Entrepreneurs are not afraid of taking both a personal risk and a financial risk when they set up their own business. They work long hours and invest their money in the business. Aimee invested her money and time when she opened Sculpted.

Innovative: Entrepreneurs are inventive when they come up with new ideas for their business. They have to think outside the box to continue to develop these new ideas. Aimee at the age of 23 launched her own brand.
Decisive: Entrepreneurs have to be able to make good decisions quickly, so that they don’t miss out on any opportunities that may arise. Aimee wanted to make her products more accessible.

Reality Perception: Entrepreneurs need to see things as they are and not how they might like to see them. When things go wrong, they must identify this quickly and act. Aimee created products that were missing from the market.

Flexible/Adaptable: Entrepreneurs must be capable of changing their approach to business as situations change. The business environment is constantly changing, and successful entrepreneurs must adapt to these changes. Aimee realised that selling online was as important as selling her products in shops. Aimee exports to 68 countries.
Human Relations: Entrepreneurs need to be good with people and bring out the best in them. Aimee has 55 employees working for her.

rows.contextNote: Each characteristic is worth 5, split 4 + 1: naming the characteristic and explaining what it means, then linking it back to Aimee and Sculpted. Only three are marked — a fourth scores nothing however good it is.

notes: Section 2 Q5(C), scheme p.29. The Marks column prints 15m for the part and then 4 + 1 three times, once each beside Risk Taker, Innovative and Decisive — the same value three times over a six-entry menu, which is three answers at 5 rather than three named characteristics at anything, so best-3-of-6 at 5. One anyN row: the scheme lists six and the candidate picks three. Each option carries the characteristic, the sentence or two explaining it AND the closing sentence applying it to Aimee, because the scheme prints all three together and the 1 is what the application is paid for; an option cut back to Risk Taker alone would let a candidate who wrote two words award themselves the whole five. The application sentences are the scheme's own — they draw on the stimulus in the stem (her money and time, launching at 23, making products more accessible, the missing products, selling online and exporting to 68 countries, the 55 employees) but the stem names no characteristic, so it gives none of the six away. No figure needed.

questionText: Explain the term stock control.
stem: Enterprise / Managing. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. Aimee Connolly is honoured as the Emerging Entrepreneur of the Year. Aimee Connolly, a makeup artist and beauty entrepreneur, founded Sculpted by Aimee in 2016. At the age of 23, she launched her own brand, driven by her desire to create products she felt were missing, all with a focus on making them more accessible. Today, Sculpted by Aimee is one of the fastest-growing brands in its field. It reported a 50% increase in revenue, reaching €22.23 million last year. It has 55 employees, over 500 stockists, and, together with its booming online shopping website, it exports to 68 countries. Adapted from thinkbusiness.ie

rows.verbatim: Stock control means ensuring that the business has optimum stock. This means the right amount of stock, at the right time. A business should not have too much or too little stock.
rows.contextNote: Part (E) carries 15 between its two halves and the scheme prices this definition at 3. Optimum stock is the idea being paid for — the right amount of stock, at the right time, neither too much nor too little.

notes: Section 2 Q5(E)(i), scheme p.30. The Marks column prints 15m against the whole of part (E) and then a bare 3 against the definition, leaving 12 for (E)(ii), which is exactly the two 5 + 1 answers the scheme prices there — 3 + 12 = 15, so the definition is worth 3 and is carded on its own as the smallest part. The row quotes the definition across all three of its lines, including the closing sentence about not having too much or too little, because that sentence is part of what the examiner printed as the answer. openList is set because the scheme's front matter says its model answers are not exhaustive and variations may also be acceptable, so a candidate who defined optimum stock in their own words still earned the 3. Stem carries the same stimulus panel as the rest of the question; this part alone could be asked without it.

questionText: Outline two reasons why stock control is important to a business like Sculpted.
stem: Enterprise / Managing. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. Aimee Connolly is honoured as the Emerging Entrepreneur of the Year. Today, Sculpted by Aimee is one of the fastest-growing brands in its field. It reported a 50% increase in revenue, reaching €22.23 million last year. It has 55 employees, over 500 stockists, and, together with its booming online shopping website, it exports to 68 countries. Adapted from thinkbusiness.ie

rows.verbatim: Any two of these reasons, each outlined

options: Use cash wisely – It ensures money is not tied up in stock that could be used to reduce debts or avail of discounts elsewhere.
Reduces costs – Storage of stock costs money, e.g., warehousing, insurance, security.
Ensures quality is maintained – Stock can become obsolete (out of date) or damaged making it difficult to sell.
Ensure optimum stock levels – Stock control involves ensuring the business always has sufficient stock to meet customer requirements.
Reduce risk of theft – If stock is left lying around in a shop or warehouse there is more risk of theft.
Maintaining customer satisfaction and loyalty – If a business does not have enough stock customers will move to a different supplier resulting in loss of sales and profit.

rows.contextNote: Each reason is worth 6, split 5 + 1: the reason itself earns the 5 and the sentence developing it earns the 1. Only two are marked. With the 3 for the definition in (E)(i) these twelve make up the 15 the whole of part (E) carries.

That is also why this card totals 12 and not 15 — the other 3 belongs to (E)(i), which is its own card. questionText: Outline one duty of the Chairperson of a club.

questionText: Outline two benefits to Cadbury of having a good brand name.
stem: Question 8 — Business in Action. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. “Cadbury is constantly coming up with new and innovative ideas and increasing its product portfolio”

rows.verbatim: The first benefit you gave: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: Tick here for the first benefit you wrote. The examiner marks the first benefit 7 + 3 and the second 4 + 1, and that split follows the ORDER you answered in, not which benefit you picked — so any of these five can be the ten-mark one. The two figures are the point and the development of it, so a benefit named without the sentence that follows it does not reach the 10. The word set as “oŌen” in the Price bullet is “often” — a font fault in the SEC PDF, not a different word.

options: Recognition: Helps identify the chocolate range making it more recognisable / differentiates it from competitors’ brands.

Price: A well-known brand name oŌen has the image of higher quality; therefore, the store can charge a higher price. Premium pricing.

rows.verbatim: The second benefit you gave: any one of the following

These five are a sample: the scheme's front matter says the model answers are “not intended to be exhaustive” and that “Variations and alternatives may also be acceptable”, so a real benefit of a good brand name that the scheme did not print still scores.

(1) GRADING. This is a pick-any-two menu and the old card modelled it as five REQUIRED point rows under an orderedSplit tariff. orderedSplit makes showsRowMarks() false, so suggestGrade() falls to its row-count path and a student who wrote two perfect benefits ticked 2 of 5 and was told "shaky". (2) STEM. The paper's panel (business-2025-OL-paper.pdf, pdf page index 44 = printed page 9) prints ONE line, "Cadbury is constantly coming up with new and innovative ideas and increasing its product portfolio", above four product photographs. The sentence beginning "The paper prints that line above photographs of Cadbury products — an 1824-2024 anniversary tin..." was authored narration and is cut. Two mark cells against five bullets means the values belong to the two ANSWER POSITIONS, not to particular benefits — but the examiner DOES say which position is which, so the split is stated, not unlabelled, and the model is `fixed` rather than orderedSplit. Carried as one menu per answer position over the same five options: claimMax 1 at 10 (7 + 3) and claimMax 1 at 5 (4 + 1), summing to the printed 15. This is the deck's established shape for exactly this case — bus-2022-ol-s1-q6 splits 15 as 8 + 7 the same way — and SessionScreen's takenByRow then greys an option already ticked in the other menu, so one answer earns marks once. bestNofParts is unavailable: 15 does not divide into two equal answers.

OPEN LIST. Kept true on both menus. A good brand name has more benefits than the five printed, and the scheme's front matter states the model answers are "not intended to be exhaustive" and that "Variations and alternatives may also be acceptable".

FIGURE. None bound, and none is available: the Q8 stimulus sits on pdf page index 44 and 2025-ol-figs.json publishes nothing for that page (it jumps p44 -> p46). questionText: Explain two factors that a business should consider before setting the price of a product or service.
stem: Cadbury is constantly coming up with new and innovative ideas and increasing its product portfolio

rows.verbatim: The first factor you explained: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 7 + 3 against the first bullet: 7 for the factor and 3 for explaining it. Only two mark cells are printed against seven factors, so the 10 and the 5 follow the order you gave your two factors in — they do not attach to particular factors on this list. The scheme heads the list "Possible Responses", so another sensible pricing factor, explained, would be paid too.

options: Competitors' Prices: Analyse competitors' pricing strategies. Decide whether to match, undercut, or set a higher price than competitors.
Cost of Product: Ensure the price covers production costs and provides a profit.
Target Market: Identify the specific group of people each product is aimed at (e.g., products for children). Consider what consumers are willing and able to pay.
Image: Reflect on the image the business wants to create when setting prices.
Cost of Production and Research & Development: Factor in manufacturing and development costs for each item when pricing.
Taxes and Tariffs: Include all applicable taxes and tariffs in the price.
Economic Conditions and Demand: Consider the economic climate; higher prices may be feasible in a booming economy.

rows.verbatim: The second factor you explained: any one of the following
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 4 + 1 for the second answer: 4 for the other factor and 1 for explaining it. It has to be a different factor from the first, and only two are marked — a third scores nothing.

notes: REPAIRED. The scheme (2025-ol.md, p.38) lists SEVEN factors and prints only TWO mark cells against them — 7 + 3 beside the first bullet, 4 + 1 inside the third — so 10 and 5 price the two ANSWER POSITIONS, not particular factors: a student who explains Taxes and Tariffs first is paid 7 + 3 for it. The card now carries one anyN menu per answer position, each listing all seven factors verbatim (10 for the first answer, 5 for the second, 15 in all). That closes the defect: the previous five-row version demoted 'Cost of Production and Research & Development' and 'Taxes and Tariffs' into a contextNote where a student who wrote either could not claim them. Section 2 allows 14 options, so seven fit with room over. SessionScreen's takenElsewhere already blocks the same factor being ticked in both menus, so one answer still earns marks once. TARIFF stays orderedSplit: no mark attaches to a named factor, only to the order the two answers came in; the per-position values live on the groups. This is the shipped house shape for a 10-then-5 split — 55 OL cards use it, including bus-2025-ol-s2-q1a and bus-2025-ol-s2-q2b on this same paper — and it is why a single claimMax-2 menu is wrong here: no one perOption is true when the two answers are worth 10 and 5. openList stays true; the scheme's own header is 'Possible Responses' and pricing factors are genuinely open (an examiner would pay for, say, the stage of the product life cycle, which the list never names). STEM: the authored narration of the photographs is gone. What is left is the single line of stimulus prose the paper actually prints above the picture strip, which is verbatim and hands over no marking point on (A), (B), (C)(i), (C)(ii) or (D). The photographs are real (a 200-years 1824–2024 anniversary tin, a personalised HAPPY BIRTHDAY JORDAN bar, a Double Deck selection box — checked against the rendered page) but describing them is our wording, not the SEC's, and this part asks about 'a business', not Cadbury, so it can be answered without them. NO FIGURE: the published 2025-ol-figs.json emits no candidate for paper page 45, and the panel is not needed to ask the question. All seven options traced to the scheme with the build's own normalise/comparableScheme; group gates (options >= claimMax, claimMax x perOption <= 15, options <= 14, no tariff prose in verbatim) all pass, and orderedSplit's rows-carry-no-marks rule holds.

questionText: Explain the term Target Market, with reference to Cadbury.
stem: Question 8 — Business in Action. Read the information supplied and answer the questions which follow. "Cadbury is constantly coming up with new and innovative ideas and increasing its product portfolio."

rows.verbatim: A target market is the group of people at whom a particular product or service is aimed.
The target market may be characterised by age, income level, gender, location and lifestyle.
Cadbury's chocolate targets a wide and diverse market, ranging from children to adults.
rows.contextNote: The scheme heads this "Example:" and illustrates the Cadbury target market five ways, any of which serves: 1. Children and Teenagers – Cadbury Dairy Milk, Cadbury Heroes, and selection boxes. 2. Young Adults – adventurous flavours, sharing packs, and limited-edition products. Campaigns oŌen highlight lifestyle, relationships, and fun moments. 3. Families – larger family packs, variety boxes e.g., Cadbury Celebrations. 4. GiŌ Givers – affordable giŌs for various occasions, such as birthdays, events. Cadbury Celebrations, personalised chocolates, customised selection boxes. 5. Health-conscious Consumer – health-conscious people offering dark chocolate, sugar-free, or reduced-calorie options. The words set as "GiŌ", "giŌs" and "oŌen" are "Gift", "gifts" and "often" — a font fault in the SEC PDF, not different words.

notes: Section 2 Q8(C)(i), scheme p.39. STEM REPAIRED. The previous stem ended "The paper prints that line above photographs of Cadbury products — an 1824–2024 anniversary tin, personalised bars and a selection box." No such sentence is printed anywhere on the paper: page 45 carries the header box (Question 8 / Business in Action), the instruction line, one line of type inside the panel and four product photographs, and nothing else in words. On a target-market card that description is also a pre-reveal nudge toward two of the scheme's own illustrations, which print "selection boxes" (Children and Teenagers) and "personalised chocolates, customised selection boxes" (Gift Givers). Cut rather than reworded — the photographs carry no marking content, and a bland paraphrase would still be authored description of a page. What remains is the paper's own words, and none of it states a marking point on this card or on Q8(A), (B), (C)(ii) or (D): the panel line says only that Cadbury keeps launching products, which names no brand benefit, no pricing factor, no advertising medium, no research type and no market segment. The identical fabricated sentence sits on all five Q8 stems in the shipped deck and needs the same cut on each, or it returns on the sibling. No figure bound: the product photographs are scene-setting the question can be asked without, and no crop of paper page 45 has been published for this paper in any case. Tariff: the paper prints (15) against part (C) as a whole; the scheme's mark column splits it 4 + 2 + 1 for (i) and 6 + 2 for (ii), so this card carries 7 and its sibling 8. The single bracket ⟨4 + 2 + 1⟩ sits at the end of the definition block and covers the definition, the characteristics and the Cadbury illustration without saying which earns which, so it is an orderedSplit and no row states its own marks. questionText is the PAPER's wording; the scheme restates it mispunctuated as "Explain, the term Target Market with reference to Cadbury." and I did not use that. The five Cadbury illustrations printed under "Example:" stay in r-3's contextNote rather than becoming rows or an anyN menu — they are five ways of doing the one thing r-3 asks for, not five separate marking points, and an anyN group on an orderedSplit card would print a per-option mark value this tariff says does not exist. They are now quoted in full and in the scheme's own characters: the earlier note had dropped option 2's second sentence and the whole of option 4's product list, and had respelled the SEC PDF's "GiŌ"/"giŌs"/"oŌen" font fault as "Gift"/"gifts"/"often", which is wording the scheme file does not contain (checked with the build's own normaliser — the respelt form does not trace). The gloss at the end of the note tells the student what those glyphs are, exactly as the Q8(A) card does. openList stays true on all three rows: the definition and the characterisation are both paid in the candidate's own words, the scheme's own "may be characterised by" invites bases it does not list, and the Cadbury reference is explicitly headed "Example:", so a segment the scheme never names still scores.

questionText: Name and explain two types of market research a business like Cadbury could have used before launching new products.
stem: Cadbury is constantly coming up with new and innovative ideas and increasing its product portfolio.

rows.verbatim: Desk Research (Secondary): Desk research involves using information that has already been gathered by someone else. It is secondary data and can be both internal and external. Desk research is relatively cheap, keeping business costs down.

Field research (Primary): Field research involves going into the marketplace to gather first-hand or new information. It involves making direct contact with customers or potential customers. Field research tends to be expensive and time consuming, but it provides specific information on the behaviour of the target market.

notes: STEM: the paper (p.9) prints a single line of stimulus in the Question 8 panel — "Cadbury is constantly coming up with new and innovative ideas and increasing its product portfolio" — above a photo strip of a 200-years anniversary tin, a personalised bar and a selection box. The old stem quoted that line and then narrated the photographs in the author's own words, which is not text the paper prints; the narration and the rubric boilerplate are now cut and the stem is the printed line alone (the printed headline carries no full stop; a sentence-final one is added for reading). Checked against every sibling before keeping it: it hands over no marking point on (A) brand-name benefits, (B) pricing factors, (C)(i) target market, (C)(ii) advertising media or on this part. FIGURE: none bound — no Q8 figure was published for this paper, and the product photographs carry no information the question needs to be asked. TARIFF: stays orderedSplit. The brackets ⟨7 + 3⟩ and ⟨4 + 1⟩ do sit beside the first and second entries here, but the same scheme prints ⟨4 + 1⟩ beside the THIRD of seven bullets in Q8(B) and beside the second of five in Q8(A), so the brackets are column typesetting for the standard Ordinary Level 10-then-5 split by answer POSITION, not a fixed value pinned to Desk versus Field. A candidate who wrote Field research first earns the 10 for it, so pinning 10 to Desk Research would misprice the card. openList: now FALSE on both rows. The LC taxonomy of market research is exactly two types — desk (secondary) and field (primary) — the scheme prints both, the question demands two, and the synonyms a student may have used are already inside the quoted headings; there is no third type the examiner could have paid for, so marking the list open would tell a student a wrong third answer might have scored. Both points are quoted whole, development included: the closing sentences ('Desk research is relatively cheap, keeping business costs down'; 'expensive and time consuming, but it provides specific information on the behaviour of the target market') are what the +3 and +1 pay for, and cutting the card back to the two headings would let a two-word answer claim the development marks.
